1. Course App, Prerequisites and Project Structure Angular

Angular › 1. Course App, Prerequisites and Project Structure

  • Prerequisites: TypeScript, HTML/CSS, npm. Any modern browser and OS.
  • Dev environment: GitHub Codespaces (cloud VS Code). Start with npm start. Codespaces port forwarding needs the host bound to 0.0.0.0 with the host check disabled (see the start script in section 2).
  • Example app Gem Finder: All Players page (search by name), Profile page (score, gems, ID), Leaderboards (top 5 scores and gem counts), Message inbox (unread, delete), routing with page titles and browser history.
  • app-root in index.html is where Angular mounts the app. The name is a convention. Bootstrap CSS is optional styling. styles.css holds global styles. JSON files in assets/mocks/ stand in for a backend.

Root files: angular.json (CLI config), package.json (deps and scripts), tsconfig.json (TypeScript), .eslintrc.json (lint rules).

2. Angular Overview: Versioning, License, Tooling Angular

Angular › 2. Angular Overview: Versioning, License, Tooling

Philosophy. Keeps HTML templates separate from JavaScript controllers and extends HTML with custom attributes and dynamic content. Angular is positioned as a platform (routing, standard libraries, reusable components, scalable architecture), not only a UI library. It builds single-page applications (SPAs) that update content without a browser refresh. Maintained by a full-time Google team plus an open-source community, MIT licensed.

Decorators Angular

Angular › 3. Decorators and Modules › Decorators

  • Functions that return functions. Not Angular-specific, but Angular cannot be used without them. They supply metadata that tells Angular what a class is and how to inject it.
  • Syntax: @Name() or @Name(config). Starts with @, always has parentheses, no semicolon.
  • Common mistakes: @Component (no parentheses), @Component() (missing required config), @Component({}); (semicolon). Modern Angular reports these at compile time (ng build / ng serve); older versions failed at runtime.
← Previous8 / 55Next →
Modules (NgModule) Angular

Angular › 3. Decorators and Modules › Modules (NgModule)

  • A module groups closely related components, services, pipes and directives. Files are named *.module.ts.
  • Standalone (Angular 14+) lets you use these pieces without a module. Modules are still the norm in existing projects.
  • The module class body is empty. The decorator metadata does the work; the class only tells Angular what to load.
  • Only the root module has bootstrap (usually one component). Use one root module plus feature modules.
PropertyMeaning
declarationscomponents, directives, pipes owned by this module. Each can belong to one module only (compiler error otherwise)
importsexternal modules whose exports are usable in this module's templates
exportscode made available to modules that import this one
providersservices for dependency injection. Rule: modules go in imports, services in providers
bootstrapcomponent(s) to load at launch, root module only

exports, providers and the other properties are optional and can be omitted or left as empty arrays.

Angular › 5. Templates and Data Binding › Structural directives

Start with * and add or remove elements from the DOM (not CSS hide/show).

  • *ngIf="cond": renders when truthy. else templateRef renders the alternate when falsy. *ngIf="obs$ | async as value" unwraps an observable into a local variable.

Angular › 6. Standalone Components and Zoneless › Standalone (Angular 14+)

Use a component, directive or pipe without assigning it to a module. Simpler structure, and compatible with module-based code so migration can be gradual.

  • Set standalone: true (default is false as of Angular 16). Applies to components, pipes and directives.
  • The piece declares its own imports (built-in CommonModule, other standalone pieces, router directives, pipe modules) and optional providers. Imports are not inherited from a module.
  • CLI: ng generate component component-name --standalone.

Angular › 6. Standalone Components and Zoneless › Zoneless Angular (18+)

Architecture without ZoneJS. Experimental and opt-in at the time of the course, with an incomplete, unstable API. Benefits: fewer change detection cycles, smaller bundles, faster startup, better debugging, better third-party API compatibility. Risks: API can change, may require dependency, code and unit-test changes. Try it on new projects; wait for stability on existing ones.

Angular › 7. Pipes › Custom pipes

A pipe is a class decorated with @Pipe that implements PipeTransform, ends in Pipe, and has a transform method (build error if missing). The first argument is the template value, extra arguments are pipe arguments, and it must return a value.

PropertyNotes
namecamelCase, no hyphens (build error)
puredefault true: runs only when the input reference changes (fast). false runs on every change detection cycle, so use sparingly
standalonetrue for standalone architecture, false for module architecture

8. Services Angular

Angular › 8. Services

Services separate and reuse code: API calls, calculations, business logic, anything that does not change the UI directly. They keep components small. Services and dependency injection go together. Files: *.service.ts.

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) creates one singleton for the whole app, so every consumer sees the same data (caching, shared state). It is the CLI default. providedIn: null (or bare @Injectable()) means you must add it to a providers array. See section 11.

Canonical HTTP service Angular

Angular › 8. Services › Canonical HTTP service

  • Class name ends in Service. Constructor injects dependencies; private is recommended (easy to spot dead code), public if the template needs it, protected for subclasses.
  • Module-based apps import HttpClientModule in AppModule.imports.
  • $ suffix marks observable-returning methods or properties (convention, not required).
  • http.get<Type>(url, options?): URL is local or remote, the generic gives type safety and autocomplete.
  • .pipe(...) composes operators. delay simulates network lag, map transforms the data.
  • Return observables from services and let components (or the async pipe) subscribe.

  • @Input receives a value from the parent through binding. Simplest pattern: the property name equals the selector name. Alias form: @Input('customName') public appOnlineStatus: boolean;.
  • ElementRef<T>.nativeElement is the underlying DOM element, injected via the constructor.

11. Dependency Injection Angular

Angular › 11. Dependency Injection

DI is a design pattern where a class requests dependencies from an external source instead of creating them. Angular cannot be used without it.

← Previous32 / 55Next →
How it works Angular

Angular › 11. Dependency Injection › How it works

  • Angular keeps an injector: a collection of key-value pairs, each key a unique token.
  • For constructor(private api: ApiService), the type annotation is the token. Angular looks it up in the injector and injects the instance.
  • What can be injected: services (most common), strings, booleans, object literals, anything with a provider.

Change detection Angular

Angular › 12. Change Detection and Lifecycle Hooks › Change detection

How Angular checks application state and updates the UI. Two strategies set through changeDetection:

StrategyBehavior
Defaultruns on data mutation inside objects and arrays, property redefinition, and events (API calls, click handlers). Starts at the root component, compares the new state tree to the old with strict equality, and reruns only what changed. Works everywhere, but checks all components, so it is slower with many components
OnPushskips the component and its sub-tree unless a property is redefined, an event fires, or change detection is called manually. Faster, but requires immutable data (never mutate in place)

Use OnPush for components with many children, immutable data, and where performance matters.

HighScoresComponent in section 6 is a working OnPush example: players$ is declared once, set once in ngOnInit, never mutated.

OnPush + async pipe is the best pairing: the observable emits a new reference and the async pipe triggers detection, so no manual change detection is needed.

← Previous37 / 55Next →
Lifecycle hooks Angular

Angular › 12. Change Detection and Lifecycle Hooks › Lifecycle hooks

Run code at specific moments of a component or directive lifecycle. Implement the matching interface from @angular/core (autocomplete, type safety, compile checks; optional but recommended) and add the public method.

HookWhen
ngOnChangesinput properties change
ngOnInitonce, after construction, with injected dependencies and inputs available
ngDoCheckevery change detection run
ngAfterContentInitafter projected content is initialized
ngAfterContentCheckedafter content is checked
ngAfterViewInitafter the view is initialized
ngAfterViewCheckedafter the view is checked
ngOnDestroyjust before destruction

Order: constructor, ngOnChanges (if inputs), ngOnInit, ngDoCheck, ngAfterContentInit, ngAfterContentChecked, ngAfterViewInit, ngAfterViewChecked. On updates: ngOnChanges, ngDoCheck, ngAfterContentChecked, ngAfterViewChecked. Finally ngOnDestroy.

  • ngOnInit (most common): initialization and API calls. Prefer it over the constructor, which should only inject dependencies and do trivial assignments, because ngOnInit is guaranteed access to the injector and inputs. Example in section 4.
  • ngOnDestroy (second most common): clean up by unsubscribing, stopping timers, unregistering callbacks.

Several hooks: implements OnInit, OnDestroy, AfterViewInit, then add each method.

Lazy loading Angular

Angular › 13. Routing and Navigation › Lazy loading

Loading modules or components only when a route is first visited is Angular's default for routes (loadChildren / loadComponent). It uses a dynamic import:

The arrow function returns a Promise, import() loads an ES module asynchronously, and .then extracts the exported class.

  • Upside: faster first load, smaller initial bundle.
  • Downside: network lag on first navigation to a page, noticeable on slow connections.
← Previous42 / 55Next →
Preloading strategies Angular

Angular › 13. Routing and Navigation › Preloading strategies

Preloading loads lazy modules in the background after the initial page load, giving fast startup and low navigation lag. Set it through preloadingStrategy:

  • NoPreloading (default): everything lazy on demand.
  • PreloadAllModules: loads everything on launch. Fine for small apps, slow launch with many modules.
  • Custom class implementing PreloadingStrategy with a public preload(route, fn) method returning an Observable. Call fn() to preload, return of(null) to skip.

Bracket access route.data['preload'] is required by Angular's type definition. Mark routes with data: { preload: true } as in the route table above.

Network result with that setup: first load fetches main.js and the current page module (players), and preloads messages in the background. leaderboards has no flag, so it is fetched only when visited. Navigating to messages causes no request.

Angular › 14. Reactive Programming: Signals, effect, async Pipe, RxJS › Signals (Angular 16+, developer preview at recording)

Reactive pattern: data is wrapped in getters and setters so Angular tracks changes and updates only what changed, instead of checking every component. The API may change, so check the docs.

signal(initialValue) returns a WritableSignal; the type is inferred, or given explicitly. Read a signal by calling it.

MethodUse
set(value)replace the value
update(fn)return a new value from the current one (immutable, recommended)
mutate(fn)change the current value in place (mutable, no return).

MessageService with these calls is in section 8.

computed() derives a read-only value from other signals. It is cached (recalculates only when dependencies change) and lazy (evaluated only when read), which suits filtering large arrays and heavy calculations.

Patterns:

total and average computed signals follow the same computed(() => this.items().reduce(...)) shape.

Signals vs Observables. Signals are synchronous, always hold a current value, have a simpler API and suit local state. Observables are asynchronous streams over time with a rich operator set and suit async work.

← Previous47 / 55Next →
effect() Angular

Angular › 14. Reactive Programming: Signals, effect, async Pipe, RxJS › effect()

Runs a side effect whenever the signals it reads change.

  • Call signals inside the callback to read them.
  • Runs at least once, then again when its signals change. Runs asynchronously during change detection. Should not update the UI or do blocking work.
  • Needs an injection context, so create it in the constructor of a component, service or directive.
  • Use cases: analytics, logging, syncing to storage.

async pipe Angular

Built-in pipe for Promises and Observables. It subscribes, triggers change detection, unwraps the value and unsubscribes automatically, which avoids leaks and duplicate subscriptions. Prefer async as so the pipe is referenced once:

RxJS and observables Angular

Angular › 14. Reactive Programming: Signals, effect, async Pipe, RxJS › RxJS and observables

Reactive programming handles data that changes over time. An Observable is a stream of values over time from the RxJS library; Angular's HttpClient returns them. pipe() composes operators where each output feeds the next. The service in section 8 shows delay and map.

Common operators:

  • Transformation: map, pluck, scan
  • Filtering: filter, take, skip
  • Combination: merge, concat, combineLatest
  • Errors: catchError, retry
  • Utility: tap (side effects), delay, timeout

Observables vs Promises. Observables: multiple values, lazy (run only when subscribed), cancellable, rich operators. Promises: single value, eager, not cancellable, limited transformation.

Unit testing basics Angular

Angular › 15. Testing and Linting › Unit testing basics

Default stack: Jasmine (framework) and Karma (runner). Specs live in *.spec.ts, generated by the CLI.

Karma builds the app, opens a browser, reruns tests on file save (watch mode). Green is pass; red shows expected vs actual and a stack trace. If Karma shows "No binary for Chrome browser", close and reopen the Karma tab.

  • describe('Name', () => {...}) groups specs into a suite (use the class name).
  • beforeEach(() => {...}) runs before every spec for a fresh instance. Declare shared variables with let at suite level and assign them in beforeEach.
  • it('should ...', () => {...}) is one spec; start the label with "should".
  • expect(actual).toBe(expected) asserts. Follow Arrange-Act-Assert, with named expected/actual variables.

Testing with DI (services) (1/2) Angular

Angular › 15. Testing and Linting › Testing with DI (services)

Services use DI, so configure TestBed, fetch instances with TestBed.inject, replace HTTP with HttpClientTestingModule, and stub the HTTP method with a Jasmine spy. Put configureTestingModule in beforeEach so each test gets a clean copy. declarations can be empty or omitted.

Without the spy, the test times out because the testing module never answers the request. With spyOn(...).and.returnValue(of(data)) the call returns immediately with no network. Observable tests need done so Jasmine waits for the subscription.

LangChain Chatbot 29 cards Building a personalized chatbot with OpenAI and LangChain
1. Big picture LangChain Chatbot

LangChain Chatbot › 1. Big picture

Goal: a chatbot that answers from your own data (hotel PDF + website) using OpenAI and LangChain, wrapped in a Flask web app. No model training; the data is injected through the prompt.

Pipeline: extract text -> save to a text file -> prompt template with that text + persona -> prompt | llm chain -> Flask route -> HTML/JS front end.

Stack: Python, OpenAI API, LangChain, PyMuPDF, requests + BeautifulSoup, Flask, HTML/CSS/JS.

Two ways to feed your data to the model (key interview distinction):

ApproachHowTrade-off
Prompt stuffing (Sections 5-6)Entire extracted text in the promptSimple; fails when data exceeds the context window; pays tokens for all text every call
RAG (Section 8)Chunk, embed, store in a vector store, retrieve top-k per questionScales to large data, cheaper per call; more moving parts

8. RAG upgrade: chunking, vector store, retrieval, memory LangChain Chatbot

LangChain Chatbot › 8. RAG upgrade: chunking, vector store, retrieval, memory

Use when data is too big for the prompt. Flow: load, split into overlapping chunks, embed, store in FAISS, retrieve top-k similar chunks per question, LLM answers from them.

  • RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200): overlap preserves context across chunk edges.
  • OpenAIEmbeddings: text to vectors; as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 3}): top 3 chunks.
  • chain_type="stuff": retrieved chunks go into one prompt.
  • ConversationBufferMemory: chat history so follow-ups work.

Caution: the snippets use older import paths and APIs (langchain.vectorstores, langchain.memory, ConversationChain, llm(prompt)) that newer LangChain moved or deprecated; check current docs.

1. Overview, Prerequisites & Setup LangChain Level Up

LangChain Level Up › 1. Overview, Prerequisites & Setup

Why RAG? LLMs generate text and answer questions but often lack current and specific knowledge, which gives inaccurate outputs. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) connects the LLM to external data sources. Course arc: LangChain basics → similarity search/RAG → Streamlit UI → multi-source Q&A agent → MongoDB Atlas Vector Search → NoSQL (MongoDB) interaction → LangServe REST API → cloud deployment.

Prerequisites: Python 3.10+ (syntax, control flow), CLI/venv/pip, 1–2 years of web development, VS Code, an OpenAI account with credits.

PackagePurpose
langchainFramework for building LLM apps by composing chains
langchain-openai / openaiOpenAI integration / API client
langchain-communityCommunity integrations (FAISS, Chroma, loaders)
python-dotenvLoad env vars from .env
coloramaColored terminal output
faiss-cpuFacebook AI Similarity Search (vector search)

OpenAI API key: platform.openai.com → Project API Keys → Create new secret key (copy immediately; it is shown once). Put it in a .env file at the project root.

OpenAI() / ChatOpenAI() read OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment automatically once load_dotenv() has run.

Exercise repo: branches are named <chapter>_<video>b (beginning) and <chapter>_<video>e (end).

3. Embeddings, Vector Store (FAISS) & Retriever LangChain Level Up

LangChain Level Up › 3. Embeddings, Vector Store (FAISS) & Retriever

Similarity search retrieves dataset content similar to a query (used in information retrieval, image recognition, recommenders, NLP). Embeddings are vector representations of text that preserve semantic relationships; text → embedding model → vector → vector store. Query vectors are compared with stored vectors (cosine similarity) and the top-k closest are returned.

Step 1: RAG prompt template

Step 2: Embeddings + FAISS store

Direct similarity search returns a list of Document objects (page_content = text, metadata = source/page/etc.). k (top_k) is the number of results.

Vector store as a retriever in an LCEL RAG chain — the dict runs in parallel: the retriever fills {context}, RunnablePassthrough() forwards the raw question unchanged to {question}.

ConceptDescription
similarity_search()Direct method to find similar documents
as_retriever()Wraps a vector store as a retriever usable in chains
RunnablePassthrough()Passes input through unchanged (the question in RAG chains)
← Previous7 / 35Next →
4.1 Why RAG / architecture LangChain Level Up

LangChain Level Up › 4. RAG: Architecture & the Red30 Shoes Q&A Chatbot › 4.1 Why RAG / architecture

LLM limits: training-data cut-off, no specialized domain knowledge, no access to your private data. RAG combines retrieval with generation to fix this.

BenefitDescription
Up-to-date informationRetrieves context from external sources
Improved accuracyAnswers aligned with the actual data
Domain-specific knowledgeLLM knows your products, services, policies

Two components: information retrieval from an external source, and augmented generation (retrieved context added to the prompt).

StageWhat happens
1. Document indexingSplit documents into smaller chunks
2. Create embeddingsChunks → numeric vectors
3. Store in vector storeSave embeddings for efficient similarity search
4. User queryTriggers search
5. RetrievalSearch the store, retrieve relevant documents
6. Context integrationCombine retrieved docs with the original query
7. Augmented generationLLM answers using query + retrieved docs

Project: Q&A chatbot for fictitious Red30 Shoes, data source is a .txt FAQ (opening hours 24/7, return policy, shipping costs, product info). Layout: .env, requirements.txt, main.py, docs/ FAQ file, README. Extra install: pip install chromadb.

4.4 Chain without vs with context LangChain Level Up

LangChain Level Up › 4. RAG: Architecture & the Red30 Shoes Q&A Chatbot › 4.4 Chain without vs with context

Without context (generic answer): chat prompt = system message + human message {user_query}.

With context: add {context} to the system message and wire the retriever in with RunnablePassthrough.

RunnablePassthrough forwards the user query unchanged to {question} while the retriever searches the store and fills {context}; both reach the prompt, then the LLM, then the parser.

AspectWithout contextWith context (RAG)
ResponseGeneric, vagueSpecific, accurate
KnowledgeLLM training data onlyLLM + your data

LangChain Level Up › 8. Agents & Tools over MongoDB (OpenAI Tools Agent) › 8.1 Defining tools

Tools are functions decorated with @tool (name = function name, description = docstring, arguments = typed parameters). The docstring is mandatory; the LLM reads it to decide when/how to use the tool, and validation fails without it.

Vector search tool: vector_search_index.py holds the RAG chain from Section 7 ({"context": retriever, "question": RunnablePassthrough()} | custom_rag_prompt | llm | StrOutputParser()); agent.py wraps it as a tool.

  • Not normalizing vectors when using cosine; wrong metric for the data.

  • Keep the embedding model version-controlled; keep preprocessing consistent.

Why not a traditional DB Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 3. Vector databases: concepts › Why not a traditional DB

Row/column databases are not optimized for high-dimensional vectors: slow similarity search, no ANN support, poor scaling. A vector DB provides optimized vector storage, ANN search, built-in distance metrics, and scales to billions of vectors.

  • CRUD on vectors. Consistency: transaction isolation exists but not RDBMS-level; tuned for read-heavy loads.
  • Distinguishing feature: built-in similarity search (L2, Cosine, IP) with no custom code.

  • Avoid: complex transactions, heavy aggregations/reporting/warehousing, purely relational data (users, orders, catalogs).
  • Hybrid approach: metadata in RDBMS, embeddings in the vector DB, join in the app.
  • Future: better transactions, more built-in functions, faster ingestion, lower memory, richer integrations, hybrid DBs.

4. Milvus: deployment, architecture and setup Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 4. Milvus: deployment, architecture and setup

Milvus: open-source vector database for storing, indexing and searching vectors; a leading choice for GenAI apps. SDKs: Python, Node.js, Go, Java. Stores vector and scalar fields together, so you can combine similarity search with metadata filters. Supports L2, IP, COSINE.

← Previous18 / 73Next →
Architecture Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 4. Milvus: deployment, architecture and setup › Architecture

  • Access layer: gRPC API, port 19530.
  • Coordinator: cluster management.
  • etcd: metadata (schemas, users, indexes).
  • Message queue (RocksMQ default; Kafka/Pulsar): DML.
  • Worker nodes: data processing, index loading, search.
  • MinIO: object store for vector data and logs.

Request flows:

  • DDL (create DB/collection/user/index): client -> access layer -> coordinator -> etcd.
  • DML (insert/update/delete): client -> access layer -> message queue -> worker node -> MinIO.
  • Query/search: client -> access layer -> coordinator (metadata check) -> worker node (load index, search, return).

Collection schema Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 5. Milvus objects › Collection schema

A collection has a schema of scalar + vector fields, exactly one primary key, optional dynamic fields.

  • FieldSchema parts: name, dtype, is_primary, max_length (required for VARCHAR), dim (vector).
  • Vector dim must equal the embedding model's output and cannot change later. Check with len(embeddings_model.embed_query("test")).
  • shard_num: DML parallelism (small data 1-4, large 4-16).

Primary key: one scalar field, unique, can be auto-generated.

Dynamic fields: extra ad hoc fields supplied at insert time with enable_dynamic_field=True (flexible, may cost performance; enable only if needed).

Data types

ScalarNotes
INT8/16/32/64, FLOAT, DOUBLE, BOOLEANnumeric/boolean
VARCHARneeds max_length
JSON, ARRAYARRAY needs element_type and max_capacity
VectorNotes
FLOAT_VECTORstandard embeddings (most common)
BINARY_VECTORdim must be a multiple of 8; compressed

Collection operations

Schema modification restrictions: you cannot change field types, names, the primary key, vector dimension, or remove fields. Workaround: create a new collection with the new schema, migrate data, drop the old one. (You can add dynamic fields at insert and edit the description.)

← Previous27 / 73Next →
Partitions Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 6. Partitions and indexes › Partitions

  • A partition is a physical subdivision of a collection that stores related data together, so queries scan fewer data blocks (fewer disk reads, better cache use).
  • Every collection has an automatic _default partition (data goes there when none is given).
  • Typical keys: tenant ID (multitenancy), date/month (time series), region, device ID, user ID.
  • Guidance: partition by frequently filtered fields, keep the number of partitions small (<100), search specific partitions.
← Previous28 / 73Next →
Indexes Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 6. Partitions and indexes › Indexes

  • Speed up retrieval. One index per field; no composite indexes. Scalar indexes (RDBMS-like) and vector indexes (ANN).
  • A vector index must exist and the collection must be loaded before vector search.
IndexDatasetRecallSpeedNotes
FLATsmall (<10K)100%slowbrute force, exact
IVF_FLATlargehigh (not 100%)fastmost popular, balanced
IVF_SQ8largehighfasterless memory
HNSWlargevery highvery fasthigher memory
GPU_IVF_FLATlargehighvery fastneeds GPU deployment
IVF_PQvery large (>1M, per Best Practices lesson)compressed

nlist / nprobe trade-off

SettingEffect
Higher nlistfaster search, lower recall (use for large datasets: 4096+)
Lower nlistslower, higher recall (small datasets: 128-512); 1024-2048 general
Higher nprobebetter recall, slower (5 = fast, 10 = balanced, 20 = higher recall)

Same metric_type must be used for the index and the search.

Search always returns results: use a threshold Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 8. Query vs Search › Search always returns results: use a threshold

Even an unrelated query returns Top-K. Demo: "machine learning" gave distances 0.33-0.50; "best movies of the year" gave 0.62-0.65. So pick a similarity threshold from observed distances, or push it into the search with radius.

Ideas for choosing it dynamically (source): percentile of distances, mean minus std, or fixed per metric (L2 ~0.5, COSINE ~0.8). A "fallback" pattern: if nothing passes the threshold, show the top 3 anyway.

Why Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 9. Use case 1: LLM semantic cache › Why

  • LLMs are costly (per-token API pricing, heavy compute) and slow (decoder generates one token at a time, so long answers mean high latency).
  • Users send similar prompts (same questions across users, common org queries, paraphrases), so responses overlap.
  • An exact-match cache misses paraphrases ("What is ML?" vs "What is machine learning?"); a vector-DB cache matches by meaning, so more hits.
  • Benefits: lower API cost, lower latency (~50-100 ms vs 2-5 s, quoted as 20-50x), less LLM load, better UX.
← Previous44 / 73Next →
Workflow Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 9. Use case 1: LLM semantic cache › Workflow

User prompt -> embed -> search cache (top-1) -> distance below threshold? Hit: return cached response. Miss: call LLM, store prompt + embedding + response, return response.

What is stored per entry: prompt text, prompt embedding (vector), response text. Requirements: one embedding model for all prompts, a distance threshold, a vector DB.

Auto-generated primary key; the prompt is embedded (not the response); L2 + IVF_FLAT.

Field sizes: 2048 for short, 4096 medium, 8192 long prompts/responses. Raise max_length for longer responses.

Vector Databases › 9. Use case 1: LLM semantic cache › Inference loop (notebook code_04)

The radius parameter acts as the threshold: if the cache returns any hit, it is within the similarity threshold (0.3 for L2), so "hit" is simply len(results[0]) > 0.

Explicit-check variant from the lesson (when you do not use radius): if results[0] and results[0][0].distance < SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD: hit, else miss.

Threshold (L2 distance) Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 9. Use case 1: LLM semantic cache › Threshold (L2 distance)

DistanceMeaning
0.1-0.3very similar: hit (0.3 is the recommended start)
0.3-0.5somewhat similar: miss
> 0.5not similar: miss
  • Too low: few hits (strict). Too high: false positives (wrong cached answer returned). Examples from the lesson: "Height of elephant" vs "Weight of elephant" = 0.48, "Capital of France" vs "Population of France" = 0.52 (must miss).
  • Tune on a benchmark set; lesson numbers: 0.1 -> ~20% hit / 98% accuracy; 0.3 -> ~70% / 90% (recommended); 0.5 -> ~95% / 65% (too loose). Score = hit ratio x accuracy.
← Previous48 / 73Next →
Measuring effectiveness Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 9. Use case 1: LLM semantic cache › Measuring effectiveness

  • Cache hit ratio = hits / total requests; grows as the cache fills. Typical by use case: FAQ 80-90%, customer support 60-80%, general chatbot 40-60%, creative writing 10-30%.
  • Cost example (1000 req/day, $0.002/call, 70% hits): no cache $2.00/day; with cache $0.60/day; saves $1.40/day (~$42/month).
  • Gains are small in the local demo (small prompts, local DB) and bigger in production.
← Previous49 / 73Next →
Cache management (production) (1/2) Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 9. Use case 1: LLM semantic cache › Cache management (production)

  • Timestamp (last_used) field: update on every hit (upsert) so you can prune LRU / by age.
  • Pruning strategies: age-based (simple, may delete popular old entries), LRU (keeps popular, needs timestamp updates), size-based (predictable, may delete recent), hybrid (best, more complex).
  • User feedback field (+1 thumbs up / -1 thumbs down) and delete negative entries.
  • TTL, cache warming (pre-populate with common prompts), multi-model cache (add model_name field and filter on it).

Cache management (production) (2/2) Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 9. Use case 1: LLM semantic cache › Cache management (production)

  • The prune_cache snippet queries with sort_by="last_used"; treat it as pseudo-code (verify the pymilvus 2.3.5 query signature before using).
  • Troubleshooting: low hit ratio (<30%) -> loosen threshold, check embedding-model consistency, analyze query patterns; high false positives -> tighten threshold, add feedback; fast-growing cache -> prune more, set size limits; slow lookups -> collection loaded? index built? tune nlist/nprobe.
  • Production checklist: threshold set via benchmark, size limit, timestamp tracking, pruning schedule, feedback, hit-ratio monitoring.
← Previous51 / 73Next →
LLM capabilities and limits Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 10. Use case 2: RAG concepts › LLM capabilities and limits

  • Capabilities: language (understand, generate, translate, keep conversation flow) and knowledge (answer from training data).
  • As a knowledge source, an LLM:
    1. only knows its training data (no company-specific info);
    2. is outdated (training cut-off date);
    3. hallucinates (confident, plausible, false answers: legal/compliance and trust risk);
    4. has no access to private/enterprise data (internal docs, customer records, specs);
    5. is expensive to update (a custom LLM costs ~$100K-$1M+ to train, plus GPUs, data prep, talent; daily retraining is impractical).

What RAG is Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 10. Use case 2: RAG concepts › What RAG is

Retrieval-Augmented Generation = curated knowledge base (context) + LLM (language skills). Retrieve relevant context, augment the prompt with it, let a standard LLM generate a grounded answer. Most popular enterprise LLM use case.

  • Enterprise data access, multiple formats (PDF, tickets/DB, HTML, CSV), curated (only relevant, clean content), continuously updated (new doc is searchable minutes after processing; no retraining).
  • Reduces hallucination because the answer is grounded in retrieved facts.
  • Hybrid search: vector similarity plus scalar filters (e.g. product == 'Product A' AND date > '2024-01-01').
  • Uses off-the-shelf LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama 2): no training, provider updates, lower cost, faster deployment.

Knowledge curation pipeline Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 10. Use case 2: RAG concepts › Knowledge curation pipeline

Data sources -> acquisition and filtering -> standardization -> chunking -> embedding -> store in knowledge base.

  1. Sources: websites (HTML), ticketing systems, databases, document hubs (SharePoint, Drive), PDFs/DOCX. Structures differ widely.
  2. Acquisition module: fetch, filter relevant data, cleanse noise, handle incremental updates (initial load, then monitor source changes and fetch only new/updated).
  3. Standardization: uniform structure; segregate structured data into scalar fields, unstructured text into vector fields, metadata into filter fields.
  1. Chunking: vector fields have size limits, and retrieving only relevant portions improves precision. Use overlap to keep context across chunks; preserve sentence boundaries; keep metadata (e.g. doc_id) with each chunk.
Use caseChunk size
Short answers512
General1024
Technical docs1536
Long context2048
  1. Embedding: same model for curation and inference; consistent dimensions; batch for efficiency.
  2. Store: insert (or upsert to avoid duplicates and handle document updates), then flush.
  • Entity per chunk: {id, chunk, embedding, doc_id}.
  • Advanced / ensemble knowledge base: vector DB (semantic) + RDBMS (structured) + knowledge graph (relationships, e.g. Neo4j).
  • Curate: include accurate, current, relevant, structured content; exclude outdated, irrelevant, duplicate, low-quality sources.

Question-answering pipeline Vector Databases

Vector Databases › 10. Use case 2: RAG concepts › Question-answering pipeline

User prompt -> validation and metadata -> embed -> query knowledge base (top-K, with scalar filters) -> build context -> augment prompt -> LLM -> answer (plus sources).

(Build filter expressions from validated values; interpolating raw user input into expr invites injection.)

Top-KTrade-off
1precise, may miss context
3balanced (recommended start)
5more comprehensive, more noise
10too much context

Prompt augmentation: instruct the model to use only the context, allow "I don't know", ask for citations.

Temperature: 0.0 deterministic/factual, 0.3 recommended for RAG, 0.7 general chat, 1.0 creative.

1. RAG Overview & Use Cases RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 1. RAG Overview & Use Cases

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances an LLM by connecting it to external data sources, including private datasets.

LLM limitationWhyHow RAG helps
Stale informationTrained on static internet scrapesRetrieves current data from external stores and injects it into the context window
No source attributionKnowledge is baked into weightsThe answer can be traced back to retrieved sources

RAG in three steps: Retrieve context from an external source → Augment the prompt with it → Generate the answer with the LLM.

3. LlamaIndex Fundamentals RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 3. LlamaIndex Fundamentals

LlamaIndex is a data framework for context-augmented LLM apps (LLM + private/domain data). Python and TypeScript SDKs exist; the course uses Python.

CapabilityWhat it is
Data connectors (Readers)Ingest from APIs, PDFs, SQL, etc.
IndexesIntermediate data structures optimized for LLM retrieval
Query enginesRetrieval interface that returns a synthesized answer
Chat enginesMulti-turn conversational interface over your data
Data agentsLLM-powered workers augmented with tools

Three kinds of packages: llama-index-core (loading, indexing, querying, evaluating; no integrations), integrations (LLMs, embeddings, vector stores, readers; each installed separately), and Llama Packs (community templates, often implementing techniques from papers). LlamaHub (llamahub.ai) catalogs all of them (150+ data loaders, 35+ agent tools, 50+ packs, 50+ LLMs, 25+ embeddings, 40+ vector stores); sort packs by downloads to find the popular ones.

Pipeline: Your data → Reader → Index (backed by a vector store such as Qdrant) → Query/Chat engine → LLM → Response.

← Previous8 / 64Next →
3.1 Using LLMs RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 3. LlamaIndex Fundamentals › 3.1 Using LLMs

LLMs are used at two stages: indexing (judge relevance, summarize) and querying (retrieval: fetch data, choose a source, use tools; then response synthesis).

MethodUse
llm.complete(prompt)Single text completion
llm.chat(messages)Chat with message history
llm.stream_chat(messages)Streaming chat
chat_engine.chat(msg) / .chat_repl() / .streaming_chat_repl()Conversational interface / REPL / streaming REPL

Tip: dir(obj) lists available methods on any LlamaIndex object.

← Previous9 / 64Next →
3.2 Loading Data RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 3. LlamaIndex Fundamentals › 3.2 Loading Data

Ingestion has three stages: Load (Reader → Documents) → Transform (Documents → Nodes: chunking, metadata, embeddings) → Index & store (vector DB). It resembles ETL / ML data cleaning.

A Reader (data connector) formats data into Document objects (text + metadata + id + embedding slot). SimpleDirectoryReader reads markdown, PDF, Word, PowerPoint, images, audio, video; one Document per page for PDFs.

Nodes are chunks of documents and the first-class citizen in LlamaIndex (Document is a subclass of Node). A node holds text, metadata, relationships to other nodes, and a link to its source document. Node parsers turn documents into nodes.

Node relationships link chunks sequentially (NEXT/PREVIOUS) or hierarchically (PARENT/CHILD). Useful for books with chapters, legal docs with clauses.

← Previous10 / 64Next →
3.3 Indexing (1/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 3. LlamaIndex Fundamentals › 3.3 Indexing

An index is a data structure for fast retrieval of relevant context for a query. Indexes build Retrievers, Query Engines, and Chat Engines. Flow: raw text → Document → Nodes → embeddings → vector DB.

An embedding is a fixed-length numeric vector representing the meaning of a text. The length depends on the model, never on the input length.

ModelDimensions
Cohere embed-english-v3.01024
Cohere embed-english-light-v3.0384
Cohere embed-english-v2.04096
OpenAI text-embedding-3-small1536

Local embedding alternatives (check the MTEB leaderboard); FastEmbed models are lightweight, quantized, CPU-optimized:

VectorStoreIndex creation

MethodUse when
VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs)You have documents to embed and store (computes embeddings)
VectorStoreIndex.from_vector_store(store)Embeddings already live in an external vector store such as Qdrant
VectorStoreIndex(nodes)You parsed nodes yourself (more control)

Embedding calls cost time and money, so the notebook indexes only a 10,000-character slice of one book.

3.4 Storing RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 3. LlamaIndex Fundamentals › 3.4 Storing

By default an index lives in memory. Re-indexing costs time and money, so persist it. The simplest option is index.persist() to disk; the course uses a vector database (Qdrant).

Steps: initialize Qdrant client → create a vector store bound to a collection → assign it to a StorageContext → build the index from that context.

StorageContext tells LlamaIndex where to put each kind of data: vector_store (embeddings), docstore (nodes/documents), index_store (index metadata), graph_store (knowledge graphs). The Qdrant dashboard shows the collection, vector dimension (1536 here), a visualization tab, and "Find Similar".

← Previous13 / 64Next →
3.5 Retrieving RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 3. LlamaIndex Fundamentals › 3.5 Retrieving

A retriever is the interface an index exposes to fetch relevant nodes. The query is embedded with the same model used at indexing, a similarity search runs, and the top-k nodes come back with scores. Retriever types include vector, fusion, and recursive (hierarchical via node relationships).

The lesson notes pass similarity_cutoff=0.75 to as_retriever; the notebook uses similarity_threshold=0.75. For a reliable cutoff use a SimilarityPostprocessor(similarity_cutoff=...) on a query engine (sections 3.6 and 7.1).

Retrieval returns raw nodes and scores. A query engine is needed for a synthesized answer.

← Previous14 / 64Next →
3.6 Querying (1/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 3. LlamaIndex Fundamentals › 3.6 Querying

Querying is a prompt call to the LLM with retrieved context. Under the hood: Retrieval (top-k) → Postprocessing (rerank/filter/transform nodes) → Response synthesis (query + context + prompt → LLM).

Chat engine = multi-turn querying with memory.

chat_modeBehavior
simplePlain LLM chat, no knowledge base (SimpleChatEngine)
condense_questionRewrite history + last message into a standalone question, then query the engine (CondenseQuestionChatEngine)
contextRetrieve text for each user message and use it as context (ContextChatEngine)
condense_plus_contextCondense to a standalone question, retrieve context for it, then answer (CondensePlusContextChatEngine)
reactReAct agent loop with query-engine tools
bestPicks the best engine for the LLM: OpenAIAgent if function calling is supported, otherwise ReActAgent

Customizing the query pipeline (low-level composition): control retrieval top_k, add postprocessors (e.g., minimum similarity), choose a response synthesizer.

3.7 Agents RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 3. LlamaIndex Fundamentals › 3.7 Agents

An agent is an LLM-powered entity that decomposes complex queries, selects tools and parameters, plans, and executes. Agentic behavior is essentially a sophisticated prompting strategy plus tool access. ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) reasons step by step and decides when to call tools.

Tool docstrings matter: the agent reads them (and the type signature) to decide when and how to call the tool.

Different LLMs differ in tool use. In the demo Command-R beat Command-R+ here, so test multiple models.

4.2 Ingestion Pipeline RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 4. Introduction to RAG: Pipelines, Prompts, Data Prep › 4.2 Ingestion Pipeline

A higher-level abstraction over the low-level load/parse/index APIs: applies transformations (split, embed, extract metadata), returns nodes or inserts them into a vector store.

  • Caching: each (node, transformation) pair is hashed and cached; identical later runs reuse results.
  • Docstore attached = document management: tracks doc_id → document_hash. Same id + changed hash → reprocess; same id + same hash → skip. Without a vector store it can only detect/remove duplicate inputs; with a vector store it handles upserts of updated documents.
  • Persistence: pipeline.persist() saves the cache and docstore (default ./pipeline_storage).
Low-level APIIngestion pipeline
ProsFull control per stepLess boilerplate, caching, dedupe/upserts
ConsMore codeLess granular control
← Previous19 / 64Next →
4.3 Query Pipeline RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 4. Introduction to RAG: Pipelines, Prompts, Data Prep › 4.3 Query Pipeline

A declarative API to chain LLMs, prompts, retrievers, rerankers, and other pipelines, either as a sequential chain or a DAG. Fewer lines, better readability.

Pattern 1: chain. Use when each module takes one input. Here two prompts wrap a retriever.

Pattern 2: explicit modules and links. Needed when one input feeds several modules (use InputComponent) or for DAGs.

Control how retrieved chunks are combined and sent to the LLM. Listed by dir(ResponseMode).

ModeBehaviorTrade-off / use

compact_accumulatePack chunks first, then accumulateFaster than accumulate

Naive RAG workflow: index (chunk and index raw data) → retrieve (search with the query) → generate (query + retrieved context).

StageProblems
IndexingIncomplete or inaccurate extraction; suboptimal chunking; inefficient indexing; poor semantic representation
RetrievalLow precision (retrieved chunks that don't match); low recall (relevant chunks missed); ineffective user queries; redundant or overlapping chunks
GenerationHallucination not grounded in context; hard to judge relevance of retrieved context; over-reliance on context (echoing without synthesis); biased, inconsistent, or irrelevant output

The rest of the course addresses these with advanced and modular RAG.

Evaluation gives numbers for accuracy and relevance. It lets you compare models, prompts, contexts, and retrieval strategies, track quality over time, and find which part of the pipeline to fix.

5.1 What to evaluate RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 5. RAG Evaluation › 5.1 What to evaluate

ComponentPhasesEvaluation challenge
RetrievalIndexing (organize documents) + searching (fetch by query)Is the filtering effective? Is the retrieved data relevant and useful?
GenerationQuery + retrieved context → answerDoes the LLM use the context well? Is the answer factual, relevant, coherent?
AspectDimensions
QualityRelevance (precise context, answers related to the query); Faithfulness (answer consistent with the retrieved context, no contradictions)

5.2 Metrics RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 5. RAG Evaluation › 5.2 Metrics

MetricMeaning
FaithfulnessAnswer stays true to the context; key for catching hallucinations
Answer relevanceAnswer addresses the question and stays on topic
Context relevanceRetrieved context is accurate and targeted, without irrelevant text that wastes LLM capacity
MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank)Reciprocal of the rank of the first correct result, averaged across queries

Faithfulness, context relevance, and answer relevance use the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm: a strong LLM scores other LLM outputs to approximate human judgment. Benefits: scalable, cheap, fast iteration. Limits: position bias, verbosity bias (prefers longer outputs), weak reasoning on topics like math. GPT-4 reaches over 80% agreement with human preferences.

Further reading: ARAGOG (advanced RAG output grading, recommended), ARES, "Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey", and the Hugging Face cookbooks on RAG evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge.

5.3 Building an evaluation set (synthetic Q&A from your own data) (1/3) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 5. RAG Evaluation › 5.3 Building an evaluation set (synthetic Q&A from your own data)

The hard part of RAG evaluation is a high-quality evaluation dataset, not the metrics. Pipeline: sample documents per author → chunk → LLM writes a question per chunk → LLM answers from the chunk → critic LLM scores question groundedness → filter → publish.

OpenAI is used here because Cohere's free tier is rate-limited (the dataset is published, so rerunning is optional).

The helpers behind that (helpers/utils.py): group_documents_by_author builds a defaultdict(list) keyed by doc.metadata['author'] (warns and skips docs with no author). sample_documents keeps only docs longer than 500 characters, then random.samples num_samples per author (warns if an author has too few).

Prompts (helpers/prompts.py): the question prompt asks for a short, first-person, search-engine-style question answerable from the context; the answer prompt answers in second person using only the context.

6.1 Three RAG paradigms (from the "RAG for LLMs: A Survey" paper) (1/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.1 Three RAG paradigms (from the "RAG for LLMs: A Survey" paper)

ParadigmWhat it does
Naive RAGIndex (clean, extract, chunk, vectorize) → retrieve (similarity between query and chunks) → generate (query + docs into a prompt)
Advanced RAGPre-retrieval: better indexing (granularity, structure, metadata, alignment, mixed retrieval), fine-tuned or dynamic embeddings. Post-retrieval: re-ranking (diversity, best-document placement, recomputed similarity), prompt compression (importance estimation, summarization)
Modular RAGAdds modules (search module, memory module), allows serialized pipelines or end-to-end training across modules, builds on Advanced RAG
Optimization areaTechniques
Pre-retrievalData granularity (standardize text, remove ambiguity, domain annotations); index structure (varied chunk sizes, multiple index paths, graphs); metadata (dates, chapters) for filtering; alignment (hypothetical questions matched to document content); mixed retrieval (keyword + semantic + vector)
EmbeddingsFine-tune embedding models for the domain (not covered in the course); dynamic embeddings that adapt to context
Post-retrievalRe-ranking; prompt compression to cut noise
PipelineHybrid search; recursive retrieval and query engines (start small, expand); step-back prompting (broader reasoning); sub-queries and HyDE

Course map: pre-retrieval (chunk size, small-to-big, semantic chunking, metadata, document summary index, query transformations) → post-retrieval (node post-processing, reranking, FLARE, prompt compression, self-correcting) → modular (hybrid retrievers, agentic RAG, ensemble retrieval, ensemble query engine).

6.2 Optimizing chunk size (1/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.2 Optimizing chunk size

Chunking commandment (Greg Kamradt): don't chunk for chunking's sake; get data into a form that can be retrieved for value later.

The lowest-hanging fruit: chunk size affects response time, faithfulness, and relevancy. LlamaIndex defaults: chunk size 1024 tokens, overlap 20.

Effect
Smaller chunks (e.g., 128)More precise, focused embeddings; granular but may lack context
Larger chunks (e.g., 512+)Broader context, good for overviews; may include irrelevant text, miss detail
OverlapShared tokens between neighbors preserve context across boundaries
Chunk size vs similarity_top_kSmaller chunks → raise similarity_top_k to compensate (halving 1024→512 means retrieve more chunks)

TokenTextSplitter splits by token count (tokenizer default cl100k_base); SentenceSplitter keeps sentences/paragraphs whole (NLTK Punkt), so chunk sizes vary.

TokenTextSplitterSentenceSplitter
Splits byToken countSentence boundaries
Sentences preservedNoYes
Chunk lengthUniformVaries
Use whenStrict token limitsSentence context matters
← Previous38 / 64Next →
6.2 Optimizing chunk size (2/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.2 Optimizing chunk size

End-to-end with 256-token sentence chunks, MMR, and compact synthesis:

Gotcha: the notebooks spell it similiarty_top_k. The correct retriever argument is similarity_top_k; the misspelled keyword is silently passed through as a kwarg, so the default (2) may be what actually applies. The default similarity_top_k is 2.

MMR (Maximal Marginal Relevance) balances relevance and diversity: iteratively pick items that are relevant to the query but different from already-selected items.

MMR = argmax [ λ · Relevance(item, query) − (1 − λ) · max Similarity(item, selected) ]

λ near 1 favors relevance, near 0 favors diversity (mmr_threshold is λ). It depends on embeddings, so chunk size affects it. Enable with vector_store_query_mode="mmr".

← Previous39 / 64Next →
6.3 Small-to-big retrieval (recursive retrieval) (1/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.3 Small-to-big retrieval (recursive retrieval)

Retrieve small, query-specific chunks, then follow references to larger parent chunks (or inject surrounding context) so the LLM gets both precision and context. Three parts: recursive retrieval, node post-processing, response synthesis.

Option A: sentence window. SentenceWindowNodeParser makes one node per sentence and stores a window of surrounding sentences in metadata (window_size sentences each side; the sentence itself under original_text). Both are excluded from what the embedding model and LLM see by default, so only the single sentence is embedded. Splitting uses NLTK Punkt. At query time MetadataReplacementPostProcessor swaps the sentence for its window before the LLM sees it.

Note: the notebook sets window_metadata_key="window_size" while the post-processor targets "window" (the parser's default key); keep the keys consistent when you write your own.

Option B: parent-child chunks. Smaller child chunks (several sizes) point to a bigger parent via IndexNode. Retrieval matches a small child, then follows the reference to the parent.

← Previous40 / 64Next →
6.3 Small-to-big retrieval (recursive retrieval) (2/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.3 Small-to-big retrieval (recursive retrieval)

RecursiveRetriever is not created via index.as_retriever(): it is a standalone class that takes a root id plus dicts of retrievers/query engines/nodes, follows links, deduplicates nodes, and returns them. RetrieverQueryEngine wraps a retriever, applies postprocessing, and synthesizes the answer.

TechniqueHow it worksBest for
SentenceWindowNodeParser + MetadataReplacementPostProcessorEmbed one sentence, give the LLM its surrounding windowSentence-level precision with wider context
Parent-child IndexNodes + RecursiveRetrieverMatch small chunks, follow references to the parentMulti-granularity, hierarchical content

6.4 Semantic chunking RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.4 Semantic chunking

Instead of fixed N tokens/sentences, use embeddings to find breakpoints where meaning shifts (popularized by Greg Kamradt). Keeps related sentences together; chunk size is dynamic.

How SemanticSplitterNodeParser works: (1) split into sentences (default split_by_sentence_tokenizer, NLTK Punkt) → (2) group adjacent sentences by buffer_size (1 = each sentence alone) → (3) embed each group → (4) cosine similarity between adjacent groups, converted to distance (1 − similarity) → (5) a breakpoint is made where distance exceeds the breakpoint_percentile_threshold percentile → (6) sentences between breakpoints become one node.

ArgumentMeaningDefault
embed_modelModel used for similarityfrom Settings
buffer_sizeSentences grouped together when comparing1
breakpoint_percentile_thresholdPercentile of distances that triggers a split; lower → more nodes95
sentence_splitterPre-splittersplit_by_sentence_tokenizer

Design choices to experiment with: embedding model and its dimensions, buffer size, breakpoint threshold, sentence splitter.

Fixed chunkingSemantic chunking
BreakpointsFixed N tokens/sentencesWhere similarity drops
Related sentencesMay be splitKept together
CostFastSlower (embeds sentence groups)
Best forSimple docs, speedComplex docs, retrieval accuracy

6.5 Metadata extraction RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.5 Metadata extraction

Chunks can look alike; metadata disambiguates them and enables filtering. Effectiveness depends on the quality of the tags.

Manual metadata: add a dict entry per document.

Automatic extraction: extractors use an LLM and run as transformations in the ingestion pipeline.

ExtractorAdds
SummaryExtractorSummary of the node, optionally of previous/next nodes (summaries=["prev","self","next"])
QuestionsAnsweredExtractorQuestions the node can answer (questions=N)
TitleExtractorA title over node context (nodes=5)
KeywordExtractorUnique keywords, comma separated (keywords=10)

Design choices: which extractors; extraction LLM (gpt-4o quality vs gpt-3.5-turbo cost); questions per node; summary scope; splitter; chunk size/overlap. More metadata means a slower, costlier ingestion.

← Previous43 / 64Next →
6.6 Document Summary Index RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.6 Document Summary Index

Embed document summaries and link them to their chunks. Limits of chunk-only retrieval: chunks lack global context, similarity thresholds need tuning, embeddings may miss relevance, keyword filtering has its own problems. The index stores an LLM summary per document, the document's text chunks, and a mapping between them. Retrieval operates at the document level first, then synthesizes over the linked chunks (different optimal representations for retrieval vs synthesis).

The high-level as_query_engine() route uses embedding-based retrieval by default. The low-level retrievers allow either mode:

LLM-based (DocumentSummaryIndexLLMRetriever)Embedding-based (DocumentSummaryIndexEmbeddingRetriever)
Selects byLLM scores summaries in batches (choice_batch_size, default 10; choice_top_k, default 1)Cosine similarity of query vs summary embeddings (similarity_top_k)
Speed / costSlower, more expensiveFaster, cheaper
QualityHigher via LLM reasoningDepends on embedding quality
Custom hookschoice_select_prompt, format_node_batch_fn, parse_choice_select_answer_fnsimilarity_top_k

The retrievers also support adding/deleting documents from the index.

6.7 Query transformations (1/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.7 Query transformations

Rewrite or decompose the user query before retrieval. Three techniques:

1. Query expansion / rewriting: an LLM generates several alternate queries (few-shot prompt), each sent for retrieval.

2. SubQuestionQueryEngine: decomposes a complex query into sub-questions, each aimed at a specific data source (a QueryEngineTool), runs them, then synthesizes the final answer. Suited to compare/contrast, multi-part, and multi-document questions.

← Previous45 / 64Next →
6.7 Query transformations (2/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 6. Advanced RAG: Pre-Retrieval & Indexing › 6.7 Query transformations

3. HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings): the LLM writes a hypothetical answer; that text is embedded and used for the search. A hypothetical answer is semantically closer to real answers than the question is. It is zero-shot (no labels or fine-tuning) and performs comparably to fine-tuned retrievers. The generated document may contain inaccuracies, but the embedding only has to land in the right neighborhood. Paper: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels.

TechniqueUse when
Query expansionUsers articulate poorly; you need broader recall
SubQuestionQueryEngineMulti-part or cross-source questions
HyDEVague or broad queries; better query-document embedding alignment

7. Advanced RAG: Post-Retrieval & Other Techniques RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 7. Advanced RAG: Post-Retrieval & Other Techniques

Setup for these notebooks: sample 10 documents per author, chunk with SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=256, chunk_overlap=16), ingest into an in-memory Qdrant collection (QDRANT_URL = ":memory:"), create_index(from_where="vector_store", ...). Same code as sections 4 and 6.

Order of operations in a LlamaIndex query: ingestion → indexing → retrieval → reranking → post-processing → response generation. Reranking reorders nodes (most relevant first); post-processing transforms or filters nodes (drop low scores, replace text, compress). Both run on retrieved nodes before the LLM.

← Previous47 / 64Next →
7.1 Node post-processing (1/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 7. Advanced RAG: Post-Retrieval & Other Techniques › 7.1 Node post-processing

A node postprocessor takes the retrieved nodes, transforms or filters them, and returns them, after retrieval and before response synthesis. All subclass BaseNodePostProcessor, so they share one usage pattern. They plug into a query engine, not into as_retriever().

← Previous48 / 64Next →
7.1 Node post-processing (2/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 7. Advanced RAG: Post-Retrieval & Other Techniques › 7.1 Node post-processing

PostprocessorUnder the hoodKey arguments
SimilarityPostprocessorKeep nodes whose score ≥ cutoffsimilarity_cutoff
KeywordNodePostprocessorSkip a node if it lacks required keywords or contains an excluded one (spaCy matching)required_keywords, exclude_keywords, lang
MetadataReplacementPostProcessorSwap node text for a metadata valuetarget_metadata_key
LongContextReorderSort by score desc; even-indexed nodes inserted at the front, odd-indexed appended at the end, so best nodes sit at both endsnone
SentenceEmbeddingOptimizerSplit nodes into sentences, embed, keep top sentences (int(n * percentile_cutoff)) and/or those with similarity ≥ thresholdpercentile_cutoff, threshold_cutoff, context_before/after, tokenizer_fn

Lost in the Middle: LLMs use information at the start or end of a long context best and degrade for facts in the middle (paper: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts). LongContextReorder targets this, useful when top_k is large.

← Previous49 / 64Next →
7.2 Re-ranking RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 7. Advanced RAG: Post-Retrieval & Other Techniques › 7.2 Re-ranking

Reorder retrieved nodes by relevance with a dedicated model. Retrieve many (e.g., similarity_top_k=15), rerank, keep the best top_n. Rerankers use the same usage pattern as postprocessors.

Alternatives with the same pattern: ColBERT rerank (pip install llama-index-postprocessor-colbert-rerank; from llama_index.postprocessor.colbert_rerank import ColbertRerank) and Flag Embedding reranker (pip install llama-index-postprocessor-flag-embedding-reranker; from llama_index.postprocessor.flag_embedding_reranker import FlagEmbeddingReranker). Cohere Rerank is the most popular.

← Previous50 / 64Next →
7.3 FLARE (Forward-Looking Active REtrieval) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 7. Advanced RAG: Post-Retrieval & Other Techniques › 7.3 FLARE (Forward-Looking Active REtrieval)

Most RAG retrieves once. For long-form generation one retrieval is not enough. FLARE retrieves actively during generation, deciding when and what to retrieve (paper: Active Retrieval Augmented Generation).

  1. Predict (look ahead to) the upcoming sentence. 2. Use it as a retrieval query. 3. If it has low-confidence tokens, regenerate it with the retrieved documents. 4. Repeat until the response is complete or max_iterations is hit.
VariantBehavior
FLAREInstructPrompts the LLM with retrieval-encouraging instructions to emit search queries when needed (implemented in LlamaIndex as FLAREInstructQueryEngine)
FLAREDirectUses the LLM's own generated sentence as the query if it contains uncertain tokens

Confidence-based retrieval triggers only when the model lacks knowledge; queries can be masked sentences (implicit) or generated questions (explicit).

Other FLAREInstructQueryEngine options: llm, instruct_prompt, lookahead_answer_inserter.

Standard RAGFLARE
RetrievalOnce, before generationRepeatedly, when confidence is low
Hallucination controlLimitedRegenerates low-confidence sentences
LLM callsFewerMany
Best forShort, focused answersLong-form, knowledge-intensive output
← Previous51 / 64Next →
7.4 Prompt compression (LongLLMLingua) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 7. Advanced RAG: Post-Retrieval & Other Techniques › 7.4 Prompt compression (LongLLMLingua)

Shorten the prompt while keeping the relevant information: faster, cheaper, and counters "lost in the middle". Reported gain: up to 21.4 points at 4x compression in RAG settings. Components:

  1. Question-aware coarse-grained compression: relevance of each context to the question based on perplexity.
  2. Question-aware fine-grained compression: contrastive perplexity to keep key tokens (not implemented in LlamaIndex).
  3. Adaptive granular control: different compression ratios per document, driven by the coarse-grained ranking.
  4. Subsequence recovery: maps response subsequences back to the original prompt content.

Requires a GPU: model_name defaults to NousResearch/Llama-2-7b-hf, device_map defaults to "cuda". Other arguments: model_config, open_api_config, metadata_mode.

← Previous52 / 64Next →
7.5 Self-correcting RAG RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 7. Advanced RAG: Post-Retrieval & Other Techniques › 7.5 Self-correcting RAG

Query engines that evaluate their own output and retry when it isn't good enough.

EngineEvaluatorOn failure
RetryQueryEngineRelevancyEvaluatorTransforms the query using the evaluation result and re-queries, up to max_retries
RetrySourceQueryEngineRelevancyEvaluatorEvaluates each source node, builds a new index from only the passing nodes, retries on it
RetryGuidelineQueryEngineGuidelineEvaluator (custom guidelines)Transforms the query from feedback (FeedbackQueryTransformation, optionally resynthesize_query=True) and retries

Each retry engine takes max_retries; if the response passes evaluation it is returned, and if max_retries is 0 the first response is returned unevaluated. Each retry costs extra LLM calls (evaluation plus re-query).

8. Modular RAG RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 8. Modular RAG

Modular RAG treats retrieval and generation as composable modules: hybrid retrievers, agents that choose filters, ensembles of retrievers or query engines, routers. Same setup as sections 6-7 (10 sampled documents per author, SentenceSplitter(256, 16)).

← Previous54 / 64Next →
8.1 Hybrid retrieval (1/3) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 8. Modular RAG › 8.1 Hybrid retrieval

Combines vector search (semantic similarity) with keyword / full-text search (BM25).

SearchStrengthWeakness
Vector (dense)Finds semantically similar text without exact keywordsCan miss exact keyword matches
Keyword (BM25)Fast exact keyword matchingMisses semantic relationships
HybridBothMore setup

Hybrid search needs a docstore (BM25 reads from it) plus a vector store created with enable_hybrid=True.

vector_store_query_mode values

ModeBehavior
defaultPure dense vector search
hybridVector + keyword search; alpha weights them (alpha=0 → BM25 only, alpha=1 → vector only)
semantic_hybridHybrid plus a semantic reranking step
sparseSparse vectors (mostly zeros, good for exact keywords/details); needs a sparse embedding model (e.g., FastEmbed prithvida/Splade_PP_en_v1) and sparse_top_k (nodes fetched from each of the sparse and dense queries)
text_searchExact keyword matches only

similarity_top_k is the final node count after fusion; hybrid_top_k is the top-k for hybrid mode.

← Previous55 / 64Next →
8.1 Hybrid retrieval (2/3) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 8. Modular RAG › 8.1 Hybrid retrieval

Hybrid fusion retriever (QueryFusionRetriever) runs three steps: (1) generate or rewrite several queries from the user query, (2) retrieve with each query across an ensemble of retrievers, (3) fuse and rerank.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): for each unique node, take 1/rank from every list it appears in, sum them, and reorder by that total. Nodes that rank consistently high across retrievers rise to the top, with no extra model or heavy computation (paper: Cormack et al., SIGIR 2009).

Fusion modeHow scores are combined
reciprocal_rerankRRF; best general choice
relative_scoreMin-max scale each retriever's scores to 0-1, weight per retriever, combine
dist_based_scoreLike relative_score but scales using mean and standard deviation (less sensitive to outliers)
simpleReorder by original scores
← Previous56 / 64Next →
8.1 Hybrid retrieval (3/3) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 8. Modular RAG › 8.1 Hybrid retrieval

BM25 + vector with reciprocal rank fusion is one of the most effective, cheapest upgrades to a RAG system.

8.2 Agentic RAG (1/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 8. Modular RAG › 8.2 Agentic RAG

Data agents are LLM-powered workers that go beyond query engines: they read from static data and can also call external APIs and modify state. A data agent needs a reasoning loop and tool abstractions; given a task it decides which tools to call, in what order, with which parameters.

Here the agent turns the user's question into metadata filters + a query against the vector DB (auto-retrieval). Pieces: metadata on nodes (manual known_for plus extractors) → a VectorStoreInfo describing the schema → a Pydantic schema for the tool arguments → a function tool → an agent.

← Previous58 / 64Next →

RAG with LlamaIndex › 8. Modular RAG › 8.2 Agentic RAG

Behavior to note: a full question tends to filter on questions_this_excerpt_can_answer, a "find text that mentions…" prompt on excerpt_keywords, and a named thinker on author.

Lower-level agent API

ComponentRole
AgentRunnerOrchestrator: manages state (conversation memory), creates and maintains tasks, runs steps, exposes the chat interface

8.3 Ensemble retrieval RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 8. Modular RAG › 8.3 Ensemble retrieval

Try several retrieval strategies at once (here: four chunk sizes), merge their results, and rerank. Steps: build a vector index per strategy → wrap each retriever in an IndexNode → put the index nodes in a SummaryIndex (simple list-based structure) → a RecursiveRetriever fans the query out to every retriever → rerank the combined nodes.

(The index node text still says "Llama 2 paper" because the notebook is adapted from the LlamaIndex docs; the wording is only a label.)

Reranking also tells you which strategy matters: compute the reciprocal rank of the first node from each chunk size in the final ranking. Higher MRR means that chunk size tends to rank earlier, i.e., more relevant. In the demo, chunk size 128 ranked highest.

← Previous60 / 64Next →
8.4 Ensemble query engine (1/2) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 8. Modular RAG › 8.4 Ensemble query engine

Run several query engines (top-k vector, keyword table, knowledge graph, etc.) and let an LLM rate each result's relevance and synthesize one answer. Steps: build indexes over the same nodes → query engines with a QA prompt that asks for a relevance score → wrap each as a QueryEngineTool with a clear description → RouterQueryEngine with LLMMultiSelector (the LLM can pick more than one tool) → TreeSummarize combines the answers. A selector can choose a data source, decide between summarization and semantic search, or combine multiple choices.

Comparative analysis of RAG techniques (ARAGOG paper) RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG with LlamaIndex › 9. Wrap-up › Comparative analysis of RAG techniques (ARAGOG paper)

ARAGOG: Advanced RAG Output Grading compared techniques with LlamaIndex abstractions.

AspectDetail
Data423 arXiv papers on AI/LLMs; 107 QA pairs (GPT-4 generated, human validated); detailed analysis on 13 papers plus noisy extras
Runs10 per technique for statistical reliability (ANOVA, then Tukey HSD for pairwise comparisons)
MetricsRetrieval precision (0-1, relevance of retrieved context); answer similarity (0-5, match to reference answer)
TechniquesSentence window retrieval, document summary index, HyDE, multi-query, MMR, Cohere reranker, LLM reranker
ResultFinding
Best retrieval precision and answer similarityHyDE + LLM reranking
Strong, but inconsistent answer similaritySentence window retrieval
ModerateDocument summary index, multi-query
LowerMMR, Cohere reranker

Takeaways: prioritize retrieval precision (it drives faithfulness); answer similarity also depends on the LLM and prompting, not only retrieval. Reasonable baseline: HyDE + LLM reranking; sentence window retrieval for precision-critical use; combine hybrid search + reranking + query transformation; evaluate with repeated runs and significance tests. Faithfulness needs the LLM to understand retrieved meaning, not just match keywords.

2.5 LangGraph building blocks (1/3) LangGraph

LangGraph › 2. Concepts: Chatbots, Agentic AI, State vs Memory, LangGraph › 2.5 LangGraph building blocks

LangGraph (LangChain ecosystem) is a workflow orchestration engine for stateful multi-agent apps: it manages agent interactions and state, integrates LLMs, tools and third-party apps, and streams intermediate results.

  • Nodes: LLM node (analyzes prompt, creates actions), tool node (runs function tools), action node (invokes other agents), logic node (custom code).
  • Edges: basic (sequential) and conditional (routes on a check). Start and End blocks mark entry and exit.
  • Agent state: shared structure nodes read and write. Data moves through state, not through edges.

3.1 What ReAct is LangGraph

LangGraph › 3. ReAct Agent (prebuilt and from scratch) › 3.1 What ReAct is

ReAct = Reason + Act. From a research paper; the LLM drives an iterative loop, which also makes agent actions explainable.

User input → Thought → Action → Observation → repeat until done → Final answer

  1. Thought: the LLM analyzes the input and decides the next step.
  2. Action: the agent runs a tool or computation.
  3. Observation: the LLM checks the result and decides whether more steps are needed.

Course example: a math agent with tools find_sum and find_product. "What is the sum of 2 and 3?" calls find_sum(2, 3) and returns 5.

5.1 When to build a custom graph LangGraph

LangGraph › 5. Custom Orders Agent (hand-built graph) › 5.1 When to build a custom graph

create_react_agent is a ready-made graph. Build your own StateGraph for control over nodes, edges, state and routing. Nodes communicate through agent state, not edges.

Use case: Orders chatbot over data/Laptop Orders.csv (Order ID, Product Ordered, Quantity Ordered, Delivery Date) that gets order details and updates quantities (DataFrame standing in for an RDBMS).

Graph: orders_llm → conditional edge (tool call?) → yes: orders_tools → back to orders_llm; no: END. The LLM loops until it answers without a tool call.

5.3 The custom agent (native tool calling) (1/3) LangGraph

LangGraph › 5. Custom Orders Agent (hand-built graph) › 5.3 The custom agent (native tool calling)

  • State: Annotated[list[AnyMessage], operator.add]. The operator.add reducer appends each node's returned messages instead of overwriting.
  • model.bind_tools(tools) lets the LLM emit structured tool_calls.
  • is_tool_call is the conditional edge: {True: "orders_tools", False: END}.
  • call_tools wraps each result in a ToolMessage with the tool_call_id, which matches results to requests.
  • The system prompt is prepended on every LLM call, not stored in state.
  • compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver()) gives per-thread_id memory.

9. Gotchas & Version Notes LangGraph

LangGraph › 9. Gotchas & Version Notes

  • Versions matter. The notebooks pin langgraph==0.2.59, langchain==0.3.12. create_react_agent(..., state_modifier=...) is the argument name in that version; newer LangGraph releases renamed it to prompt. Match the pinned versions when running the course code.
  • Tool docstrings are the tool's API for the LLM. Vague docstrings give wrong tool choices. Retriever tool description plays the same role.
  • Tool return conventions: the course uses -1 for "not found" so the LLM can tell the user clearly.
  • Annotated[list, operator.add] is what makes state updates append. Without a reducer a node's return value replaces the field.
  • Thread ID = conversation. MemorySaver is in-process and lost on restart. Reuse the same thread_id for follow-ups, use a new one per user conversation. The router graph has no checkpointer and forwards the thread ID to inner agents.
  • Agent state vs conversation memory (section 2.4): per-prompt, internal, discarded vs session-long, owned by the chatbot, persisted.
  • Cap loops. ReAct and reflection both loop; use an iteration limit (max_iterations, message-count check) to avoid infinite cycles.
  • Router prompt/key coupling. A router that returns the raw LLM text as the edge key breaks on any wording drift. Constrain the output to one word, or normalize in find_route.
  • Streaming vs invoke. stream(..., stream_mode="values") shows each step as it happens; invoke returns only the final state.
  • Notebook quirks: call_tools returns inside its for loop (handles only the first tool call); chunk settings differ between lesson (overlap=100, k=3) and notebook (overlap=256, k=1); the notebooks contain a hard-coded Azure key, so use your own environment variables.

Overview Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › Overview

Pretrained transformers from Hugging Face shorten the model lifecycle and allow quick deployment. The course covers question answering, summarization, text generation (chat, translation), and transfer learning for sentiment analysis. It does not cover transformer math or building transformers from scratch.

2. Question Answering Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 2. Question Answering

Extractive QA: given a context and a question, the model returns the span of the context that best answers it. Flow: the corpus is tokenized and vectorized, the question goes through the same steps, the model compares them, scores candidate answers, and returns the best one.

Open Domain (ODQA)Closed Domain (CDQA)
ScopeAny topic (Google Search)Specific domain (pharma, product FAQs)
CorpusVery large (all of Wikipedia)Limited, domain-specific
Model sizeLargeSmaller
AccuracyLowerHigher
CostHigher training and inferenceLower
Use casePublic searchEnterprise self-service, product Q&A
