QA pipeline Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 2. Question Answering › QA pipeline

Model: deepset/minilm-uncased-squad2 (BERT-based, trained on SQuAD 2.0). pipeline(...) downloads it to the local cache.

Output fields: score (confidence 0 to 1), start/end (character positions in the context), answer (extracted text).

Gotcha: a low score (0.26 here) signals a weak answer. Use the score as a threshold to filter out low-confidence answers before returning them to users.

← Previous4 / 26Next →
SQuAD metric Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 2. Question Answering › SQuAD metric

Regular accuracy often does not fit NLP outputs. The SQuAD metric (Stanford Question Answering Dataset) scores predicted answers against correct ones and reports Exact Match and F1, per answer and for a whole dataset. It comes from Hugging Face's evaluate package.

Workflow: build an evaluation set (context, questions, correct answers), run it through the model, compare predictions with the correct answers using the metric.

  • Exact match gives F1 = 100, no overlap gives 0, partial overlap reflects token overlap.
  • Cumulative keys: exact (percent exact matches, 1 of 3 = 33.33), f1 (average F1), total (answers evaluated), HasAns_exact / HasAns_f1 (only questions that have answers).
← Previous5 / 26Next →
3. Text Summarization Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 3. Text Summarization

Condenses a large text into a short summary that keeps the context and key points (documents, meeting transcripts, article/email previews).

ExtractiveAbstractive
HowScores sentences, extracts the top ones verbatimGenerates new human-like sentences capturing the gist
CompletenessSome information may be left outBetter at overall meaning
ComplexitySimpler to train and useMore complex to build
ExampleConversation summary, skipping small talkReducing large documents to concise new text

BART (Bidirectional Auto-Regressive Transformers, from Facebook): encoder-decoder like T5. Encoder is BERT-like, decoder is GPT-like. Works for summarization, QA, and generation.

Default model: sshleifer/distilbart-cnn-12-6 (DistilBART, a distilled BART, BartForConditionalGeneration; 12 encoder layers, 6 decoder layers). Real input may need cleanup of formatting first.

Output keeps three of the original sentences (life, ocean 71%, land 29%).

  • min_length / max_length: min and max tokens in the summary. Model defaults are 56 and 142; tune per use case.

ROUGE score Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 3. Text Summarization › ROUGE score

Accuracy and F1 do not work well for summaries. ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) measures similarity between the generated summary and the reference text. It is a family of metrics scored from 0.0 (no overlap) to 1.0 (perfect match):

MetricMeasures
ROUGE-1Unigram overlap
ROUGE-2Bigram overlap (phrase-level meaning)
ROUGE-LLongest common subsequence
ROUGE-LsumSentence-level ROUGE-L

Scores near 0.6 indicate a good summary here. Try examples to find the threshold for your use case, then track it on production inference. ROUGE is also used to compare summarization models or configurations.

4. Natural Language Generation Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 4. Natural Language Generation

NLG produces text that is meant to be indistinguishable from human writing, from a phrase to several paragraphs. It uses the transformer decoder stack (GPT, BART, T5). Use cases: content creation, chatbots and voice bots, translation, personalized emails, text reports from structured data, product descriptions. Three tasks below: content generation, conversation, translation.

GPT-2 uses only the decoder stack and can produce several different continuations from the same seed sentence. Model: gpt2.

  • num_return_sequences: number of separate outputs from the same input.
  • max_new_tokens: max tokens generated beyond the input.
  • set_seed(): reproducible output.

Hugging Face Transformers › 4. Natural Language Generation › Conversation generation

A bot understands the user's intent and replies, can ask follow-up questions, and keeps conversation history as context. Real bots combine services: Named Entity Recognition, Sentiment Analysis, Question Answering, and Text Generation. Example: order-status request, NER extracts the order number, backend lookup, text generation produces the reply.

Model: Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (small instruction-tuned model that answers general questions and asks follow-ups).

← Previous11 / 26Next →
Machine translation Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 4. Natural Language Generation › Machine translation

Translates with attention to context, not word-for-word. Typical architectures: GPT-3 and T5. Challenges: many languages and variants, and large models (smaller custom models can be built for narrow cases). Applications: real-time speech translation, enterprise documents, multilingual customer service, multilingual text analytics.

Here an explicit tokenizer and model are used instead of the translation pipeline, which helps when a tokenizer/model combination is not supported by the pipeline. Model: t5-base. T5 is text-to-text: one model does summarization, QA, and translation, chosen by a task prefix on the input.

  • return_tensors="pt": PyTorch tensors. input_ids: IDs into the embedding matrix. max_length: output token limit. skip_special_tokens=True: strips <pad>, </s> from the output.

5. Transfer Learning (Sentiment Model) Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 5. Transfer Learning (Sentiment Model)

Transfer learning: take a base model from the Hub, fine-tune it on a small task-specific dataset, and train a classifier (or sequence generator) on top. Encoder/decoder weights can be frozen or retrained. This turns days of base training into minutes.

5.1 Load the dataset Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 5. Transfer Learning (Sentiment Model) › 5.1 Load the dataset

poem_sentiment is in Apache Arrow format, downloaded and cached like models. Schema: id, verse_text, label. Splits: train (892), validation (105), test (104). For your own data, convert to a Hugging Face Dataset (see 5.5).

← Previous14 / 26Next →
5.2 Tokenize and encode Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 5. Transfer Learning (Sentiment Model) › 5.2 Tokenize and encode

The data is already clean, so go straight to tokenizing. Use the tokenizer class that matches the checkpoint (DistilBertTokenizer).

Tokenizing adds two features, input_ids and attention_mask:

  • input_ids: IDs from the embedding matrix. Start with 101 (begin of string), end with 102 (end of string), right-padded with zeros to the max length.
  • attention_mask: 1 for real tokens, 0 for padding. The model only attends to tokens with mask 1.
← Previous15 / 26Next →
5.3 Model architecture and freezing Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 5. Transfer Learning (Sentiment Model) › 5.3 Model architecture and freezing

Loading a base checkpoint copies its architecture, hyperparameters, and weights, so nothing is built from scratch. num_labels sets the size of the new classification head.

Freezing a layer means its weights are not updated in backpropagation, which keeps what the base model already learned.

Layer 0 is the DistilBERT encoder (most parameters), then pre_classifier and classifier (Dense). Layers can also be added, inserted, or removed through the layers object.

Without a pipeline you handle pre-processing (tokenize, convert to tensors) and post-processing (labels from logits) yourself. Dataset.from_dict() converts data in any format into a Hugging Face Dataset.

When to customize a pretrained model Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 6. Deploying Models in Production › When to customize a pretrained model

  • Low accuracy out of the box.
  • Domain vocabulary or grammar (medical, legal, tweets, regional variants).
  • Reduce size by cutting encoder/decoder layers, then check performance still holds.

Transfer learning guidance: small, specific datasets covering all scenarios equally; accurately labeled, high-quality data; change the architecture one step at a time and check impact; validate across scenarios; monitor production for drift and bias; retrain as new data arrives.

← Previous20 / 26Next →
Model compression Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 6. Deploying Models in Production › Model compression

Goal: smaller trained model for production. Two routes: fewer layers, nodes, and parameters; or smaller storage types (FLOAT32 to integers). Both cut math operations, memory, and compute.

TechniqueDescription
QuantizationConverts floats to smaller types such as integers. Supported out of the box by most frameworks
PruningRemoves selected nodes and connections
Low Rank ApproximationReduces data dimensions by dropping unneeded information
Knowledge DistillationAdvanced. Shrinks the model while retaining learned knowledge (DistilBERT, DistilBART)
Neural Architecture SearchFinds the best architecture for a problem (compute intensive)

After compression, retest on the original test/validation data. Start with quantization and pruning before the advanced options, which need more time and expertise.

← Previous21 / 26Next →
Serving multiple models Hugging Face Transformers

Hugging Face Transformers › 6. Deploying Models in Production › Serving multiple models

PatternHow it worksExample
Chain (sequential)Output of one model feeds the nextChatbot: intent detection, then NER, then QA
Parallel (independent)Same input goes to all models at once, outputs are collectedReview analysis: sentiment, topic extraction, obscenity detection
Alternate (conditional)Condition picks one modelLanguage detector picks the matching translator into English

Best practices: test models together as one solution; parallelize where possible to cut latency; validate that one model's output suits the next; exit chains early when intent confidence is too low; scale each model independently; measure end-to-end latency.

3.3 The four steps (every task uses the same loop) Fine-Tuning LLMs

Fine-Tuning LLMs › 3. FLAN-T5 & the 4-Step Prompting Workflow › 3.3 The four steps (every task uses the same loop)

  1. Define the prompt (task prefix matters). 2. Tokenize it. 3. model.generate. 4. Decode with the tokenizer.

Parameters: return_tensors="tf" (TensorFlow tensors), max_length=512 (model's input token limit), truncation=True (cut long inputs), padding=True (pad short ones), num_beams=5 (beam search width: higher = better quality, slower), early_stopping=True (stop when beams finish), skip_special_tokens=True when decoding. Output max_length is tuned per task (summarise 150, translate 40, QA 50). temperature controls randomness (0 = deterministic, 1 = creative) and only applies with do_sample=True.

5. Few-Shot & In-Context Learning Fine-Tuning LLMs

Fine-Tuning LLMs › 5. Few-Shot & In-Context Learning

Few-shot learning = put worked examples in the prompt so the model learns task format and output style. In-context learning (ICL) is essentially the same technique. Works across tasks and helps smaller models most. No weights change (contrast with Sections 8+).

Rules of thumb: 2–3 high-quality examples, separated by blank lines, matching the desired output format; mind the 512-token input limit.

8. Transfer Learning vs Fine-Tuning Fine-Tuning LLMs

Fine-Tuning LLMs › 8. Transfer Learning vs Fine-Tuning

Transfer learningFine-tuning
AnalogyChef adapting existing skills to a new kitchenChef learning an entirely new cuisine
TechnicalPre-trained model + new task-specific head; base mostly frozenUpdate all weights and biases on the new dataset
ApproachKeep structure intact, train only new componentsFurther train the whole model
Use whenSimilar tasks, little data/compute, quick adaptation, prototypingDifferent task/domain shift, large dataset, maximum accuracy, specialised domain

Decision rule from the lecture (high task similarity + small data → frozen transfer; medium similarity + high compute → progressive fine-tuning; low similarity + large data → full fine-tuning; otherwise partial transfer):

Success factors: model pre-trained on a similar domain; freeze according to task similarity; lower learning rate when fine-tuning; start frozen, then unfreeze gradually; quality labelled data; compare against a baseline.

12.1 PEFT in one view Fine-Tuning LLMs

Fine-Tuning LLMs › 12. PEFT & LoRA Concepts › 12.1 PEFT in one view

Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) modifies a small subset of parameters (or adds small modules) instead of retraining the whole model, getting strong task performance with limited data and compute.

Analogy: full fine-tuning = reworking the recipe; transfer learning = adding a sauce (new head); PEFT = specialised tools (adapters) that enhance the dish without altering the recipe.

Traditional fine-tuningTransfer learningPEFT
Parameters updatedAllNew layers + some base layersSmall adapter modules only
Data neededLargeMediumSmall
Compute / training timeHigh / longMedium / mediumLow / fast
Storage per taskFull model copyModified model per taskBase model + small adapters

Advantages: works with limited data, lower cost, faster training, one shared base model with swappable per-task adapters. Lecture rules of thumb: ~0.1–1% of parameters trained, ~10x faster, ~5x less memory, 95–99% of full fine-tuning quality. Use PEFT when compute or data is limited, you serve many tasks from one model, or you are prototyping.

← Previous45 / 76Next →

Fine-Tuning LLMs › 12. PEFT & LoRA Concepts › 12.2 Adapters (the idea LoRA refines)

A bottleneck module inserted into a transformer layer: down-project → non-linearity → up-project, added back through a residual connection.

12.3 LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): the math Fine-Tuning LLMs

Fine-Tuning LLMs › 12. PEFT & LoRA Concepts › 12.3 LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): the math

  • Keep the original weight matrix W frozen (e.g. 512×512 = 262,144 parameters).
  • Learn a low-rank update ΔW = A × B where A is (in × r) and B is (r × out) and r (rank) is tiny. Output = W·x + (x·A·B) (scaled by alpha / r in the PyTorch version).
  • For r = 1: 512×1×2 = 1,024 trainable parameters, ~256x reduction.
  • B is initialised to zeros in the PyTorch version, so training starts exactly at the pre-trained behaviour.

PyTorch LoRA wrapper (freezes the original layer, scales by alpha/rank):

14.2 The Keras LoRALayer (1/2) Fine-Tuning LLMs

Fine-Tuning LLMs › 14. LoRA in TensorFlow: Implementation & Experiments › 14.2 The Keras LoRALayer

output = dense(x) + (x @ A) @ B: A is (input_dim × rank), B is (rank × units), both trainable; the wrapped dense layer is frozen. rank is the bottleneck width (default 4).

  • inputs @ A @ B is the low-rank update; original_output + lora_output is W·x + A·B·x; the original weights stay non-trainable.
  • Note: unlike the PyTorch version in Section 12.3, both matrices use random_normal here (no zero-init for B) and there is no alpha/rank scaling.
  • Lecture sketches (explore_model_layers, apply_lora_to_model, recursive_lora_replacement) say in their own comments that real layer replacement "requires more complex model reconstruction"; the notebook approach below is the working version.

Find the dense layers, then freeze everything but LoRA. Inspect the structure first:

SettingEffect

17.2 Advanced topics and trends Fine-Tuning LLMs

Fine-Tuning LLMs › 17. Course Wrap-Up & Where the Field Is Heading › 17.2 Advanced topics and trends

  • Few-shot / zero-shot learning: good performance from minimal examples, better generalisation, lower data barrier (see Section 5).
  • Federated learning: data stays on local devices and only model updates are shared; privacy-preserving, decentralised; used for healthcare, on-device mobile learning and cross-organisation collaboration.
  • Multimodal AI: text + image (visual QA, captioning), text + audio (speech-to-text with context); encode each modality, fuse features, feed one model:
  • Efficient training/deployment: pruning (remove unneeded parameters), quantisation (lower numeric precision), knowledge distillation (teach a smaller model); benefits are lower latency, lower cost, edge deployment.
  • Next topics named in the course: chatbot cloud deployment, model optimisation (distillation, quantisation, pruning), scalable production AI services, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Constitutional AI, Mixture of Experts.

Model Context Protocol 65 cards Hands-on MCP with agentic AI
1. Core Concepts and Architecture Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 1. Core Concepts and Architecture

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a simple protocol that gives any data source or software a natural-language interface for AI models. Anthropic open sourced it in November 2024. It lets a model retrieve data, run tools, use resources beyond its training data, and execute actions from natural-language commands.

Three defining traits:

  • Open source: anyone can build a server; community driven; free to use and modify.
  • Client agnostic: any LLM-powered app can hook in (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor); no vendor lock-in.
  • Protocol based: standardized communication that supplies context and enables interaction with external resources.

USB-C analogy: before USB-C every device had its own connector and standard. MCP is USB-C for AI: one universal protocol between AI apps and data, working with any MCP-compatible app.

1 / 65Next →
Components Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 1. Core Concepts and Architecture › Components

The request flows down the chain and the result returns up the same chain.

ComponentRoleExamples
MCP HostApplication that wants data accessClaude Desktop, Cursor
MCP ClientExtension inside the host that maintains the protocol connectionBuilt into the host
MCP ServerPackage that exposes resources/tools/promptsWeather MCP, GitHub MCP, your code
Data source / toolThe thing being accessedDatabase, API, file system

Flow: User -> AI chat app (host + client) -> MCP server -> data source/tool, then back.

MCP servers are language-agnostic: function calling where the functions are plugins. SDKs exist for Python and TypeScript. The server can run locally on your machine or be published for others.

Example 1: Weather MCP Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 3. Examples, Use Cases and Finding Servers › Example 1: Weather MCP

Prompt: "My family's going on a two-day roadtrip to Squamish tomorrow. What clothes should we bring to fit with the weather?"

Point: language models have no access to current weather; MCP bridges that gap.

Multiple servers, mixed languages, env vars Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 4. Using MCP Servers in Claude Desktop › Multiple servers, mixed languages, env vars

Each server is a uniquely named object inside mcpServers, separated by commas.

  • command is the executable: uvx (Python package runner), npx (Node package runner), or any executable.
  • args: for npx, -y auto-confirms, then the package name, then (for filesystem) the allowed directories.
  • env passes environment variables such as API keys. Generic form: "env": {"API_KEY": "...", "BASE_URL": "..."}.
  • The same JSON structure works across languages, clients, and operating systems, so configs are portable between clients.

Official reference servers: fetch (Python), filesystem, github, slack, google-maps, postgres (TypeScript). Repo: github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers.

Tool anatomy Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 5. Building a Python MCP Server (FastMCP) › Tool anatomy

  • @mcp.tool() registers the function as a tool.
  • The docstring is a prompt for the LLM. It tells the model when and how to use the tool and what each argument means.
  • async functions with type hints and clear parameter names.
  • Return raw data, do not pre-format it. The LLM processes raw data better, can pick out what matters, and writes the natural-language answer itself.

Complete server.py (final version; three tools) Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 5. Building a Python MCP Server (FastMCP) › Complete server.py (final version; three tools)

Helper plus tools. get_location exists because LLMs may guess wrong coordinates; geocoding gives accurate ones. The first-pass get_current_weather/get_forecast in the lesson (string error messages) are earlier steps of this file.

The helper returns None on any failure, so each tool returns an error value instead of crashing the server.

The exercise file open-meteo-weather/server.py is the same helper with two tools, but its get_forecast formats the daily arrays into a text string (the "don't pre-format" anti-pattern above) and its get_current_weather returns the raw dict.

Meaning: the app cannot find uv because the config uses the bare command uv, which is not on its PATH. Fix: get the absolute path (which uv or where uv, for example /Users/your-username/.local/bin/uv or C:\Users\your-username\.local\bin\uv.exe), put it in command, and restart Claude fully.

Logs and debugging workflow Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 6. Testing with MCP Inspector and Troubleshooting › Logs and debugging workflow

  • Settings -> Developer shows each server's status ("Failed"/"Disconnected"). Open Logs Folder has one file per server, such as mcp-server-weather.log.
  • Log example for this error: [ERROR] UV returns error no entity, [ERROR] spawn uv ENOENT, [ERROR] Unable to start MCP server.
  • Workflow: check status, open the log, find [ERROR] lines, check claude_desktop_config.json (command path, args, env), run the command manually in a terminal (/path/to/uv run server.py; if it works, the config is the problem), then restart and verify.
  • Other tools: Chrome DevTools (client interactions), server-side logging, Claude Desktop logs, and modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/debugging.

Config best practice: absolute paths for command, --directory for the project, and env for secrets (full example in section 7). Checklist when a server fails: status, logs, absolute command path, manual run, venv/dependencies, API keys, restart, Inspector first.

7. Running Local Servers in Claude Desktop Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 7. Running Local Servers in Claude Desktop

Published servers (npm/PyPI) need simple args such as the package name. Local servers (on your disk) need complex args because Claude Desktop must create a virtual environment and install dependencies itself. Claude Desktop is a good test bed before publishing.

The args array is this terminal command:

PartPurpose
command (absolute path to uv)Find with which uv / where uv
uv runStart uv
--with mcp[cli]Add the MCP CLI to a temporary environment
mcp runRun the server via the MCP CLI
last argAbsolute path to server.py (get it with pwd in the project)

What happens: Claude reads the config, runs the command, uv creates a temporary venv, installs mcp[cli], runs the server, and the server is ready. The LLM app is running software inside itself.

Mix local and published servers freely in one config (local weather with uv run ..., plus fetch via uvx, as in section 4).

Blast radius Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 9. Security › Blast radius

Blast radius is the potential scope of damage or unintended consequences when AI agents execute actions on your computer. "The blast radius of AI agents and MCPs is unlimited until we limit it." Even if you read a server's code you may not know what is really happening on it.

RiskExample
Unintended actionsDeleting files instead of reading them
Hidden operationsCode runs behind the scenes, data manipulated without awareness
Excessive accessFull file system access when only read is needed
LLM extensionsThe model uses the server in unexpected ways
← Previous51 / 65Next →
As a user, before installing an MCP Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 9. Security › As a user, before installing an MCP

  • Trust the developers: who built it, is the source reputable, is the code open source and reviewed?
  • Understand capabilities: read-only retrieval is safest; write, modify/delete, and execute need much more trust.
  • Review permissions, read the docs, test in a safe environment, and monitor actions during use.

New paradigm Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 9. Security › New paradigm

Traditional rule: never trust the user. MCP rule: never trust the user or the LLM. The LLM is now effectively the user making requests, so validate and limit permissions for AI requests like human ones.

Project Documenter example Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 10. Using MCP in Cursor and the Documenter Workflow › Project Documenter example

Automates documentation: read project files, summarize them into project.md, generate/update README.md, and assess README quality. Real implementation: mcp-server-examples/projectDocumenter (TypeScript, SDK ^1.7.0, zod, fs/promises).

KindNameBehavior
Toolgenerate-project-mdCollect project code into project.md, respecting .gitignore (adds project.md to it)
Tooldocument-projectGenerate project.md and a README; updateExisting boolean defaults to true
Toolupdate-readmeWrite given content to README.md
Toolassess-readme-qualityReview the README against modern documentation standards
Resourcesproject-md://{projectPath}, readme://{projectPath}Read the files, or return a "not found" text
Promptsgenerate-readme, assess-readmeInstruct the model to read project.md first, then write or evaluate the README (criteria: comprehensiveness, clarity, structure, accuracy, usefulness)

Pattern shared by every tool: validate that projectPath is a directory (fs.stat), return isError: true with a message on failure, and wrap the work in try/catch.

(Condensed from the exercise file, which wraps each step in nested try/catch.) The server starts with new StdioServerTransport() inside an async main() that logs to console.error (stdout is reserved for the protocol) and exits with code 1 on failure.

test-server.sh builds with npm run build, creates a temp project with sample files (or uses a path you pass), and launches npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node dist/index.js so you can try the generate-readme prompt/tools.

Development workflow for such an MCP: identify a repetitive task (README creation, 30-60 minutes per project), design the tools (read, write, validate), implement with least privilege (read-only where possible, validated paths, limited directories, sanitized inputs), test extensively (normal use, traversal, invalid input, edge cases, adversarial prompts), deploy and monitor (log operations, review unexpected behavior).

Security and responsibility framework Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol › 11. Conclusion: Mindset and Responsibility › Security and responsibility framework

Unlimited potential comes with unlimited risk, so limit it at every stage: design, implement, test, deploy, monitor. MCPs should follow three principles:

  1. Do what they are supposed to do: clear purpose and scope.
  2. Do not do what they are not supposed to do: explicit restrictions.
  3. Do not put users at risk: validate and sanitize input, encrypt sensitive data, log security events, require approval for risky actions, give clear errors, never expose credentials.

"When you build MCPs, you are quite literally building the future for other people." Users trust you to protect their data and privacy, act in their interest, be transparent, handle errors, and stay reliable.

PowerResponsibility
Access to user dataProtect privacy
Execute on user's computerEnsure safety
Automate user tasksVerify correctness
Make decisionsProvide transparency
Scale capabilitiesMaintain control

  • During development: least privilege, validate inputs, handle errors, add logging, test adversarial prompts, review security implications.
  • Before deployment: test thoroughly, document capabilities and limits, give usage instructions, set up monitoring, plan incident response.
  • After deployment: monitor usage and errors, respond to security issues quickly, update from feedback, maintain docs, communicate changes.

Start small and test; expand gradually while keeping security in focus; push boundaries; share what you learn; build responsibly. Balance mindsets: "is it possible?" becomes "let's find out", but "can we?" must be followed by "should we?" and "does it protect users?". Innovation plus responsibility is sustainable progress.

Amazon Bedrock 17 cards Building AI applications with Amazon Bedrock
1. What Bedrock Is Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock › 1. What Bedrock Is

Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed AWS service with a unified API to many foundation models (FMs) from different providers (Anthropic Claude, Amazon Titan, Mistral and others). No infrastructure to manage. You can pick model variants, fine-tune, and use everything through one API.

Course flow: chat interface, then agents, then knowledge bases (RAG), then agents + knowledge bases, then programmatic access (Bash, then Rust or Go). The console is the fastest way to learn new features: experiment there first, code later. Instructor: Noah Gift.

Cost optimization is a recurring theme: move an expensive prompt from a high-cost model to a cheaper one with equivalent results (see section 4).

Amazon Bedrock › 2. Core Features and Concepts

Foundation modelsPre-trained, ready to use. Text, image, embeddings, analysis. Each model needs explicit access authorization before use

4. Compare Mode and the Dracula Pattern Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock › 4. Compare Mode and the Dracula Pattern

Compare Mode runs the same prompt against two models side by side (quality, speed, cost, style). Setup: Playground > Chat, select the first model and system prompt, click Compare Mode, select a second model, paste the same system prompt, close both config panels, then type a prompt. Each model's config panel can be toggled independently.

Example system prompt used on both models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 vs Claude 3 Haiku):

Techniques in that prompt: placeholders for task/input/output, a length limit, "just code", a required one-line comment, and a working compilable example with expected output. A concrete code example beats natural-language description. Reliability ranks: natural language only (low), plus format instructions (medium), plus working code example (high).

AspectClaude 3.5 SonnetClaude 3 Haiku
Code qualityCorrect, reproducibleCorrect but missing elements and formatting issues
Prompt adherenceFollows all instructions, consistent across "add", "subtract"Varies per prompt, needs prompt refinement
CostHigherLower
SpeedSlowerFaster

This is a classic engineering tradeoff: best performance now, cheaper later. Other factors: energy use, carbon footprint, latency, reliability.

← Previous4 / 17Next →
The Dracula Pattern (cloud to cloud) Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock › 4. Compare Mode and the Dracula Pattern › The Dracula Pattern (cloud to cloud)

You "suck the logic out" of the better model and move it to a cheaper one through prompt refinement. Develop once on premium, optimize for production on cheaper.

  1. Premium development. Build a robust prompt on Claude 3 Opus / 3.5 Sonnet. Document it. Add validation (XML, JSON, YAML or compilable code).
  2. Transfer testing. Use Compare Mode or API calls (for example a Rust CLI). Find quality gaps.
  3. Iterative refinement. Ask the premium model to rewrite the prompt so the cheaper model (Haiku) produces the same output. Repeat, validating with structured formats.
  4. Deploy on the cheaper model with the optimized prompt. Prompt routing in Bedrock can pick models automatically.

Rule: treat prompts as software, not human language. Validate with JSON, XML, linting and unit tests.

← Previous5 / 17Next →
The Dracula Pattern (cloud to local) Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock › 4. Compare Mode and the Dracula Pattern › The Dracula Pattern (cloud to local)

Same process, but the target is a free local model (Ollama with Qwen 2.5 Coder). Test on Bedrock Claude first, move working prompts to Ollama, refine while monitoring quality loss, iterate until local matches cloud.

Cloud (Bedrock)Local (Ollama)
Cost modelPay per call (variable)Pay per server (fixed hardware and power)
HardwareAWS managedYour own, CPU or NVIDIA GPU
InternetRequiredNot needed after setup
Data privacyData leaves your networkData stays local
UpdatesAutomaticManual

Use local for: lower API cost at high volume, privacy, legal or health compliance, offline use, batch workflows (CPU may be enough; use an NVIDIA GPU for low-latency inference).

PitfallConsequence
Skipping the cloud testing phaseNo baseline to compare against
Underestimating hardwareSlow inference, poor UX
Not documenting prompt changesCannot reproduce or debug regressions
Treating prompts as natural languageNon-deterministic output
Not monitoring quality during transferUndetected degradation

5. Deployment Choices and GenAI Misconceptions Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock › 5. Deployment Choices and GenAI Misconceptions

No single perfect option. Choose per workload and proxy between systems:

  • Complex or high-quality: premium Bedrock model (Opus, Sonnet).
  • Simple or high-volume: cheaper Bedrock model (Haiku).
  • Privacy-sensitive, offline or batch: local Ollama.
FactorPremium cloudCheaper cloudLocal (Ollama)
QualityHighestAcceptableDepends on model and prompt
CostHighest per callLower per callFixed
Compliance (legal, healthcare)May not be allowedMay not be allowedFull control
ControlAWS managedAWS managedFull

Evaluate total cost of ownership, not only per-call price. Hybrid cloud + local is the expected norm, like cloud + on-prem.

AGI is imminentLLMs are pattern-matching systems, similar to clustering that finds and labels patterns
Programming is getting easierMore powerful but more complex. DevOps, build systems, testing, lower cyclomatic complexity, logging, monitoring and continuous delivery matter more
Coding will be fully automatedMore code means more bugs and more complexity. Work shifts from writing to reviewing, testing and maintaining

7. Knowledge Bases and RAG Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock › 7. Knowledge Bases and RAG

A knowledge base is a vector store that grounds responses on your own corpus, restricting the model to your information (eliminating hallucination from outside data).

Workflow:

StepWhat happens
1. Source dataRaw text (for example transcripts made with Whisper CPP)
2. Upload to S3Store raw text in a bucket
3. Sync to vector storeBedrock creates embeddings automatically
4. RAG queryRelevant chunks are retrieved for the question
5. Synthesized responseLLM answers grounded in retrieved data

Re-sync whenever new data lands in S3 to keep the store current.

Create it: Builder Tools > Knowledge Bases > Create, choose data source (S3), Bedrock builds the vector store and embeddings, select a query model (for example Claude 3 Sonnet), test in the built-in interface.

Query modeReturnsUse
Search only (Generate responses OFF)Raw matching chunksVerify data, debug retrieval
Generate responses (ON)Synthesized answerProduction, user-facing (full RAG)

Configuration options: data manipulation, guardrails, query modification, prompt editing, model selection (Sonnet, Haiku, and so on).

9. Agents Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock › 9. Agents

An agent selects a foundation model and does a very specific task. It follows the small-function principle: clear input, one unit of work, return value. Chain simple agents rather than building one complex one.

Agent = Foundation Model + Instructions + (optional) Knowledge Base + (optional) Code Interpreter

Agents can be tested in the console, called by API (Bash, Rust, Lambda), and orchestrated with other agents and knowledge bases. All agents go through the Bedrock Foundation Model Gateway (unified API), so an agent can pick an expensive model for complex tasks and a cheaper one for simple tasks, and you can upgrade models without changing agent code.

CapabilityExample
Text extractionStrip whitespace, format messy input, resize
Summation / computationExtract numbers from text and add them
Code interpreterAnalyze a failed build traceback and generate a fix
Automated testingRun a test, iterate if it fails

CI/CD pattern: build fails with a traceback, Agent 1 extracts the error and relevant code, Agent 2 (code interpreter) generates a small fix and corrects the test, Agent 3 re-runs the build. Pass means done, fail loops back to Agent 1. This try, fail, fix, retry loop is one of the most powerful agentic patterns.

Two core components of modern Bedrock apps: agent (task execution) + knowledge base (grounded data).

Steps:

Agent design principles: keep agents small and specific, return structured output (JSON), ground with knowledge bases, test in the console first, orchestrate with code (Bash to prototype, Rust for production).

Boto3 25 cards Cloud automation with Boto3
1. Core Concepts (Q1-15) (1/3) Boto3

Boto3 › 1. Core Concepts (Q1-15)

Q1. What is boto3 and how does it talk to AWS? The official AWS SDK for Python. It gives a Pythonic interface to AWS APIs (EC2, S3, Lambda and more). It sends HTTP requests signed with your credentials, and botocore does the low-level work.

Q2. boto3.client vs boto3.resource

clientresource
LevelLow-level, maps 1:1 to the API; returns raw dicts/JSONHigher-level, object-oriented (buckets, instances as Python objects)
CoverageAll API operationsSimpler, but not every service or operation
Use whenYou need precise control or the resource abstraction is missingCommon tasks, readable code

Q3. How does boto3 authenticate? Credential sources, in resolution order:

  1. Environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN).
  2. Credentials file (~/.aws/credentials).
  3. IAM roles for EC2 instances or ECS tasks.
  4. AWS CLI SSO or temporary credentials from STS.

You can also pass credentials explicitly in code or select a named profile (Q19).

Q4. Which services can boto3 manage? Most of them:

  • Compute: EC2, Lambda, ECS, EKS
  • Storage: S3, EBS, Glacier
  • Database: DynamoDB, RDS, Redshift
  • Networking: VPC, Route 53, ELB
  • Messaging: SNS, SQS, SES
  • Monitoring: CloudWatch, CloudTrail
  • Management: IAM, CloudFormation, SSM

Q5. Pagination. Use paginators. They follow NextToken (or the equivalent marker) automatically.

1 / 25Next →
1. Core Concepts (Q1-15) (2/3) Boto3

Boto3 › 1. Core Concepts (Q1-15)

Q6. Role of the SDK; how it differs from other AWS SDKs. boto3 is built on botocore and turns low-level HTTP calls into Python methods. The JavaScript, Java and other SDKs do the same job but differ in syntax, conventions and some features.

Q7. Managing resources programmatically. Python scripts automate things like creating EC2 instances, uploading to S3 and configuring IAM. It offers both client and resource interfaces and fits scripts, CI/CD pipelines and serverless functions.

Q8. Why boto3 over the Console or CLI?

  • Automation: scripted, repeatable tasks.
  • Integration with Python tools and workflows.
  • Scale: manage many resources in code.
  • Flexibility: complex logic and conditionals.
  • Programmatic error handling and retries.

Q9. Integration with DevOps tools

  • Kubernetes: manage EKS clusters (node groups) and feed the kubernetes Python client.
  • Terraform: validate or modify Terraform-managed resources.
  • Ansible: generate inventories or pre-provision resources.
  • GitHub Actions: run boto3 scripts in workflows to deploy or manage resources.

Q10. Why IAM roles matter. Roles give temporary, scoped credentials, so keys are not hardcoded. They enforce least privilege and are the secure choice on EC2, Lambda and CI/CD.

Q11. Error handling. API errors raise botocore.exceptions.ClientError. Practices: catch specific errors with try/except, use exponential backoff for throttling, log errors, validate inputs.

Q12. Regions. Regions are isolated geographic areas. Pass region_name to the client or resource, for example boto3.client('s3', region_name='us-east-1'). If omitted, the default region from AWS configuration is used.

Q13. Limitations

← Previous2 / 25Next →
1. Core Concepts (Q1-15) (3/3) Boto3

Boto3 › 1. Core Concepts (Q1-15)

  • Needs knowledge of both AWS APIs and Python.
  • API rate limits (throttling).
  • Some services have limited resource support, so you fall back to client.
  • Needs robust exception handling.
  • Steep learning curve versus the Console.

Q14. Serverless (Lambda). boto3 runs inside Lambda functions to call S3, DynamoDB, SNS and so on. The function's IAM role supplies the credentials. Typical use is event-driven work such as processing S3 uploads or sending notifications.

Q15. What is botocore? The low-level library under boto3. It handles HTTP requests, authentication and response parsing. boto3 adds the friendly interface on top.

7. Scenario-Based Questions (Q71-85) (1/5) Boto3

Boto3 › 7. Scenario-Based Questions (Q71-85)

Q71. GitHub Actions workflow cannot authenticate with AWS. Troubleshooting checklist:

  • Verify AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in GitHub Secrets.
  • Check the IAM user/role has the needed permissions.
  • Check the aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials step config.
  • Check the region.
  • Enable debug logging with ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG: true.
  • Switch to OIDC with an IAM role.

Q72. Timeout listing thousands of S3 objects. Use a paginator and process in batches to limit memory; add retries for transient errors. (Gotcha: MaxItems caps the total results returned, so it truncates rather than speeds up. Use PageSize to tune per-request size.)

Q73. Create an EKS cluster with boto3, then configure it with Ansible.

  1. boto3 creates the cluster and node group and waits for ACTIVE.
  2. boto3 reads the cluster details and generates a kubeconfig.
  3. Ansible uses the kubeconfig and the k8s module to deploy resources.
  4. Run both in a GitHub Actions workflow.

Q74. "Rate Exceeded" when creating many EC2 instances. Exponential backoff with retries, limit concurrent calls, use batch operations (for example MinCount/MaxCount instead of looping).

← Previous21 / 25Next →
7. Scenario-Based Questions (Q71-85) (2/5) Boto3

Boto3 › 7. Scenario-Based Questions (Q71-85)

Q75. Detect Terraform drift. Query AWS, compare with state-file data, report discrepancies (missing resources, modified attributes).

Q76. Credentials exposed in workflow logs.

  • Keep credentials in GitHub Secrets.
  • Use OIDC to assume an IAM role instead of long-term keys (workflow below).
  • Mask sensitive values with ::add-mask::.
  • Do not log sensitive data in scripts.

(OIDC also needs the job to have permissions: id-token: write.)

Q77. Monitor CloudWatch alarms and trigger an Ansible playbook. Query alarms, and on ALARM state run ansible-playbook via subprocess. Run on a schedule in GitHub Actions.

Q78. EKS cluster not scaling as expected. Diagnose:

  • Check node group config (desired, min, max) with boto3.
  • Check that the Cluster Autoscaler is deployed and configured.
  • Review CloudWatch logs.
  • Validate IAM permissions for scaling.
  • Fix by updating the node group scaling config.

Q79. Automate cleanup of unused S3 buckets. List buckets, delete those matching a tag or age, schedule in GitHub Actions, and add safeguards (dry run, confirmation). (Gotchas: delete_bucket fails on non-empty buckets, and get_bucket_tagging raises an error for buckets with no tags.)

Q80. IAM role lacks DynamoDB permissions. Inspect the AccessDenied error, describe the role's policies with boto3, attach a policy allowing the needed dynamodb:* actions (scope it tighter in practice), rerun.

Q82. Slow boto3 script in a workflow. Paginate, cache results to avoid repeat calls, parallelize with ThreadPoolExecutor, use batch APIs.

Q83. Ansible fails because boto3-created resources are not ready yet. Use boto3 waiters, add retries in the playbook, and run boto3 and Ansible as separate dependent workflow steps.

MLOps 36 cards MLOps essentials: model development and integration
Overview MLOps

MLOps › Overview

Scope is build-side MLOps: requirements, data, training, model management, integration. Deployment and monitoring belong to a separate course.

1 / 36Next →
1. Scope & Big Picture MLOps

MLOps › 1. Scope & Big Picture

Build activitiesRun activities
Core MLFeature engineering, training, testing, packagingDeployment, inference
MLOpsRequirements, data/training pipelines, data governance, experiment tracking, integrations, model managementInfrastructure, deployment, serving, monitoring, responsible AI
  • This course covers the build column only.
  • The tools landscape changes fast. Re-evaluate tools when you start a project. AWS, GCP and Azure each have their own MLOps tooling.
← Previous2 / 36Next →
ML life cycle MLOps

MLOps › 2. MLOps Foundations › ML life cycle

A cyclic process. Retraining is triggered by new training data, new user requirements, or model decay.

  1. Requirements: product owner defines the problem.
  2. Design: workflow for executing the project.
  3. Data acquisition: training data made available.
  4. Feature engineering: cleanse, transform, extract features.
  5. Model training.
  6. Testing & evaluation: refine until performance goals are met.
  7. Deployment & inference: used in business workflows.
  8. Data collection: production data is collected and labeled, which becomes new training data (back to step 3).

MLOps is the ecosystem of processes around this cycle, not the model building itself.

← Previous3 / 36Next →
Why ML is harder than software engineering MLOps

MLOps › 2. MLOps Foundations › Why ML is harder than software engineering

  • Software has 2 artifact types: code and records (requirements, design, test plans/results).
  • ML has 4: code, records, data (training, production, labeled) and models (trained artifacts).
  • Artifacts depend on each other: requirements guide data prep, data plus requirements build the model, the model is integrated into code, and code execution produces new training data.
ChallengeDetail
Independent life cyclesEach artifact has its own life cycle but depends on the others
CoordinationDependencies need careful coordination
CollaborationData engineers, ML engineers, product owners must work together
Extra toolingTools and workflows to manage and govern every artifact type
Different skill setsEach artifact needs specialized skills
Integrated workflowNeeds an end-to-end workflow across all life cycles
← Previous4 / 36Next →
DevOps vs MLOps MLOps

MLOps › 2. MLOps Foundations › DevOps vs MLOps

  • DevOps: combines development, testing and operations in one integrated workflow with agile practices and heavy automation. The same team owns all three, unlike traditional separate teams. Cycle: Plan → Code → Build → Test → Release → Deploy → Operate → Monitor → Plan.
  • MLOps: a set of best practices (not a product or technique), supported by automation and tools. It:
    • extends DevOps to building and serving ML;
    • integrates data engineering and model development into the software life cycle;
    • manages all 4 artifact types;
    • enables continuous model development and integration, which shortens time to market;
    • includes deployment, serving, monitoring, performance analytics and feedback.
← Previous5 / 36Next →
MLOps life cycle (software engineering + ML + operations) MLOps

MLOps › 2. MLOps Foundations › MLOps life cycle (software engineering + ML + operations)

Requirements & Design splits into two parallel tracks: non-ML development (APIs, services, DBs, UIs) and data engineering.

ActivityDescription
Requirements & DesignML project needs; design of ML and non-ML parts
Data EngineeringRaw data to usable features
Continuous TrainingBuild and refine the model until it meets requirements
Model GovernanceTrack, evaluate, manage models under a governance framework
Continuous IntegrationIntegrate model with non-ML code at regular intervals (sprint/week)
Package & DeliverBundle model plus non-ML code
Continuous DeploymentDeploy approved packages
Serving / MonitoringServe users; keep the model within performance thresholds
Feedback loopPerformance, drift and bias info goes to model governance and requirements
Data captureProduction feature/label data goes to data engineering for new datasets

If governance decides retraining is needed, it kicks off a new training cycle with new data.

← Previous6 / 36Next →
Principles of MLOps MLOps

MLOps › 2. MLOps Foundations › Principles of MLOps

Goal: an optimal end-to-end workflow that integrates teams, modules and artifacts. Use these as goals when adding any policy, process or tool.

PrincipleMeaning
ModularClear boundaries and ownership; artifacts evolve simultaneously
ContinuousContinuous development, modeling, integration, deployment
AutomatedKey to efficiency and scale
IncrementalQuick time to market via incremental development
End-to-end managedVisibility into the state of all artifacts
ReproducibleArtifact and the code/steps to build it are both managed
ScalableBigger datasets, models, teams, deployments
ObservableMonitoring and diagnosis of workflows and artifacts
TraceableLineage of an artifact back to data and model origins
SecureAccess controls and privacy protection
IntegratedArtifacts move seamlessly across the workflow
ResilientProcess changes don't cascade
TransparentAnyone can understand the inner workings
CollaborativeTeams and artifacts collaborate
OrganizedClear interfaces to outside teams, systems, processes

When to start MLOps MLOps

MLOps › 2. MLOps Foundations › When to start MLOps

StageTeamWhat happensMLOps investment
1. Exploration2–3 engineersStudy ecosystem, explore use cases, build an initial model, pitch strategy to executives. Project may be dropped.None (ad hoc)
2. ExperimentationBigger teamPick one use case, process data, extract features, run training experiments, review against business expectations and cost. Project may be dropped.Incremental: add data/training pipelines as needed; postpone deployment/operations
3. EngineeringFull team (data engineers, scientists, software engineers)Concrete requirements, design workflow, build non-ML software, methodical training/testing/integration, deploy and monitorFull MLOps system (needs people and technology investment)
  • Too early wastes effort if the project is dropped. Too late brings inefficiency and integration pain.

Selecting ML projects MLOps

MLOps › 3. Requirements & Design › Selecting ML projects

The goal is to improve business outcomes (more sales or lower cost). Invest only if benefits outweigh costs.

CriterionDetail
Core business valueMust give strategic differentiation
Training data availabilityGood data including labels is essential; without it projects fail
Technology ecosystemAlgorithms, libraries, frameworks, pre-trained models must exist and be affordable
Budget & teamUnderstaffed projects drag on and outlive their usefulness
Time to marketCompetitors may overtake you
Risk appetiteThe org must accept that performance or cost targets may not be met

Creating requirements MLOps

MLOps › 3. Requirements & Design › Creating requirements

Requirements cover the whole ML application (ML and non-ML parts together). They keep experimentation from drifting.

Non-ML requirementDescription
User experienceGUIs and APIs
FunctionsData collected, transformations, reporting, analytics
DeploymentHow it is served to customers
ScaleMaximum capacity
SecurityProtection from unauthorized access and damage
ServiceabilityObservability and issue handling
ML-specific requirementDescription
Problem statemente.g. "predict customer propensity"
Performance goalsTarget model performance
Operational goalsHow the model is accessed and used
Cost requirementsCost limits for the model

State ML requirements as minimum metric values the model must achieve and maintain, in two dimensions:

Performance / effectivenessOperational / efficiency
Model metricsAccuracy ≥ 90% in trainingLatency ≤ 1 s (90th percentile)
Product metricsConversion rate ≥ 30%Max 500 concurrent sessions

Good metric goals are measurable (include instrumentation requirements), minimum required, and reasonable. Base them on known performance of existing models in the domain, other market technologies, customer expectations, and what is achievable in the time available.

← Previous10 / 36Next →
Designing the ML workflow MLOps

MLOps › 3. Requirements & Design › Designing the ML workflow

An ML workflow is a sequence of processes and iterations that develop, manage and improve ML products.

PracticeDetail
TraceabilityTrack data, models, processing steps; lineage helps measure progress and troubleshoot
Repeatability"Data as code" and "model as code" pipelines; rebuild from scratch with the same results
AutomationWherever possible
Access controlsWho can create, promote, use, discard artifacts
FlexibilityPlug-and-play; replace one part without affecting the rest
OwnershipDefined owner for each pipeline part
AutoscalingScale with data, models, teams

Decoupled sub-pipelines: data engineering, model development, product development, deployment & operations. Decoupling lets each evolve independently, progress in parallel, and be owned by its own sub-team. Tight coupling blocks everyone when one part has a problem.

← Previous11 / 36Next →
Assembling the team MLOps

MLOps › 3. Requirements & Design › Assembling the team

Role% of teamFocus
Data engineers30%Data processing and wrangling
Data scientists20%Building models
Software engineers20%Wrapper services and APIs around the model
ML engineers20%Productizing, scaling, packaging, integrations
Operations engineers10%Deployment and operations
  • Myth: "a couple of data scientists is enough." They are only about 20% of the team.
  • Aim for about 10 engineers for the right balance. With a team of 3, hire people who wear multiple hats.
  • Don't hire everyone upfront. Start with data engineering and data science, add the rest once the model proves viable.
  • Include 1–2 domain experts and 1–2 integration leads.
  • Expect attrition (ML skills are in demand): cross-train and document.
← Previous12 / 36Next →
Choosing tools MLOps

MLOps › 3. Requirements & Design › Choosing tools

The MLOps tools market is nascent, growing, and immature. Examples: open source (MLflow), commercial (Weights & Biases), cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure). Most tools are function-specific, not end-to-end, and no dominant vendor has emerged.

  • Decouple tools from the main pipeline so they can be swapped.
  • Match tools to the use case (classical ML, NLP and vision differ).
  • Try trial/free versions before buying.
  • Check the vendor roadmap and enterprise support.
  • Look for programmability and extensibility.
  • Research the ecosystem at implementation time.
← Previous13 / 36Next →
Managed data pipelines MLOps

MLOps › 4. Data Processing & Management › Managed data pipelines

Data issues are the most common blocker for data scientists, so invest in a managed pipeline early.

Flow: raw data (batch/streaming) → cleanse/filter/validate → transform/enrich → feature store → model training → production → new data → repeat.

What makes a pipeline "managed":

ElementDetail
Engineering life cycleTreat pipeline code as production code (agile, not ad hoc)
Environments & promotionSeparate dev/test/prod with promotion policies and deployment pipelines
Data traceabilityLineage: source, timeline, processing steps, exceptions
Code versioningVersioned pipeline code and deployment tracking
ObservabilityLogging, audits, monitoring
ReproducibilityReproduce feature store contents by reprocessing raw data
Version-controlled stepsAll transformations are version-controlled code, with no ad hoc manipulation (data as code)
AutomationTrigger on new data or schedule; auto-rollback on errors; auto-reprocess
Consistent stateFeature store stays consistent; all errors reported and analyzed
← Previous14 / 36Next →
Automated data validation MLOps

MLOps › 4. Data Processing & Management › Automated data validation

New data keeps arriving after deployment. Validate it against the original training-set patterns to catch deviations before they hurt the model.

ValidationWhat to check
FeatureMissing/erroneous data, formats, ranges (machine-generated data can be wrong too)
DistributionMean, std, quartiles vs baseline; class distribution of categoricals, so new data belongs to the same population as training data
Out-of-distributionOutliers beyond quartiles (continuous); new class values (categorical)
CorrelationFeature-target and feature-feature correlation vs baseline (detects multicollinearity changes)
← Previous15 / 36Next →
Managed feature stores MLOps

MLOps › 4. Data Processing & Management › Managed feature stores

A centralized store of pre-processed features ready for ML, often shared by several teams and models.

  • Central store: shared ownership with defined responsibilities. Saves cost and enables reuse.
  • Flexible schema: add features without breaking consumers.
  • Separate datasets: keep related datasets separate and let consumers join at query time via linking attributes.
  • Updated registry: shows what exists and avoids duplicate processing.
  • Common format: teams customize at query time, not by changing the store (avoid last-minute customization requests).
  • Multiple storage types: files, tables, images, media, with low storage cost.
← Previous16 / 36Next →
Data versioning (e.g. DVC) MLOps

MLOps › 4. Data Processing & Management › Data versioning (e.g. DVC)

Version control for data. It creates an immutable baseline for raw, intermediate or feature datasets, at feature, record or dataset level (tool-dependent). A version can be referenced for training and testing.

BenefitDetail
TraceabilityLink a data version to a specific model and experiment number
ReproducibilityRecreate a model with an older data version even after the data changed
Change logWhat changed in the feature store over time
RollbackReturn to last known good state after bad processing
Parallel workScientists use a fixed version while data evolves, so data evolution is decoupled from model development
← Previous17 / 36Next →
Data governance MLOps

MLOps › 4. Data Processing & Management › Data governance

Ensures integrity, security and usability of data via people, policies and processes. It applies to all data (raw, intermediate, temporary, features, metadata), at rest or in motion.

ElementDetail
ConsistencyEveryone sees a consistent snapshot once data is committed
IntegrityComplete, accurate, conforming, error-free
SecurityOnly authorized users can view/create/modify/delete; protection from adversarial attacks
PrivacyProtect sensitive personal info; comply with laws/standards; redaction and obfuscation in the pipeline
ResiliencyBackups, standbys, redundancy; recovery to last known good state
Life cycle managementPolicies and automation from creation to cleanup

Implementing it:

  1. Identify a governance team (data owners and custodians).
  2. Reuse existing production-data policies.
  3. Identify all data elements in the ML pipeline.
  4. Classify data by security and privacy needs.
  5. Enforce through automation (scale, fewer human errors).
← Previous18 / 36Next →
Tools for data processing MLOps

MLOps › 4. Data Processing & Management › Tools for data processing

CategoryTools
Big data processingHadoop, Apache Spark, Apache Kafka
DatabasesMySQL (RDBMS); MongoDB, Cassandra (NoSQL)
Data versioningDVC, lakeFS, Neptune

Managed training pipelines MLOps

MLOps › 5. Continuous Training › Managed training pipelines

Flow: feature store → set hyperparameters → plan experiment → train → validate against performance goals → test with an independent test set → review results → if needed update parameters and retrain, until the goal is reached.

PracticeDetail
Agile life cycleStructured process adapted for continuous experiments
Separate environmentsDev/test for training; final run in a controlled environment
Experiment trackingTraceability of all experiments (a key MLOps activity)
Version controlCode, data and models versioned and tied together
ReproducibilityRebuild the model from training data plus input parameters
Model as codeNotebooks are baselined and versioned; rerunning gives the same model
Versioned dataTrain on versioned datasets
AutomationHyperparameter tuning (grid search), auto-trigger training on new data, compare new model to baseline
← Previous20 / 36Next →
Creating data labels MLOps

MLOps › 5. Continuous Training › Creating data labels

Labeling (annotation) adds contextual tags that serve as ML targets. Example: a movie review can carry a sentiment label ("positive") and a rating label (4.5).

Why it matters: unstructured data (text, images, media) often has no labels, available labels may be inaccurate or incomplete, and one dataset may need extra labels for different use cases (sentiment and recommendations).

MethodScaleAccuracyCost
Domain expertsLowHighHigh
CrowdsourcingHighVariable (knowledge/bias)Low
Professional annotatorsMediumHighHigh
Programmatic labelingMassiveDepends on the labeling modelLow (but time to build)

Recommended: combine methods. Label a base dataset with experts or professionals, then use it to train volunteers or programs to label a much larger corpus. Programmatic labeling is a fast-growing MLOps area.

← Previous21 / 36Next →
Experiment tracking MLOps

MLOps › 5. Continuous Training › Experiment tracking

Each training run is an experiment; tracking manages the model's evolution toward the stated goals.

CategoryTrack
Model setupAlgorithm, architecture (deep learning), hyperparameters
InputsDataset and version, train/validation/test splits
OutputsSerialized model (e.g. pickle), metrics (accuracy, errors, F1)
AnalysisComparison with earlier experiments, findings, next steps
  • With config plus inputs tracked, any experiment can be recreated and reproduced.
  • Benefits: measure the impact of parameter or data changes, verify progress toward requirements, decide whether to promote a model, and automate promotion decisions.
  • Manual tracking is slow and error-prone. Use tools integrated into the training pipeline.
← Previous22 / 36Next →
AutoML MLOps

MLOps › 5. Continuous Training › AutoML

Automation of ML activities across the life cycle, enabling development, analysis and decisions without human intervention.

ActivityHow AutoML helps
Feature engineeringDetect and fix issues, analyze feature-target correlation, select best features
Model trainingSelect algorithm, tune hyperparameters, ensembles (train several, pick best)
DeploymentJudge from results if ready for production; on drift/bias, retrain and redeploy
Custom modelsCustomize a base model per customer/use case, managing hundreds of models without manual work
BenefitsShortcomings
Automated retraining without humansErrors if automation isn't fully validated
Faster training and deploymentNew data/feature relationships may cause issues
Better results via grid searchBias may go untracked without special checks
Doesn't need trained data scientists to operateCapacity problems with multi-round grid search
Custom models at scaleExplainability may suffer

Best practices: achieve manual repeatability first, pick the right pipeline tools, use experiment tracking alongside, add automated sanity tests on outputs, monitor production for degradation, and review regularly.

Model versioning MLOps

MLOps › 6. Model Management › Model versioning

Versions establish lineage and manage the life cycle. The scheme should resemble software versioning (numbering is org-specific).

  • Linked baselines: model version, data version and code version tied together.
  • Traceability: from a model version, find its input data and hyperparameters.
  • Performance tracking across versions.
  • Stable references for integration and testing until they finish.
  • Enables structured life cycle management.

Model registry MLOps

MLOps › 6. Model Management › Model registry

A repository for storing and tracking models: a queryable database of the model plus metadata, with status changes and audit trails. It is to models what the feature store is to data and a code repo is to code. Usually one central registry is shared by all ML teams.

StoredDetail
Model artifactSerialized model (e.g. pickle)
MetadataUnique ID, version, description
HyperparametersThose used for this model
StatusCurrent life cycle stage
Audit trailTimestamps of state changes, test pass/fail, deployment
Lineage linksInput data version, code/notebook version, experiment-tracking results

MLOps benefits: traceability (recreate the model), life cycle tracking, collaboration across teams and time, automation of model creation and consumption, governance (access control, auditing).

Benchmarking models MLOps

MLOps › 6. Model Management › Benchmarking models

Compares a model and its versions against baselines and competing models after it passes its fitness test and before integration. It runs in an environment closer to production, measuring both performance and operational metrics. A model that looks good in a notebook may need more resources or add latency here.

Setup componentDetail
HardwareProduction-like CPU, memory, disk
Isolated environmentSoftware and network isolated from other activity
Test harnessSame test dataset and expected results for baseline and new model
Test executorsRun cases with required pacing and capacity
Tracking platformLog predictions, latency, errors, resource use; compute metrics
ModeBoth models simultaneously, or one model vs a stored baseline

Metrics: performance (accuracy, F1, precision, recall) and operational (latency, scaling, resource utilization).

Best practices: apples-to-apples conditions, log everything at the finest granularity, automate and integrate into pipelines, use experiment tracking tools for long-term analytics.

← Previous28 / 36Next →
Model life cycle management MLOps

MLOps › 6. Model Management › Model life cycle management

A model moves through states and transitions. Sample flow (customize per organization): Training → Created → Benchmarking (pass: Passed, fail: Discarded) → Integration testing (pass: Approved, fail: Archived) → Deployment (Deployed) → replaced by a new version (Retired).

StateHow the model gets there
CreatedTraining produces it
PassedPasses benchmarking
DiscardedFails benchmarking
ApprovedPasses integration testing
ArchivedFails integration testing
DeployedApproved model goes to production
RetiredA new version replaces it

Promotion best practices:

  • Define the life cycle and promotion criteria during requirements.
  • Base promotions on the performance and operational metrics from requirements.
  • Integration-test pass criteria include ML metrics and non-ML criteria (e.g. total issues found).
  • Automate promotions on metric thresholds. Add human oversight at first and reduce it as the pipeline matures.
  • Record decisions and promotion history in the registry.

Solution integration pipeline MLOps

MLOps › 7. Continuous Integration › Solution integration pipeline

A model must be embedded in other code (APIs, UIs, databases, microservices) to deliver a solution.

  1. Feature store plus hyperparameters → train model → model registry.
  2. Notebook to software conversion → regression testing → ML service ready for integration.
  3. Non-ML code (APIs, UIs, DBs) evolves independently in parallel.
  4. Integration testing → performance testing → package & deliver (model executable plus non-ML code).

Convert notebook code into a deployable, executable model that faithfully reproduces notebook processing and performance.

ModeForms

Regression test after conversion: use the model's benchmark results as the baseline and the same benchmark input data, and verify the same performance as the notebook. If not, fix and retest. Pay special attention to pre- and post-processing. Some tools convert notebooks to services automatically, so try those first.

Intent Recognition Azure AI Services

Azure AI Services › 3. Speech › Intent Recognition

Connects spoken text to what the user wants to do. Successor to LUIS (deprecated, absorbed here).

CategoryDescriptionExample
Pattern MatchingStrict, accurate, fast, works offline; no match returns an error"Go to floor nine", IVR "Press 1 for billing"
CLU (Conversational Language Understanding)Natural language; extracts overall intent and entities"What is the stock price of Microsoft?"

CLU: many phrasings ("stock price of", "current price of", "trading at") map to the same intent (get_price; could also be buy, sell) with an entity (MSFT, swappable with GOOG, ORCL). Workflow: define intents with example utterances, build a model, feed it to a recognizer, submit an utterance, read the intent + entity. "What is the stock price of Oracle?" gives intent get_price, entity ORCL.

Azure AI Services › 5. Search

Azure AI Search is an enterprise-class search engine over your data, with AI added.

OfferingSearchesUse case
Microsoft SearchM365 / SharePoint contentAuthenticated users, internal content

Choose it for: relevance tuning, heterogeneous sources, heavy indexing/query workloads, offloading search from the DBMS, or content that is neither on the internet nor in SharePoint.

Vectors Azure AI Services

Azure AI Services › 5. Search › Vectors

  • Vector embeddings map words, phrases, or documents into a multidimensional space, so similarity can be computed. Benefits: semantic similarity, finding relevant documents, ranking by relevance.
  • At index creation, add a vector search section: algorithm (HNSW or exhaustive KNN), compression (scalar and binary quantization, oversampling, re-ranking with original vectors), and profiles (combinations of algorithm + compression).
  • At query time: POST the natural-language query to an embeddings endpoint to get a vector query, then POST that to the search endpoint.

Foundry is the enterprise platform to build, test, deploy, and manage AI apps (full MLOps/DevOps lifecycle), at ai.azure.com. It uses models from across the industry, beyond what AI Services alone offer.

Typical AI project lifecycle (can be done visually in Foundry):

  1. Data: ingest, clean, transform, visualize.
  2. Split (e.g., 20% train / 80% validate, as stated in the course).
  3. Train (given these inputs, produce this output).
  4. Validate on held-out data.
  5. Deploy as an API protected by Entra ID, scaled with Kubernetes.
  6. Monitor inference and loop back (more data, retrain, tweak).

1. Core Concepts and RAG Pipeline (1/2) Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 1. Core Concepts and RAG Pipeline

Vector database: works with unstructured data as vectors. "Database" is a misnomer; it is a compute engine for vector data. Embeddings are long lists of numbers (hundreds to thousands).

Why "embeddings": they come from the second-to-last layer of a deep neural network. That layer holds what the network learned, before the predictive layer is applied.

Embedding models: deep neural networks that turn data into vectors. Two rules:

RuleWhy
Match data type to model typeImage models for images, text models for text. Even multimodal models need the input type specified.
Same model for indexing and retrievalOnly same-size vectors can be compared, so the query must use the model that vectorized the data.

LLMs in RAG: the interface to your data. Most (incl. GPT-4) are transformers that predict the next token. They are trained on public data and have no access to yours, which is the gap RAG fills.

RAG pipeline: question → embedding model → vector DB similarity search → relevant context → LLM (question + context) → answer.

2. Preprocessing: Chunking, Embeddings, Metadata Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 2. Preprocessing: Chunking, Embeddings, Metadata

Three components of RAG data preprocessing:

ComponentWhat it is
ChunkingBreaking big text into smaller blocks
EmbeddingsVectors from embedding models; semantic meaning in quantifiable form
MetadataData stored alongside embeddings; critical for customizable RAG apps

Why chunk: humans read one coherent sentence or paragraph at a time, and LLMs work the same way. The context window (max tokens an LLM handles at once; GPT-4 Turbo ~128k) is a cap, not the ideal amount.

Dense vs sparse embeddings (RAG mostly uses dense):

TypeDescriptionCreated by
DenseFew values are zeroML models
SparseMany values (>50%) are zeroAlgorithms (TF-IDF, BM25)

Metadata basics: it must include the original text, because vector DBs retrieve by similarity and an LLM cannot turn embeddings back into text. Its main use is filtering searches before similarity comparison.

TypeExamples
Processing metadataSection title, paragraph number, chunk location
Data metadataEmbedded text itself, publication date, author

Chunking considerations: the three C's Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 2. Preprocessing: Chunking, Embeddings, Metadata › Chunking considerations: the three C's

CTechnicalCommon sense
ConsumableFits the embedding model's context window; at least 3 chunks fit in the LLM's context window (depends on top-K)Readable in one go
CoherentDoesn't start/stop mid-word, clause, or sentenceMakes sense on its own ("Curiosity killed the cat" ✅, "killed the" ❌)
ContextualHolds all context needed to answer a question"Curiosity killed the cat" is coherent but out of context; full saying: "...but satisfaction brought it back"

Three chunking parameters Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 2. Preprocessing: Chunking, Embeddings, Metadata › Three chunking parameters

ParameterMeaningNotes
Chunk sizeCharacters per chunkDepends on data structure. Start at ~100 words / ~500 chars (a paragraph). May be a hard limit or a guideline depending on the method.
Chunk overlapCharacters repeated between consecutive chunksCarries context across chunks (last sentence of the previous chunk)
Special characters (separators)Characters to split on (periods, newlines)Relax size limits so chunks end at natural boundaries

How separators work: the list is a priority order.

If a chunk exceeds chunk_size without hitting a separator, the splitter relaxes the size limit and continues to the next separator. Result: more coherent chunks, slightly larger.

What to embed Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 4. Embeddings: Model Choice, What to Embed, Distance Metrics › What to embed

StrategyEmbeddedStored in metadata
Embed the chunkThe chunk textStandard metadata
Small-to-bigIndividual sentencesLarge paragraph
Big-to-smallLarge paragraphsIndividual sentences

These techniques improve retrieval even when chunks are already good.

Small-to-big: embed a sentence, store the whole paragraph. Use when sentences are very short; retrieving the paragraph adds context and coherence.

Big-to-small: embed the paragraph, store sentences. Use when sentences alone don't make sense (e.g. a period after "Mr." breaks sentence splitting); retrieving sentences separately allows post-processing before the LLM.

Non-English data needs a model trained on that language:

OptionExamplesTrade-off
Multilingual LLMGPT-3.5+, Mixtral, QwenEasy but less compute-friendly
Language-specific modelSearch MTEB for French, Polish, Chinese, etc.More efficient, better results

Challenge 2: oversized chunks (custom separator) Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 7. Challenges: Citing Sources, Fixing Chunk Size › Challenge 2: oversized chunks (custom separator)

CharacterTextSplitter defaults: separator="\n\n", is_separator_regex=False. If the text has no double newline inside the size window, it can't split, so chunks exceed the size and warnings appear. Fix: use "\n".

The separator is where the splitter may cut: "\n\n" waits for paragraph breaks, "\n" can cut at any line break, giving correctly sized chunks while keeping coherence at line boundaries.

Two types of image vectors Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 8. Image Embeddings and Vision Models › Two types of image vectors

TypeCapturesCreated byUsed in RAG?
Semantic embeddingsThe meaning of the imageDeep learning model's second-to-last layer✅ Yes
Visual / pixel embeddingsWhat the image literally looks likeCompressed image input vector (e.g. PyTorch model input)❌ Not typically

Semantic: image → input layer → hidden layers → output (prediction); the second-to-last layer holds the learned meaning, and that is the embedding. Pixel embeddings are also long number lists but encode raw pixels, not meaning. RAG uses semantic embeddings.

← Previous23 / 35Next →
Vision models 101 Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 8. Image Embeddings and Vision Models › Vision models 101

Deep neural networks for computer vision tasks (classification, segmentation, object detection).

EraModel typeKey innovation
1960sSimple neural networksFully connected layers
1993CNNsConvolution + max pooling; dominated ~30 years
2019Vision Transformers (ViT)Attention mechanism applied to vision

CNN = convolutional layer + pooling layer.

  • Convolution: slide a learnable filter (e.g. 3×3) over regions of the image; each output cell = element-wise multiply the window with the filter, then sum. Extracts local context.
  • Max pooling: compress the convolution output by taking the max of each region (e.g. max(12, 20, 8, 12) = 20).

Vision Transformer (ViT): takes attention from language transformers and applies it to images.

  • Pipeline: image → split into N×N patches (like words) → patch embeddings → add [CLS] token + positional encoding → transformer encoder (attention) → MLP head (classification, segmentation, etc.).
  • [CLS] token: special token whose output represents the whole image (the image embedding).
  • Positional encoding: tells the model where each patch sits.

Multimodal = multiple data types. Humans are multimodal (sight, hearing, ...); AI emulates mainly sight and hearing.

Widely agreed combosContested (all "sight", structured differently)
