Three ways to do multimodal RAG Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 10. Multimodal RAG › Three ways to do multimodal RAG

MethodModelsVector storesComplexityUsage
1. Single multimodal model (canonical)11LowMost common
2. Multiple models (one per data type)NNHighRare, manual
3. Multiple multimodal modelsNNVery highAlmost never

Method 1: one model (e.g. CLIP for images + text), one embedding model, one vector store, same dimensionality, so images and text compare directly. LangChain/LlamaIndex route text vs image encoding for you; natively you call different encoders.

Method 2: separate store per model. Different models give different dimensionalities, and even when dimensions match, embeddings from different training contexts are not meaningfully comparable.

Method 3 reasons: (a) too many data types (video, audio, images, tables) for one model; (b) re-ranking, using models trained on different data as a "second opinion".

← Previous30 / 35Next →
Multimodal embedding models Advanced RAG

Advanced RAG › 10. Multimodal RAG › Multimodal embedding models

They embed several data types using internal per-type functions (different preprocessing, different model parts trained on different data). Usually trained on pairs (image + text most common).

ModelSourceDescription
CLIPOpenAITwo encoders (image + text), open source
GPT-4oOpenAILLM evolved to be multimodal
LLaVAOpen sourceEnd-to-end transformer: image encoder + Vicuna LLM

CLIP = Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (most popular; free, open source, on Hugging Face):

  • Contrastive: trained on pairs; both encoders pull matching pairs close and push unpaired combinations far apart.
  • Language-Image: separate text and image encoders, but vectors land in the same embedding space with the same dimensionality.
  • Pretraining: 400 million internet image-text pairs.

(Code: same embed_documents / embed_image calls as Method 1 above; both return 1024 dims.)

1. Core Concepts (interview essentials) (1/2) AutoGen

AutoGen › 1. Core Concepts (interview essentials)

  • AI agent = LLM + tools + memory + context. Components: an LLM (language understanding), document access, a toolkit (APIs, calculators), conversation ability, and a database (memory).
  • AutoGen is a multi-agent conversational framework (Microsoft). Agents have different roles and solve tasks using different tools and patterns. An agent can send messages, receive messages, and generate replies, powered by an LLM, a code executor (e.g. IPython kernel), human input, or a combination.
  • Why multi-agent instead of one big LLM? Specialization (each agent does one thing well), collaboration/multiple perspectives (better quality), scalability (add agents), flexibility (custom roles), efficiency (parallel work).
  • Agents vs human assistants: available 24/7, no fatigue, consistent, many tasks at once, learn continuously. Framing: agents are collaborators that augment people, not replacements.
  • Design patterns taught: Reflection (self/peer review), Tool Use (functions/APIs), Multi-Agent Collaboration (sequential chats, nested chats, group chat). Also human-in-the-loop and agent memory (teachability).
  • Conversation shapes: two-way (agent ↔ agent), multi-way (group), nested (hierarchical). Collaboration shapes: sequential, parallel, hierarchical (manager-worker).
  • Problem-solving approach: break a complex problem into subtasks, assign to specialized agents, let them collaborate, synthesize the result. Example team: Researcher gathers → Analyst analyzes → Writer reports. Other teams seen in the course: architect/developer/tester/documenter (software), researcher/outliner/writer/editor (content), collector/analyst/visualizer/reporter (BI).
  • Course map: multi-agent conversations → research assistant (sequential chats) → nested chats → tool use/internet → coding copilot → teachable agents → group chat company.

5. Sequential Chats: Research Assistant AutoGen

AutoGen › 5. Sequential Chats: Research Assistant

Project: marketing-video research assistant. Roles: Manager (UserProxyAgent, supplies topic, selects ideas, decides), Idea Generator (several campaign concepts), Script Writer (full script: dialog, scenes, camera directions), Script Reviewer (coherence, engagement, alignment with the topic).

Flow: Manager → Idea Generator → Manager picks/refines an idea → Script Writer → Script Reviewer → Manager final decision.

Three phases: create agents (roles) → define tasks (list of chat dicts) → initiate chats (initiate_chats).

6. Nested Chats (Reflection pattern) AutoGen

AutoGen › 6. Nested Chats (Reflection pattern)

Nested chat = a conversation inside a conversation. An agent consults other agents before replying. Used to model multi-step processes, quality control, hierarchical decisions.

Architecture: User/Reviewer agent talks to the Writer; when the Writer replies, the reviewer runs inner chats with specialist reviewers, then sends consolidated feedback back to the Writer. The inner chats are the "inner monologue" of the reviewer.

9. Teachable Agents (Long-term Memory) (1/2) AutoGen

AutoGen › 9. Teachable Agents (Long-term Memory)

Problem with standard LLM assistants: memory is lost when the chat ends, in-context learning is not persistent, context windows fill up, and users repeat instructions every session.

Teachable agent: learns from user interaction and keeps memos in a vector database (ChromaDB) that survives restarts. A Teachability capability object is added to a ConversableAgent. Flow: teach (fact/preference/skill) → memo embedded and stored → later query is vectorized → similarity search retrieves relevant memos → response uses them.

Learnable typeExample
Facts"My birthday is June 15"
Preferences"I prefer bullet point summaries"
Skills"Always validate input before processing"
FeatureStandard agentTeachable agent
MemorySingle sessionPersistent
PersonalizationNoneGrows over time
Instruction repetitionEvery sessionOne-time teaching
ContextLimited windowExtended via DB

(installs AutoGen, ChromaDB, and teachability dependencies)

Teaching a fact: "My name is Harshit and I like miso ramen." → agent stores name and preference.

Why policies: structured communication, logical information flow, mirrors org hierarchies, fewer wasted turns (lower token cost), forces review checkpoints.

Gotchas: loops → set max_round, check circular transitions, add termination. Wrong agent speaking → check the policy dictionary, give the manager an LLM config, make sure agent names/objects match the policy keys. Poor collaboration → sharpen system messages, adjust transitions, add intermediate agents, raise max_round. Give each agent one focused role with no overlapping responsibilities, and test agents individually first.

Common failure modes: infinite loops (add termination, max_turns, max_round, timeouts); tool never called (description/registration); wrong speaker in group chat (policy dict, manager LLM); API key errors (.env, load_dotenv()); memory not loading (reset_db, path).

1. Core Concepts CrewAI

CrewAI › 1. Core Concepts

CrewAI is a Python framework for building multi-agent systems: a team of LLM-powered agents, each with a role and tools, handing results to the next agent. Prerequisites: LLM basics, knowledge of what AI agents are, Python.

Building blockWhat it is
CrewTop-level orchestrator. Holds agents and tasks, picks execution order, starts the run, collects the result (acts like a project manager).
AgentAutonomous, LLM-powered team member with a role. Uses tools, can delegate and receive tasks, makes its own decisions. The only autonomous component.
TaskActionable step that breaks down the crew's goal. Needs a clear objective, optional tools, and output that can be handed to the next agent. Good task breakdown is critical to success.
ProcessWorkflow management: how tasks are assigned and in what order. sequential or hierarchical.

Supplementary components: Tools (external actions), Memory (retain information across tasks), Knowledge (domain-specific information).

Example: an article crew = research, analyze, outline, write tasks. Email task = email agent with email tools.

Success formula: accurately defined agents + well-described tasks.

5. Agents CrewAI

CrewAI › 5. Agents

An agent is a single autonomous unit built for one specific problem. Design principle: one agent = one focused responsibility (e.g. Tax Auditor vs Tax Filer; Deal Finder vs Inventory vs Delivery agent).

Capabilities: perform a specific task, make decisions guided by role and goal, use tools, collaborate with other agents, use memory of past communications.

Agent role in a crew: the action takers and the only autonomous component, powered by an LLM. Each agent can be given a different LLM.

6. Tools CrewAI

CrewAI › 6. Tools

Agents without tools are essentially smart chatbots. Tools (skills/functions for external actions) are what make an agent agentic.

SourceExamplesNotes
CrewAI built-inFileReadTool, GitHubSearchTool, SerperDevToolBundled in crewai[tools]
LangChain toolsTavilySearchTool, TwilioToolWeb browsing, SMS
Bridge toolsComposioTool250+ tools from Composio
CustomExtend BaseToolTurn Python classes into tools

Some tools are paid (DALL-E, Composio, Serper beyond its free tier). Import tools from crewai_tools, not crewai.

SerperDevTool is a Google Search API (free tier, key from serper.dev) and needs SERPER_API_KEY. It returns JSON (credits_used, results with title/link/snippet), which agents process automatically. A tool can be tested directly with .run() before assigning it.

7. Memory CrewAI

CrewAI › 7. Memory

Memory lets agents reason better, learn from earlier interactions, keep context during a session, and improve with use (fine-tuning strategies from past errors). It goes beyond the LLM context window.

TypeStoresMechanism
Short-termRecent interactions and outcomesTemporary, uses RAG; gives context for the current task
Long-termLessons and patterns from past runsPersists insights, refines knowledge over time
EntityPeople, places, organizationsDeeper understanding and relationship mapping
ContextualBest composition of the three aboveKeeps coherence across a sequence of tasks
ExternalOutside providersMemGPT, GraphRAG, Mem0

Benefits map: contextual awareness (short-term + contextual), experience accumulation (long-term), entity understanding (entity).

Memory is off by default (memory=False). Enable on an agent, or on the crew for all agents. Default embeddings are OpenAI's; change them with embedder.

A task is the fundamental unit of work: a piece of the crew's overall goal. It encapsulates an objective, expected output, dependencies, needed data/context, and optional tools. Usually one task maps to one agent.

Managing task output CrewAI

CrewAI › 8. Tasks › Managing task output

Default output is a raw string, passed automatically to dependent tasks. Three parameters change the shape:

ParameterTakesReturnsUse for
output_pydanticPydantic model classPydantic instanceStructured data inside Python
output_jsonPydantic model classdict (JSON)External APIs

output_pydantic and output_json take the same model and differ only in return type.

After crew.kickoff(), task.output returns a TaskOutput. .raw is always available; .pydantic needs output_pydantic; .json_dict needs output_json.

← Previous19 / 32Next →
Task-level tools CrewAI

CrewAI › 8. Tasks › Task-level tools

Task tools override agent tools for that task, which reduces non-determinism. If only the agent has tools, it uses its own; if only the task has tools, the task's are used. Example uses: search tool on a research task (ground it in web data), database query tool on a summary task.

← Previous20 / 32Next →
context: dependencies between tasks CrewAI

CrewAI › 8. Tasks › context: dependencies between tasks

In sequential mode only the immediately preceding task's output flows forward. context takes a list of tasks and pulls output from several tasks or from a non-adjacent one.

← Previous21 / 32Next →
Async execution CrewAI

CrewAI › 8. Tasks › Async execution

async_execution=True runs a task in the background without blocking the main sequence. Good for long-running work (scraping, summarizing millions of records) and non-critical work (logging, notifications, emailing). If a downstream task lists the async task in context, it waits for it to finish.

ScenarioBehavior
Async task, nothing depends on itRuns in background, blocks nothing
Async task + downstream contextDownstream task waits for it
Non-async tasksSequential as normal

9. Crews and Process CrewAI

CrewAI › 9. Crews and Process

A crew is the central orchestrator: defines the objective (through its tasks), supplies agents and tasks, determines order, runs execution, collects the final result.

ParameterDescription
agentsList of agents
tasksList of tasks. For sequential, list order is execution order.
processProcess.sequential or Process.hierarchical
verboseDefault False. Detailed logs. Recommended during development.
memoryDefault False. Shared memory across agents.
manager_llmLLM for the manager agent. Required for hierarchical only.
ProcessBehavior
Process.sequentialTasks run one after another in list order. Output passes automatically. Best for linear workflows.
Process.hierarchicalA manager agent (LLM) breaks the goal into subtasks and assigns them to agents autonomously. Supports branching and complex paths. Needs manager_llm.

Custom domain Google Cloud (GCP)

Google Cloud (GCP) › 3. App Engine: Hello World, Domains, HTTPS › Custom domain

  • Default URL is a subdomain of appspot.com. Set up under App Engine, Settings, Custom Domains: link an existing domain or register a new one.
  • Verify an existing domain: pick the registrar, copy the TXT record into the domain's DNS, then Verify. DNS propagation can take minutes, and the TXT value does not change, so retrying is safe.
  • Then select the verified domain, map the domain and www subdomain, save, and add the DNS records Google lists.
  • Google then provisions a managed, auto-renewing SSL certificate automatically (about 15 minutes), so HTTPS works with no extra setup.

Bring your own SSL certificate Google Cloud (GCP)

Google Cloud (GCP) › 3. App Engine: Hello World, Domains, HTTPS › Bring your own SSL certificate

  1. Verify the domain, then disable managed security (Settings, Custom Domains, Disable managed security).
  2. Convert the key to unencrypted PEM and concatenate the certificate chain into one file. END CERTIFICATE and BEGIN CERTIFICATE must be on separate lines.
  3. Confirm that certificate and key match (both commands must print the same hash).
  4. Upload under Settings, SSL Certificates (PEM public certificate + PEM private key), assign it to the domain, save.

Multi-environment best practice Google Cloud (GCP)

Google Cloud (GCP) › 4. App Engine Components, Versions, Traffic Splitting › Multi-environment best practice

  • Use separate projects for test and production, not just separate services. Services in one project share data (Firestore, Cloud Storage), which risks cross-contamination.
  • Version naming: <timestamp>-<git-commit-hash>. Timestamp gives deployment order; the hash identifies the exact commit, which makes rollback precise.
  • Test project: default version = latest production version; each feature branch is its own version (feature-x, feature-y), so QA can test them in parallel via unique version URLs.
  • Production project: versions by timestamp + commit, used for migrations and rollbacks. Feature versions can be tried on real users via traffic splitting.
  • Natural next step: automate with CI/CD.
← Previous15 / 44Next →

App Engine, Versions, Split Traffic, choose a method, add versions with percentages, Save.

MethodHow it routesBest for
IP addressBy request IPNon-browser clients, apps without cookies
CookieBy cookie valueBrowser apps (you must add the cookie)
RandomBy percentageQuick tests (one user may hit different versions across requests)
  • Migrate Traffic: select a version, confirm, and 100% of traffic goes to it.
  • Rollback is the same operation: migrate all traffic back to an earlier version.

Service accounts (IAM) Google Cloud (GCP)

Google Cloud (GCP) › 5. Cloud SQL and Service Accounts › Service accounts (IAM)

  • A service account is a user-like identity for applications. Two kinds: user-created and Google-managed (no functional difference).
  • App Engine's default account is <project-id>@appspot.gserviceaccount.com. To let the app use another service (e.g. Cloud SQL), add a role to this account via IAM & Admin, IAM, Edit, Add Another Role (e.g. Cloud SQL Client; Cloud SQL Editor or Admin also work).
  • Create a new one under Service Accounts: name, ID, description, then roles, optionally grant users access.
  • Keys: Add Key, Create New Key, JSON. The file downloads once, so treat it as a secret.
  • Disable is temporary and reversible. Delete is permanent.

ModeDescriptionNotes
UniformBucket-level permissions, all objects inheritRecommended, tends to cost less

  • Switch under the bucket's Permissions tab. Warning: switching back to fine-grained restores previously set object ACLs, which may grant wider access than the bucket IAM policy.

Signed URLs Google Cloud (GCP)

Google Cloud (GCP) › 6. Cloud Storage (GCS) › Signed URLs

  • A signed URL gives temporary access to a private object. Flow: user asks the app, the app signs a URL using a service account, user fetches the object directly from GCS.
  • V4 URL parts: object path, signing algorithm, credentials, start date (can be in the future), expiry (seconds from start, up to 7 days), signed headers, signature.
  • Needs a service account with at least Storage Object Viewer (storage.objects.get) and its downloaded private key.
  • Locally you must pass the key file. On GCP the default service account is used automatically.
  • Signed upload URLs: same code with action: 'write'.
← Previous27 / 44Next →
Object lifecycle management Google Cloud (GCP)

Google Cloud (GCP) › 6. Cloud Storage (GCS) › Object lifecycle management

  • Rules apply to all objects in a bucket. Age counts from when the object was added. Set under bucket, Lifecycle tab, Add a Rule (action, then conditions).
  • If an object matches several rules, the least-costly-to-keep action wins: Delete beats downgrade to the lowest class, which beats downgrade to a higher class.
ActionsConditions
Set storage class (e.g. Standard to Archive), DeleteAge (days since upload), creation date, storage class, newer versions + live state (versioning)

Example (file download service): rule 1 sets class to Archive at age 30 days and class Standard. Rule 2 deletes at age 365 days, so links expire after a year.

  • Create tasks and run them in the background. Two target types: App Engine tasks (endpoints in an App Engine app) and HTTP target tasks (any public URL).

Queue settingPurpose
Rate of execution / max dispatches per secondTasks per second
Max concurrent dispatchesCap on parallel executions, protects endpoints
Max burst sizeBurstable rates via token buckets
Retry settingExampleMeaning
Max attempts100Max retries
Min backoff100 msWait before first retry
Backoff doublingup to 16 timesWait doubles on each failure
Max backoff3,600 sLongest wait between retries
  • Console queue controls: Pause/Resume a queue, Run now for one task, Delete a task, Purge all tasks.

Emailing subscribers: fan-out pattern (Exercise 06_02) (1/3) Google Cloud (GCP)

Google Cloud (GCP) › 7. Cloud Tasks and the Fan-Out Pattern › Emailing subscribers: fan-out pattern (Exercise 06_02)

Setup: enable the Cloud Tasks API, then create two queues.

Problem: sending emails in a loop is fine for few recipients, but with thousands or hundreds of thousands the loop times out.

PatternDescriptionScalability
DirectLoop and send synchronouslyDoes not scale, risks timeout
Task per emailOne Cloud Task per emailBetter, but the task-creation loop can still time out
Fan-outGenerator tasks each create the send tasks for a batchBest; parallel, App Engine auto-scales instances

Fan-out: create tasks that create tasks. Example: 100,000 emails with batch size 100 gives 1,000 generator tasks. Each receives startCount and batchSize, queries that slice from the DB, and creates the individual send-email tasks.

Timezone caveats Google Cloud (GCP)

Google Cloud (GCP) › 8. Cloud Scheduler (Cron) › Timezone caveats

  • Scheduler uses the wall-clock time of the chosen timezone. With daylight saving time, a job can run twice at the switch back or be skipped at the switch forward. Best practice: use UTC.
  • For users in many timezones (8 AM their time): run the job every hour and filter by timezone in the endpoint code.

Cloud Debugger (Exercise 08_03) Google Cloud (GCP)

Google Cloud (GCP) › 9. Operations Tools: Logging, Debugger, Trace › Cloud Debugger (Exercise 08_03)

  • Takes snapshots and inspects variable state on live traffic, useful for bugs that are hard to reproduce locally. Works with App Engine, Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run and VMs elsewhere.
  • Setup: open Debugger, make sure the version with 100% traffic is selected, pick the file, press Check to sync and activate.
  • Snapshot: click a line number. On the next request it captures the call stack and variable values. Supports conditions (e.g. i === 1 for the second loop pass) and expressions (e.g. helloArray[i]).
  • Logpoint: pick a line, give a condition (e.g. true) and a log message with {expression} syntax (e.g. "value of response is {response}"). It adds logs to the running app without changing source or redeploying.

Google Cloud (GCP) › 9. Operations Tools: Logging, Debugger, Trace › Cloud Trace (Exercise 08_04)

  • Traces requests to find bottlenecks. It samples a subset of requests. Works out of the box on App Engine and can be set up elsewhere, even outside GCP.
  • Overview page: Insights (improvement tips), Recent Traces, Most Frequent URIs (keep latency low on these), Most Frequent RPCs, Chargeable Trace Spans (free tier: first 2.5 million spans), Daily Analysis Reports (latency vs previous week).
  • Trace list: filter by time range, minimum latency, status, version. Each trace shows spans, which show which part of the code took longest, and links to the full log entry in the Logging Viewer.
  • Daily analysis reports are automatic. Custom reports are made with Create a Report.

1. Setup, Prerequisites and Cost Control GCP for Machine Learning

GCP for Machine Learning › 1. Setup, Prerequisites and Cost Control

Vertex AI covers LLM integration, custom model development/tuning/deployment, notebooks, APIs, Google AI Studio for quick prototyping, and end-to-end MLOps.

Prerequisites: ML basics, Python ML libraries, Jupyter notebooks, GCP core services (buckets, VMs, IAM/permissions).

Cost rules for learning (and for real work):

  • Use a dedicated project and delete it when done (simplest cost control).
  • Set a billing alert/budget.
  • Use only what you need. GPUs/TPUs are costly.
  • Stop services when idle. VMs and notebooks bill while running.

Variant (course conclusion): same flow with ml-continued-learning, budget 100 and thresholds 0.5/0.8/1.0, plus enabling several APIs in one command: gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com notebooks.googleapis.com bigquery.googleapis.com.

AZ-900 › 2. Cloud concepts: models and shared responsibility

Cloud computing is a bundle of ideas: shared responsibility, service models, scalability, availability, and pay-for-what-you-use.

Shared responsibility model AZ-900

AZ-900 › 2. Cloud concepts: models and shared responsibility › Shared responsibility model

  • You and the provider share responsibility. The provider never takes all of it.
  • The provider only covers what it controls. A bug in your app is your problem.
  • The service type you choose (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS) decides how much falls on you. Moving IaaS → PaaS → SaaS shifts responsibility to the provider (see Section 4).

Consumption-based model AZ-900

AZ-900 › 2. Cloud concepts: models and shared responsibility › Consumption-based model

You pay for what is allocated to you, not what you actively use. A running idle VM is still billed.

Two cost-control rules:

  1. Do not allocate more than you need (do not provision 8 cores when 2 will do).
  2. Fully use what you allocate (do not leave resources idle).

Auto-scaling, cost alerts and recommendations help with both (Sections 9 and 12).

High availability AZ-900

AZ-900 › 3. Benefits of cloud: availability, scale, reliability, governance › High availability

Availability means the app and its systems are accessible to users. High availability is 99% or higher, achieved with redundant systems.

Threats: network outage, application failure, system (VM) outage, power outage, failure of a system you depend on (such as a database server).

SLA uptime targets (worth memorizing):

Geographies, regions, region pairs AZ-900

AZ-900 › 5. Core architecture: regions, zones, resources › Geographies, regions, region pairs

  • Geography: boundary defined by country, continent or regulation, so data stays compliant with local rules.
  • Region: a physical location within a geography containing data centers and the facilities Azure needs.
  • Region pair: each region is paired with another, at least ~300 miles apart, for disaster recovery.
    • Automatic failover to the pair if you replicated resources.
    • Rolling updates: Microsoft updates one region of a pair, verifies it, then the other, so Azure updates cause no downtime.
← Previous18 / 67Next →
Sovereign regions AZ-900

AZ-900 › 5. Core architecture: regions, zones, resources › Sovereign regions

Completely isolated: separate portals, endpoints and operators.

RegionDetails
Azure Government (US)Data stays in the US. Only US citizens (screened). Separate from public Azure with dedicated networking. A DoD subset has dedicated data centers. For US government, cities and municipalities with governmental affiliation
Azure GermanyGDPR and EU rules. Available to EU, European Free Trade Association members and the UK. Operated by T-Systems International as data trustee with full control of data and infrastructure. Microsoft only manages systems that have no access to customer data
Azure ChinaOperated by Shanghai Blue Cloud Technology (owned by 21Vianet). Complies with China's regulations

Availability zones AZ-900

AZ-900 › 5. Core architecture: regions, zones, resources › Availability zones

Unique physical locations within a region, each with one or more data centers. Zone-enabled regions have at least 3 zones. Not every region supports zones.

TypeWho replicatesExample
ZonalYou choose the zonesVirtual Machines
Zone-redundantAzure replicates automaticallyAzure Storage

Zones give fault tolerance, not disaster recovery. All zones sit in one region, so a regional disaster can take them all. Use region pairs for DR.

← Previous20 / 67Next →
Data centers AZ-900

AZ-900 › 5. Core architecture: regions, zones, resources › Data centers

A data center is a physical building in a region (at least 2 per region). Each has its own climate control, power supply and generators, and network gear. Cables are owned or leased exclusively by Microsoft. None depends on another's power or water, so one failing does not affect the others.

← Previous21 / 67Next →
Resources, resource groups, management groups AZ-900

AZ-900 › 5. Core architecture: regions, zones, resources › Resources, resource groups, management groups

  • Resource: any entity you create (VM, web app, database, storage).
  • Resource group (RG): a logical container. Every resource is in exactly one RG.
    • Benefits: per-group cost view, delete the group to delete everything, tag the group and filter invoices by tag, export as an ARM template to redeploy elsewhere.
  • Management group: organizes subscriptions. It can contain subscriptions and other (nested) management groups, but not resource groups or resources.

Hierarchy: Management groups → Subscriptions → Resource groups → Resources. Organize by department, project or environment as you like.

6. Compute and networking AZ-900

AZ-900 › 6. Compute and networking

Compute is any service that consumes CPU and memory.

← Previous23 / 67Next →
Containers AZ-900

AZ-900 › 6. Compute and networking › Containers

A container is an isolated environment where an app and its dependencies run.

  1. Built from an image (like a zip of OS pieces, code, modules, web servers).
  2. Images live in a repository.
  3. A container runtime (Docker) downloads and runs the image.

Containers hold only user-mode OS components and rely on the host's kernel. A Linux image needs a Linux host, and a Windows image needs a Windows host.

  • VMs: Windows or Linux, many sizes. Azure installs the OS and you configure everything else.
  • ACI: runs containers without VMs, with container groups for several containers in one instance. For heavy or long-running workloads use AKS.
  • Azure Functions: microservices that take an input, do an operation and return a result. Event-driven (file upload, HTTP request, timer). Consumption billing, no VM costs.

App Service (PaaS): web apps in the cloud.

  • Apps run on VMs in an App Service Plan, the unit of scaling. All apps in the plan share the same VMs.
  • Lower plan tiers cost less with fewer features. Higher tiers add power and features.
  • App names must be globally unique (<app-name>.azurewebsites.net).
  • Scaling applies to the whole plan: scale up (bigger VM), scale out (more instances) or autoscale by metric (CPU, traffic).
  • Turnkey authentication: add Microsoft, Apple, Facebook, GitHub or Google sign-in with no auth code.

Virtual networking (1/2) AZ-900

AZ-900 › 6. Compute and networking › Virtual networking

A VNet is your own network in Azure with an IP address space in CIDR (for example 10.0.0.0/16, 65,534 usable IPs), split into subnets. Typical multi-tier layout: web tier (internet-facing), middle tier (business rules), data tier (no direct internet). Only the web tier should face the internet, and the web tier should not talk straight to the data tier.

VNet peering connects two VNets over Microsoft's private backbone, not the internet. Same region or different regions (Global VNet Peering). Peered traffic is not encrypted.

Azure DNS hosts DNS records (A, CNAME, MX...). Public zones are internet-facing, private zones only resolve inside Azure VNets.

Virtual networking (2/2) AZ-900

AZ-900 › 6. Compute and networking › Virtual networking

VPN Gateway: encrypted connections between Azure VNets and other networks. Azure creates a managed gateway subnet with 2+ VMs (not accessible to you). Max 1.25 Gbps, and encryption adds overhead.

Connection typeConnects
VNet-to-VNetTwo Azure VNets
Site-to-SiteAzure VNet and an on-prem network
Point-to-SiteOne device (phone, laptop) and an Azure VNet

VPN Gateway vs peering: for two Azure VNets, peering is faster (no encryption overhead, no 1.25 Gbps cap). Use VPN Gateway when you need encryption or a non-Azure network.

ExpressRoute: dedicated private connectivity from on-prem to Azure. Traffic never crosses the internet. The connection is a circuit: you → third-party provider (usually an ISP) → Microsoft Enterprise Edge (MSEE) → Azure.

VPN GatewayExpressRoute
SpeedUp to 1.25 GbpsUp to 10 Gbps (100 Gbps with ExpressRoute Direct)

Azure Migrate moves servers, databases and web apps (from on-prem or other clouds) in three steps:

Authentication methods AZ-900

AZ-900 › 8. Identity, access and security › Authentication methods

Single sign-on (SSO): authenticate once and reuse for all resources. Azure AD Connect extends SSO to on-prem. Two methods:

  • Password Hash Synchronization: the password is hashed, the hash is stored in Azure AD, and logins compare hashes.
  • Pass-Through Authentication: credentials go to an on-prem agent and are validated against on-prem AD, and the result goes back to Azure AD via AD Connect.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA): factors are something you know (password, PIN), have (phone, security key) and are (fingerprint, face, retina).

  • Two-factor = two factors. Three-factor = all three. Azure MFA uses two-factor.
  • Needs Azure AD Premium (not the free tier).
  • Enabled per user.
  • Guest users need a conditional access policy for MFA.

Passwordless replaces "something you know":

MethodHow
FIDO2 security keyCryptographic keys on a phone or USB key
Microsoft Authenticator appPush notification, enter the shown number, confirm with biometrics/PIN
Text message (SMS)Code sent by text, entered on the computer
Temporary Access Pass (TAP)Time-limited string for initial setup or a lost device
Certificate-basedDigital certificate
Windows Hello for BusinessFace biometrics on Windows devices

4. Preprocessing: the Cleanup Function ML Foundations

ML Foundations › 4. Preprocessing: the Cleanup Function

Why preprocess: most algorithms need numeric input, features should be on a similar scale, and raw data has wrong types, placeholder values, or useless columns.

Two phases: (1) a cleanup function (fix types, bad values, select columns); (2) sklearn pipelines (scale, impute, encode), covered next.

StepWhy
zipcode: int to String to CategoricalZipcode is an identifier. Left numeric, algorithms infer a false ordering (higher/lower)
date: combine year/month/dayOne proper date column. Models can't use raw dates, so extract features (month, weekday) later if needed
yr_renovated: replace 0 with None0 means "never renovated," not "year 0." Null lets imputation handle it properly
explicit .select([...]) at the endReadable, maintainable, shows exactly which features are in play

Practices:

  • Keep raw data so predictions can be traced back for explainability.
  • Build the function incrementally, then move it to the top of the notebook (load raw, run cleanup, ready).
  • Preprocessing's job is to get data into a correct, honest state. Scaling and encoding happen in the pipeline.

9.1 Linear regression and Ridge ML Foundations

ML Foundations › 9. Model Tuning › 9.1 Linear regression and Ridge

Linear regression has almost nothing to tune (fit_intercept, copy_X, n_jobs). It can't be made more complex, only simplified. Ridge adds alpha for regularization (penalizes over-reliance on any one feature): alpha=0 equals plain linear regression, default 1, higher means a simpler model.

Sweep alpha manually and plot:

Scores go from about 0.802 (alpha=0) to about 0.807, a negligible gain. The plot looks dramatic only because of the y-axis scale, so always check axis ranges. If the gain is marginal, try different data splits to confirm it's consistent.

set_params pattern: double underscore joins step name and parameter. Same pattern as dt__max_depth.

PrefixRaise the valueLower the value
max_More complex, overfittingSimpler, underfitting
min_Simpler, underfittingMore complex, overfitting
ParameterDefaultRaising it
max_depthNone (unbounded)Deeper, more complex

A validation curve sweeps one hyperparameter using cross-fold validation (each fold takes a turn as the test set) and plots train vs test score.

Reading it: train score keeps rising (memorizing); test score rises, peaks (about depth 8), then drops, so overfitting begins after the peak; a widening gap means growing overfitting.

9.3 CatBoost (2/2) ML Foundations

ML Foundations › 9. Model Tuning › 9.3 CatBoost

Reading it: depth 1-4 both scores rise, error bars tight. Depth 4 is near the test peak with the tightest error bars (most consistent). Depth 5-6 train higher, test dips then recovers. Depth 9 has very high train score, test drops, error bars very wide (inconsistent across folds). Depths 4 and 6 score similarly, so pick depth 4: when two options are close, choose the simpler one.

max_depth is blunt: it forces all 300+ trees to one depth. grow_policy, min_child_samples, max_leaves give finer control, and combining several hyperparameters can improve further.

9.4 Grid search ML Foundations

ML Foundations › 9. Model Tuning › 9.4 Grid search

Validation curves tune one hyperparameter. GridSearchCV brute-forces every combination with cross-validation.

Baseline decision tree: same as Section 7.3 (R² ≈ 0.73).

  • 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 combinations x 5 folds = 135 fits. Each added 3-value parameter multiplies the total by 3 (81 combinations, 405 fits).
  • Pass only training data; grid search makes its own 5 folds internally (train 80%, validate 20%, rotate), tracking mean and std per combination.

Attributes ending in _ are learned from fitting (sklearn convention). Apply with ** unpacking:

Default for comparison: identical pipeline but dt = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42) and no set_params, giving R² ≈ 0.74. Tuning gained +0.05 (0.74 to 0.79).

ProsCons
Simple API, built-in CVSlow, tries every combination; time grows multiplicatively per parameter
Exhaustive within the gridOnly tests values you list, may miss the optimum

Smarter alternatives:

ToolApproach
HyperoptBayesian optimization; you give distributions, it exploits good regions and explores to avoid local minima
RandomizedSearchCVSamples random combinations, faster on large grids
OptunaTree-structured Parzen estimator, similar to Hyperopt
← Previous41 / 47Next →
9.5 Challenge: grid search on Random Forest ML Foundations

ML Foundations › 9. Model Tuning › 9.5 Challenge: grid search on Random Forest

Baseline: same pipeline as 7.5, R² ≈ 0.877. Reuse the grid search code and swap the prefix dt__ to rf__:

Much slower than the tree: 3 values x 5 folds = 15 fits of 100 trees each.

Why tuning made it worse:

  • Search was incomplete (8, 10, etc. untested).
  • Grid search optimizes on CV folds of the training data, which may not match this test set.
  • Random forest averaging already counters overfit trees, so capping depth can remove useful signal.
  • One parameter isn't enough; try min_samples_split or Hyperopt/Optuna.

Lessons: tuning doesn't always help, grid search finds the best only within your grid, and different models need different tuning (trees benefit hugely from pruning, forests less).

2.1 K-Means ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 2. Clustering: K-Means, Choosing K, Interpreting Clusters › 2.1 K-Means

Unsupervised: you pass data without labels and get cluster labels back.

Algorithm:

  1. Choose k.
  2. Pick k random points as initial centroids.
  3. Assign each point to its nearest centroid.
  4. Move each centroid to the middle of its cluster.
  5. Repeat 3-4 until centroids stop moving (converge).

K-means uses distance, so features must be on the same scale.

Demo that shows the centroids moving per iteration (max_iter=i+1) on Iris:

← Previous3 / 34Next →
2.2 Choosing K (1/2) ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 2. Clustering: K-Means, Choosing K, Interpreting Clusters › 2.2 Choosing K

Elbow method. Track inertia (sum of squared distances from each point to its nearest centroid) as k grows. Inertia always falls as k rises, so look for the bend where gains become small. Trick: slide an angled ruler along the curve; where it touches the corner is the elbow.

Silhouette coefficient. How similar a point is to its own cluster versus other clusters, from -1 to 1 (higher is better). 1 = near the cluster centre, 0 = on the boundary, -1 = far away or misassigned (likely outlier).

Reading the silhouette plot:

  • Each cluster is a "blade"; each horizontal slice is one point, sorted by score. The red dashed line is the average score.
  • Good: blades bulge out (wide, rounded) and all poke past the average line.
  • Bad: pointy, narrow blades, a cluster that falls below the average, or negative scores at the bottom of a blade.
  • Iris: 2 clusters gives bulgy blades and the highest average; the average drops at 3, negatives appear at 4-5, and it recovers slightly at 6-7.
← Previous4 / 34Next →
2.2 Choosing K (2/2) ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 2. Clustering: K-Means, Choosing K, Interpreting Clusters › 2.2 Choosing K

Choosing K is judgment, not a formula. For Iris the elbow suggests 3-4 clusters and the silhouette suggests 2. When several values score about the same, choose the simpler model (fewer clusters). You must be able to explain and justify the K you chose, using domain context as well as the metrics.

Notebook variant on the Australian electricity data: the same elbow loop runs on X = elec.drop(columns=['class']), and the silhouette loop uses silhouette_visualizer(km, X.sample(1_000, random_state=42), ...). Sampling matters because the full run takes about 2 min 20 s. The elbow suggested about 5 clusters. Silhouette favoured 4 but 5 was close, so 5 was chosen.

← Previous5 / 34Next →
2.3 Interpreting the clusters ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 2. Clustering: K-Means, Choosing K, Interpreting Clusters › 2.3 Interpreting the clusters

Explaining what clusters represent matters more than producing them. Three methods:

1. Summarize by group mean (pandas). Each column is a cluster and each row a feature. Red is low and blue is high, so you can describe each cluster in business terms (for example, "cluster 4 is the high-demand, high-price cluster").

Real data used: Australian electricity (datasets library).

2. Surrogate model. Train a decision tree to predict the cluster labels (supervised: X plus cluster labels), then read the tree to explain the clusters. Start at the root; each node asks "is feature < value?" (left = yes, right = no); a leaf is the predicted cluster. The tree also shows which features matter most. In the electricity example, date was the first split, class 4 = high date/period/demand, class 2 = low across the board.

3. Visualize in 2D/3D with PCA, t-SNE, or UMAP (see section 4).

← Previous6 / 34Next →
3.1 Hierarchical and DBSCAN ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 3. Other Clustering Algorithms & the Titanic Pipeline › 3.1 Hierarchical and DBSCAN

Because of the consistent interface, you can swap the class and keep the fit/predict/label code. Process for any algorithm: choose it, determine K (if needed), evaluate and explain. The source gives no code for these two.

Hierarchical clustering: start with every point as its own cluster, repeatedly merge the two closest, and record the merge distance. The dendrogram shows those distances; cut at a height to pick the number of clusters.

  • Pro: no K upfront; the dendrogram shows structure.
  • Con: slow, since it starts with one cluster per point, so it scales poorly.

DBSCAN (density-based): like moving a flashlight around the data. Nearby points keep extending the same cluster; when no more nearby points are found, the cluster ends. Points near nothing are noise/outliers.

  • Pro: arbitrary shapes (including clusters that wrap around others), robust to outliers.
  • Con: you must tune eps (neighbourhood radius) and min_samples.
AlgorithmK required?ShapeSpeedOutlier handling
K-meansYesSphericalFastPoor
HierarchicalNo (dendrogram)AnySlowModerate
DBSCANNoArbitraryModerateGood (labels noise)

4. PCA and Other Dimensionality Reduction ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 4. PCA and Other Dimensionality Reduction

PCA is an unsupervised dimensionality reduction technique. It finds linear combinations of the original features that capture the most variance; each is a principal component (PC). Use cases: visualizing high-dimensional data in 2D/3D, cutting columns to speed up other algorithms, finding which features carry the information. PCA assumes linear relationships, and PC1 will not always hold 90%+ of the variance.

4.2 The three outputs of PCA (1/2) ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 4. PCA and Other Dimensionality Reduction › 4.2 The three outputs of PCA

  1. Principal components: the transformed data, with the same rows but PCs as columns.
  2. Explained variance ratio: information per PC, in descending order.
  3. Feature weights (components_): how much each original feature contributes to each PC.

Scree plot (variance per PC):

Cumulative sum shows the cutoff. To keep 95% of the information, take the first 2 PCs and drop the rest. Fewer columns make many ML algorithms much faster.

Feature weights. Large magnitude means the feature strongly affects the PC; near 0 means it barely matters. If features share a scale, the weights act as feature importance; otherwise standardize first. The PCs are mutually orthogonal.

Iris example (here X is the 4-feature frame, so use X_all.columns):

sepal lengthsepal widthpetal lengthpetal width
PC10.36-0.080.860.36
PC20.660.73-0.17-0.08

PC1 is mostly petal length; PC2 is mostly sepal width and sepal length.

How a PC is computed: centre each feature, multiply by its weight, sum.

5. Linear Regression ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 5. Linear Regression

Supervised: pass X and a numeric y. It fits the line (weights) that minimizes the sum of squared errors.

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + ... + \beta_n x_n$$

β₀ is the intercept and each β is the weight (slope) of one feature column.

$$\text{slope} = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \qquad \text{intercept} = \bar{y} - \text{slope} \times \bar{x}$$

6. Logistic Regression ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 6. Logistic Regression

Despite the name, this is a classification algorithm. It fits a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve and outputs a probability: above 0.5 predicts class 1, below predicts class 0.

$$y = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$$

z is the linear combination of features (as in linear regression) and y is the probability.

  • .score() is R² for regression and accuracy (% correct) for classification.
  • A positive coefficient pushes toward the positive class, a negative one away from it, and larger magnitude means more impact.
  • Accuracy trap: if fraud is 0.1% of transactions, predicting "not fraud" always gets 99.9% accuracy and is useless. Tie accuracy to business metrics.

7. Decision Trees, Random Forest, XGBoost ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 7. Decision Trees, Random Forest, XGBoost

Decision trees (classification or regression) recursively split data on feature thresholds to minimize error.

Advantages over linear models:

  • No scaling needed: they look at one column at a time.
  • Handle missing values and categoricals, depending on implementation (XGBoost does).
  • Explainable: you can visualize and walk the tree.
  • Capture non-linearity: they can split on the same feature repeatedly (bathtub, S/Z shapes).

DepthBehaviorProblem
1 (stump)Too simple, misses patternsUnderfitting
2-3Good balanceAppropriate
None (unlimited)Memorizes every pointOverfitting

7.2 Real example: aircraft elevators ML Algorithms

Uses elev from section 5.4.

The depth-3 tree splits on SaTime1 several times, capturing non-linear behaviour.

Depth sweep on training data only (misleading, since the tree can memorize):

Validation curve with a train/test split (the correct way):

  • Train score climbs toward 1.0 as depth grows (memorizing).
  • Test score peaks around depth 10-11, then falls.
  • Left of the peak is underfitting; right of it is overfitting. The peak is the sweet spot.

Here linear regression beats the single tree; trees shine when relationships are non-linear.

← Previous31 / 34Next →
7.3 Random Forest (bagging) and XGBoost (boosting) ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 7. Decision Trees, Random Forest, XGBoost › 7.3 Random Forest (bagging) and XGBoost (boosting)

Single trees overfit; ensembles combine many trees.

Random Forest: train many trees, each on a random subset of columns (and optionally rows). The final answer is the average (regression) or vote (classification). Analogy: you and 40 friends each hit a golf ball once, and the average landing spot is closer to the hole than a typical single hit.

The test score flattens around depth 11-13. When several depths score similarly, pick the shallower model.

XGBoost: train a tree, then train another that corrects the previous tree's errors, and repeat. The prediction is the sum of all trees' contributions. Analogy: hit the golf ball again from where it landed, each swing correcting the last.

Model (elevators, test R²)ScoreTechnique
Decision Tree (depth 11)~0.70Single tree
Linear Regression~0.81Line fitting
Random Forest (depth 13)~0.82Bagging
XGBoost~0.87Boosting
Bagging (Random Forest)Boosting (XGBoost)
StrategyIndependent trees on random subsetsSequential trees, each correcting errors
ParallelizableYesNo (each depends on the previous)
Overfitting riskLowerHigher (but has regularization)

Key hyperparameters: max_depth (tree complexity) and n_estimators (number of trees).

← Previous32 / 34Next →
7.4 Challenge: decision tree on Titanic (find the best depth) ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 7. Decision Trees, Random Forest, XGBoost › 7.4 Challenge: decision tree on Titanic (find the best depth)

Trees don't need standardization.

The test score peaks at depth 3, the best choice: simple, no overfitting, good on unseen data. The test curve is jagged because the split matters (changing random_state changes it). For a more stable estimate use k-fold cross validation: split into k chunks (typically 5), hold out each in turn, train on the rest, and average the scores. This is a concept only here; the course shows no code for it.

8. Summary Table, Cheat Sheet & Key Lessons ML Algorithms

ML Algorithms › 8. Summary Table, Cheat Sheet & Key Lessons

AlgorithmTypeKey concept
K-MeansUnsupervisedClusters by distance to centroids; elbow/silhouette for K
PCAUnsupervisedDimensionality reduction; explained variance; feature weights
Linear RegressionSupervised (regression)Fit a line; R²; coefficients as importance
Logistic RegressionSupervised (classification)Sigmoid; 0.5 threshold; accuracy
Decision TreeSupervised (both)Threshold splits; under/overfitting; validation curves
Random ForestSupervised (both)Bagging: many trees on random subsets
XGBoostSupervised (both)Boosting: sequential error correction

Key lessons:

  • Always visualize data before and after modeling.
  • Standardize for distance-based and curve-fitting algorithms (K-means, PCA, linear and logistic regression). Don't for trees.
  • Never evaluate on data the model has seen; use a train/test split.
  • Validation curves: sweep a hyperparameter, plot train versus test, and pick the sweet spot.
  • When models score similarly, choose the simpler one.
  • "Is this score good?" depends on the business case; higher is better between models, but sufficiency needs business context.
  • Next steps from the instructor: practice on your own data; his Feature Engineering and XGBoost courses; "Effective XGBoost" by Matt Harrison.

3. Tensors: Concepts, CPU/GPU, Moving Devices PyTorch Essential

PyTorch Essential › 3. Tensors: Concepts, CPU/GPU, Moving Devices

A tensor is PyTorch's core data structure: a multi-dimensional array whose elements share a single data type. It holds inputs, intermediate representations and outputs. Real-world data (e.g. images) is encoded into tensors; each intermediate representation is a set of floats produced by multiplying the input with the previous layer's weights.

DimensionName
0-dScalar
1-dVector
2-dMatrix
3-dStack of matrices (e.g. time series)
n-dn-dimensional tensor

Tensor vs NumPy ndarray

FeaturePyTorch tensorNumPy ndarray
GPU operationsYes, much fasterCPU only
Distributed processingMultiple CPUs/GPUs across serversNo
Computation-graph tracking (autograd)YesNo

Tensors on CPU (default device; dtype is derived from the input):

Tensors on GPU. PyTorch uses the CUDA library to detect and use the GPU. cuda:0 means the first GPU; multiple GPUs are addressed by index. Results of GPU operations stay on the GPU.

Why move between devices

DirectionReason
CPU → GPUTraining large networks and high-dimensional image tensors is far faster on GPU
GPU → CPUPost-training processing with libraries that only accept CPU data (e.g. NumPy)

CPU → GPU (three equivalent forms):

GPU → CPU. Gotcha: a tensor with requires_grad=True must be detached from the autograd graph first.

Casting (two ways: named function like .float(), .int(), .double(), or .to(dtype=...)):

Automatic casting: when operands have different dtypes, PyTorch casts to the larger type. Larger types use more memory and give more precision; smaller types use less memory and lose precision. This trade-off matters in DL.

8. DL Workflow, Datasets & Transforms (CIFAR-10) (1/2) PyTorch Essential

PyTorch Essential › 8. DL Workflow, Datasets & Transforms (CIFAR-10)

Pipeline:

StageSteps
Data preparationLoad data → convert to tensors → apply transforms → batch
Model developmentDesign → train (training data) → validate (validation data)
DeploymentSave model to file → deploy to cloud server or edge device

Learning types: supervised (labeled), unsupervised (no labels, finds patterns), semi-supervised (mix).

Dataset splits

SplitPurpose
TrainingFit model parameters
ValidationMeasure performance on unseen data and tune hyperparameters
TestingFinal evaluation

Overfitting: the model is excellent on training data but fails on unseen examples. The validation set exposes this.

CIFAR-10: 60,000 colour images (50,000 train, 10,000 test), 32×32 RGB, 10 classes (0 airplane, 1 automobile, 2 bird, 3 cat, 4 deer, 5 dog, 6 frog, 7 horse, 8 ship, 9 truck).

PyTorch data conventions: a Dataset stores samples and labels; a DataLoader feeds them into the network.

Transforms (torchvision.transforms) adjust data before it enters the model. Compose chains them; Resize((H, W)) rescales; ToTensor() converts to a tensor; Normalize(mean, std) normalizes per channel. Training and test transforms may differ (here only training is resized).

Why normalize: raw pixels are 0–255, and multiplying large values across layers makes values and gradients blow up (exploding gradients). Normalization keeps values small and gradient flow stable. The mean/std above are the standard per-RGB-channel values precomputed over the CIFAR-10 training set.

9. DataLoader, Model Definition, Training & Validation (1/2) PyTorch Essential

PyTorch Essential › 9. DataLoader, Model Definition, Training & Validation

torch.utils.data.DataLoader is an iterable over a dataset. It supports map-style and iterable-style datasets, configurable order, automatic batching, and single- or multi-process loading. Default batch_size is 1. Other parameters: dataset, sampler (custom sampling), num_workers (multi-process loading).

Why mini-batches (e.g. 64 or 128): a full-dataset pass needs lots of memory; mini-batches use less memory and train faster.

shuffle=True for training (random samples), shuffle=False for testing (repeatable results).

Model development steps: design (architecture, initial weights and biases) → training (feed data, compute error, adjust parameters) → validation (unseen data, tune hyperparameters) → testing (final check on fully unseen data).

Network definition (LeNet-style CNN for 3×32×32 inputs):

LayerIn → OutPurpose
conv1 Conv2d(3, 6, 5)3 → 6 channelsFirst convolution, 5×5 kernel
pool MaxPool2d(2, 2)Shrink spatial size
conv2 Conv2d(6, 16, 5)6 → 16 channelsSecond convolution
fc1 Linear16×5×5 = 400 → 120Fully connected
fc2 Linear120 → 84Fully connected
fc3 Linear84 → 10Output, one per class

F.relu zeroes negative values. x.view(-1, 16*5*5) flattens the feature maps for the linear layers.

1. PyTorch at a Glance PyTorch Hands-On

PyTorch Hands-On › 1. PyTorch at a Glance

Open-source deep learning framework from Meta. Four pillars: Tensors, Autograd, API, Libraries.

StrengthDetail
Dynamic computation graphGraph is built as operations run, so debugging is plain Python
PythonicFits the Python ecosystem
GPU accelerationFast training and inference
Prototyping to productionTorchServe for serving, TorchScript for optimization

Hybrid API design: Python user API (torch, torch.nn, torch.optim, torch.utils.data) on top; C++ core (ATen: tensor library, serialization) below; CUDA kernels for NVIDIA GPUs. Python ease plus C++/CUDA speed.

Tensor = multidimensional array with GPU support and autograd tracking. Interop with NumPy via .numpy() / torch.from_numpy(). Cast dtype with .to(dtype=...), move device with .to('cuda').

Autograd = automatic differentiation engine. Goal: minimize loss by adjusting weights; gradients say which direction to change each weight.

Broadcasting PyTorch Hands-On

PyTorch Hands-On › 5. Broadcasting and the NumPy Bridge › Broadcasting

Lets tensors of different shapes combine without copying data (memory efficient; e.g. applying weights across a batch). Semantics match NumPy. Compare shapes from the last dimension to the first; each pair must satisfy one of:

  • sizes are equal,
  • one of them is 1 (stretched),
  • the dimension is absent in one tensor (treated as 1).

Tensors cannot be empty (at least one dimension).

6. Autograd PyTorch Hands-On

PyTorch Hands-On › 6. Autograd

Tracks tensor operations and builds a dynamic computation graph; used to compute gradients of the loss w.r.t. parameters for backpropagation. Dynamic graph means flexible architectures (RNNs, transformers, conditional logic).

Training loop in 3 steps

StepActionPhase
1Compute loss between prediction and labelForward pass
2Compute gradients of loss w.r.t. parametersBackward pass (chain rule)
3Update weights with optimizer (SGD, Adam)Optimization

Forward: each layer's output feeds the next. Backward: traverse from the output, collecting gradients with the chain rule. A tensor with requires_grad=True is a tracked leaf; grad_fn records the op that created a tensor.

7. Advanced Autograd PyTorch Hands-On

PyTorch Hands-On › 7. Advanced Autograd

torch.autograd.grad: returns gradients without touching .grad; finer control, and the base for higher-order derivatives.

Higher-order gradients: create_graph=True keeps the graph so the derivative can itself be differentiated.

Custom autograd Function: define forward and backward yourself (debugging, experiments, unsupported ops). ctx.save_for_backward stashes tensors needed in backward.

Jacobian = matrix of first derivatives (vector-valued functions). Hessian = matrix of second derivatives.

Hooks: register_hook inspects or modifies gradients as they flow during backward.

1. Data Engineering Concepts Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 1. Data Engineering Concepts

Data engineering is designing and building systems that collect, move, process and store data at scale and low latency, so analytics and ML can use it. It is a prerequisite for ML (training data must be cleansed and transformed; inference also needs pre/post-processing). Roles: Data Engineer, Big Data Architect.

Architecture and execution flow Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 2. Spark Capabilities for ETL › Architecture and execution flow

  • The driver node runs the Spark program. Executor nodes in the cluster do the work in parallel.
  • Flow: read source, convert to DataFrame/RDD (partitioned across executors), transform (map/filter, local on each executor, no data movement), action (reduce/group by, shuffle between executors), collect (partitions merged to the driver), write to destination.
OperationData movementBottleneck risk
Transforms (map, filter)None, local on partitionsLow, fully parallel
Actions (reduce, group by)Shuffle between executorsHigh (I/O and memory)
CollectPartitions merged to driverModerate

Visualize this flow for each pipeline to find bottlenecks.

← Previous6 / 32Next →
Parallel reads, processing, writes Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 2. Spark Capabilities for ETL › Parallel reads, processing, writes

StageSource/sinkHow parallelism works
ReadJDBCPartition by column values; each executor reads a subset
ReadKafkaEach executor reads a subset of Kafka partitions
WriteJDBCEach executor writes in parallel (configurable); writes can be batched to cut network I/O
WriteKafkaExecutors write to topics in parallel
  • Predicate pushdown: filters are pushed to the data source so unwanted records are never read into memory. The optimizer does it automatically.
  • Map and filter are parallel. Reduce introduces shuffling.
  • Do map-type work and filtering early, reduce shuffling by using the right partitions, and repartition as needed.
  • Pipeline speed is set by its slowest bottleneck.
← Previous7 / 32Next →
Execution plan (lazy evaluation) Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 2. Spark Capabilities for ETL › Execution plan (lazy evaluation)

  • Spark runs code only when an action (reduce, collect) is called. It then analyzes all prior steps and builds an optimized physical plan.
  • The optimizer reduces I/O, shuffling and memory use, reads in parallel from executors (not the driver) where the source allows, and applies predicate pushdown.
  • Print and analyze execution plans to find optimizations.
← Previous8 / 32Next →
Stateful stream processing Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 2. Spark Capabilities for ETL › Stateful stream processing

  • Checkpointing: saves pipeline state to persistent storage (HDFS, S3) so a failed job resumes where it left off. Saves metadata (configuration, progress), Kafka offsets, key-based state, and RDDs for operations spanning batches (windowing).
  • Watermarks: for event-time windowing (time the event was created at the source, not when it arrived). A window must wait for all its events. The watermark is the delay to wait before processing a window. Spark tracks events until the watermark passes.
  • State tracking by key (UpdateStateByKey): tracks entity state by key (e.g., browser session ID). New events change state, and updated states are published as a DStream to downstream transformations.
← Previous9 / 32Next →
Spark SQL and ML Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 2. Spark Capabilities for ETL › Spark SQL and ML

  • Spark SQL: standard-SQL syntax that is translated to distributed operations. Works on batch and streaming. Can sit in the same pipeline, cascade (one output feeds the next), and persist to databases or streams.
  • Spark ML: pre-processing (feature extraction, transformation, dimensionality reduction), popular algorithms, and ML pipelines that chain extraction, pre-processing, training and inference inside the same Spark pipeline.
  • Spark is one integrated platform for data engineering, analytics and ML.

4. Batch Pipeline: Warehouse Stock Aggregation Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 4. Batch Pipeline: Warehouse Stock Aggregation

Use case: An enterprise has warehouses worldwide, each with its own stock app and local MariaDB (warehouse_stock.item_stock: opening stock, receipts, issues per item per day). Goal: a consolidated central stock database, collected daily, scalable to hundreds of warehouses.

Architecture:

  • Each warehouse runs a Stock Upload Job daily on its local Spark cluster. It reads the local MariaDB and writes Parquet to the central file system (HDFS/S3; local raw_data/ is the proxy).
  • Parquet is columnar and efficient for parallel reads. The folder structure is partitioned by STOCK_DATE then WAREHOUSE_ID.
  • After uploads complete, the Stock Aggregator Job on the central Spark cluster reads all Parquet, aggregates with Spark SQL, and writes to the global_stock MariaDB.
  • Flow: Acquire (local MariaDB) -> Transport (Parquet to central FS) -> Consolidate (Spark SQL GROUP BY) -> Persist (global MariaDB). Prune raw_data/ after processing.

Notebook: code_03_XX_Spark_BDE_Batch_Data_Engg.ipynb.

5. Real-Time Pipeline: Website Analytics Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 5. Real-Time Pipeline: Website Analytics

Use case: An e-commerce site tracks visits (date, country, duration, last action before exit: Catalog, FAQ, ShoppingCart, Order). Required in real time:

  1. 5-second summaries of duration by last action -> MariaDB website_stats.visit_stats.
  2. Running total of visit duration by country -> Redis sorted set.
  3. Visits ending in ShoppingCart -> Kafka topic spark.streaming.carts.abandoned.

Architecture: E-commerce app -> Kafka spark.streaming.website.visits -> one Spark job fanning out to MariaDB, Redis and the abandoned-carts Kafka topic. Kafka scales the source, Spark scales across executors, Redis sorted set scales horizontally, each executor writes to MariaDB in parallel.

Scaling processing Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 6. Best Practices › Scaling processing

  • Filter unwanted data early (less data in memory and between executors).
  • Do reduce operations as late as possible (less shuffling). Do parallel work (map, filter) early.
  • Repartition as needed, since some operations create too many partitions.
  • Cache intermediate results that are reused.
  • Avoid actions that send data to the driver. Collect only at the end.
← Previous24 / 32Next →
Building resiliency Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 6. Best Practices › Building resiliency

  • Spark handles failures at task, stage and executor level out of the box.
  • Monitor jobs and clusters and set up alerting for unhandled failures.
  • Use checkpoints on persistent stores (HDFS, S3) for streaming jobs so they resume after a restart.
  • Make input/output stores redundant and persistent, and deploy Spark on a cluster so one node failure does not stop the pipeline. The whole solution must be resilient, not only Spark.
← Previous25 / 32Next →
Batch vs real-time: choosing Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 6. Best Practices › Batch vs real-time: choosing

Real-time challenges:

  • Unbounded datasets make it hard to size memory and clusters.
  • Windowing and watermarks can cause missed events and wrong aggregations.
  • State must be maintained correctly across the cluster.
  • Reprocessing is not a rerun: checkpoints, state and offsets must be reset.
Choose real-time whenChoose batch when
Responses/actions are required within secondsLatency of minutes/hours is acceptable
Input is a continuous stream of eventsHeavy aggregation and analytics
Minimal aggregation (more steps add watermark/state complexity)Simpler to implement, debug and reprocess
Compute resources are sufficient

Hybrid pipelines (part batch, part real-time) are possible. Use real-time only when the use case demands it.

← Previous26 / 32Next →
Scaling extraction and loading Apache Spark

Apache Spark › 6. Best Practices › Scaling extraction and loading

All stages must scale, and extraction/loading (disk reads/writes) are common bottlenecks.

ExtractionLoading
Read in parallel (JDBC across executors, Kafka partitions divided between executors)Each executor writes independently to the sink
Use each source's parallel-read options. Design source schemas for parallelismUnderstand sink behavior for transactions, locking, serialization
Predicate pushdownCap parallel connections to the sink's capacity
Defend against missed and duplicate recordsRepartition to control write parallelism. Defend against missed and duplicate updates

Problem: Using the visit_stats table from Section 5, build a downstream pipeline for significant actions. Requirements:

CSRF Django

Django › 7. Forms, CSRF and Validation › CSRF

Without {% csrf_token %} a POST returns 403 Forbidden. CSRF = Cross-Site Request Forgery.

  1. Django sends a unique token to the browser with the form page.
  2. The token is submitted back with the data.
  3. Django verifies it, so only the browser that got the form can submit it. A third party has no token and is rejected.

Put {% csrf_token %} inside every <form method="POST">.

  • labels overrides labels; widgets sets the HTML tag and attributes (e.g. Bootstrap classes), all controlled from the form class without touching the template.

1. What Flask Is and the Project Flask

Flask › 1. What Flask Is and the Project

Flask is a micro web framework for Python: small core, extensions added only when needed, full control over structure. Created by Armin Ronacher in 2010 (started as an April Fools' joke). Typical uses: blogs, REST APIs, microservices, dashboards, data-visualization apps (popular in data science).

Prerequisites: basic Python, conceptual HTML/CSS, HTTP client-server basics, Git/Bash, Python + editor + GitHub account.

← Previous2 / 32Next →
Flask vs Django Flask

Flask › 1. What Flask Is and the Project › Flask vs Django

AspectFlaskDjango
TypeMicro frameworkFull-stack framework
SizeMinimal, build only what you needAdmin, auth, ORM out of the box
FlexibilityYou choose structure and componentsConvention over configuration
Learning curveGentlerSteeper, powerful for enterprise
EcosystemSmaller, growingLarger, many reusable apps
  • Use Flask: small/medium apps, flexibility and control, prototypes/MVPs, microservices, charts and dashboards.
  • Use Django: large complex apps, built-in auth/admin/CMS, teams wanting convention, high-traffic apps, strong built-in security.
  • Analogy: Flask is a blank canvas; Django is a paint-by-numbers kit.

Prompts: set up and deploy: Yes; scope: your account; link to existing project: No; project name: flask-health-tracker-project.

1. FastAPI Overview and Setup FastAPI

FastAPI › 1. FastAPI Overview and Setup

FastAPI is fast in two ways: fast to develop (little code to a working server) and fast at runtime (serves many requests efficiently).

  • Prerequisites: Python, HTTP/JSON/REST basics, command line.
  • FastAPI does not implement a web server itself. It speaks ASGI, and Uvicorn serves HTTP.
  • Pydantic handles validation and serialization; OpenAPI docs are generated at /docs.

2. REST, HTTP and JSON Fundamentals FastAPI

FastAPI › 2. REST, HTTP and JSON Fundamentals

  • REST (Representational State Transfer) is a form of RPC: client sends a request, server replies. It works on collections of things and supports CRUD over HTTP, with JSON as the encoding.
  • Frameworks hide the HTTP/JSON layers most of the time, but they leak through.
CRUDHTTP verbExample
CreatePOSTcreate a user
RetrieveGETget one user / query many
UpdatePUT / PATCHchange a user's address
DeleteDELETEdelete a user
← Previous2 / 26Next →
HTTP protocol FastAPI

FastAPI › 2. REST, HTTP and JSON Fundamentals › HTTP protocol

HTTP is a textual protocol over sockets. Raw request via Netcat:

  • Request: request line (verb, path, version), headers, empty line, body.
    • Host is the only required header.
    • Connection: close closes the connection after the response.
    • Content-Length counts body bytes only (75 here), not headers.
  • Response: status line (HTTP/1.1 200 OK), headers, empty line, body.
  • Common codes: 200 OK, 404 Not Found.

FastAPI › 2. REST, HTTP and JSON Fundamentals › JSON

JSONPython
objectdict
arraylist
stringstr
numberint / float
true/falsebool
nullNone
  • JSON has one number type; Python has int, float, Decimal, Fraction. set and tuple have no JSON equivalent.
  • JSON lacks a datetime type (sent as a string, receiver must convert) and binary data (usually Base64).
  • FastAPI does the encoding/decoding for you.

Sync vs async handlers FastAPI

FastAPI › 3. Handlers, Running the Server, Sync vs Async › Sync vs async handlers

FastAPI uses asyncio for I/O-bound concurrency. asyncio runs on a single thread, so a blocking call inside an async handler blocks every request.

Handler (10 concurrent requests)Total timeWhy
sync + sleep~1 sthread pool
async + sleep (bad)~10 sevent loop blocked, serialized
async + asyncio.sleep~1 snon-blocking

Recommendation: start with sync handlers; move to async only for performance reasons. A third-party library deep in the call chain may block without you knowing.

Query parameters FastAPI

FastAPI › 4. Accepting Data › Query parameters

Appended after ?, separated by &: GET /logs?start=2024-01-01T00:00:00&end=2024-01-02T00:00:00&level=ERROR

  • Function parameters map to query parameters; type hints drive conversion (datetime parsed from ISO).
  • A parameter with a default (level: str = None) is optional.
  • Conversion failures return 422 Unprocessable Entity automatically.
  • Raise HTTPException with the right status for your own validation errors.
  • /docs shows generated OpenAPI documentation.

Request body (Pydantic models) FastAPI

FastAPI › 4. Accepting Data › Request body (Pydantic models)

JSON in the body is the most common way to pass data. Pydantic validates it.

  • Keep API models separate from DB models; layers may store data differently (dollars vs cents).
  • Field(min_length=2), Field(gt=0) are validated automatically; failures give 422 with detailed messages.
  • A return annotation (-> Sale) adds the response schema to /docs.
  • {key} in the route is a path parameter bound to the key argument.
  • Pydantic has specialized types, e.g. PastDatetime for datetimes that must be in the past.

Raw request data FastAPI

FastAPI › 4. Accepting Data › Raw request data

Use a Request parameter for the raw body, e.g. an image whose size you return. Reading the body needs await, so the handler must be async. Never accept unbounded input from the internet: check the size.

BytesIO turns raw bytes into a file-like object for libraries such as PIL. Headers: request.headers.get('Header-Name').

Returning a dict gives JSON. A Pydantic return type also adds the response schema to /docs.

timedelta serializes to an ISO 8601 duration by default ("PT1M27S"). Override with a field serializer to return {"delta": 87}; make the serializer's return type match what clients expect.

Streaming responses FastAPI

FastAPI › 5. Sending Data › Streaming responses

For large or incremental data use StreamingResponse. JSON itself does not stream, but JSON Lines (NDJSON), one JSON object per line, does. The handler passes a generator; items are sent as produced, without buffering everything. Under the hood HTTP uses chunked transfer encoding (chunk size in hex, then data).

Custom error handlers FastAPI

FastAPI › 5. Sending Data › Custom error handlers

FastAPI handles most errors, but an unknown exception type gives 500 Internal Server Error.

Register a handler for it:

  • The handler is async def (request, exc) and returns a JSONResponse with custom status, content and headers.
  • Custom headers conventionally start with X-; header names are case-insensitive.
  • Security: do not put raw exception text in responses; it can leak tokens, addresses or other sensitive data.

FastAPI › 5. Sending Data › Example: query logs with content negotiation

Return JSON by default, CSV if Accept: text/csv, 404 if nothing matches, 400 on bad input.

  • Content negotiation: the Accept header picks the format; */* means "anything", so default to JSON; reject unsupported types with 400.
  • CSV: StringIO + csv.DictWriter, datetime.isoformat(), media_type='text/csv'.

Logging and metrics FastAPI

FastAPI › 6. Production-Ready Code › Logging and metrics

  • Metrics answer "what is happening now?" (request count, error rate, query latency). Tools: Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, Datadog.
  • Logging answers "how did we get here?" (incidents, debugging). Use Python's built-in logging.
  • If logs don't help in development, they won't help during a 4 a.m. incident.
  • Configure logging as early as possible (ideally from config). In code review ask: should we log here, at what level, with what info? Log enough to reproduce (e.g. query parameters). Format fields: see the LogRecord attributes.

Middleware runs around every HTTP request; call_next invokes the next middleware or the handler. Prefix metric lines ([metric:call.duration]) so a collector can parse and forward them.

Using Uvicorn's logger instead of the root logger (useful to separate server logs from app logs):

Security FastAPI

FastAPI › 6. Production-Ready Code › Security

Security is every developer's job. Start with the OWASP Top 10 (broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, ...). Developers think about how things should work; put on a security hat and ask how a malicious actor would abuse the code. In reviews ask: what should I validate, and what am I not checking?

Broken access controlanyone can read user details or create users; no authn/authz
No input validationlogin not checked for malicious characters
No body size limitset_icon reads the whole body; attacker can send gigabytes
Can overwrite usersset_user doesn't check existence
No admin checkcreating users should require admin

1. Course Overview and the Planetary API RESTful API

RESTful API › 1. Course Overview and the Planetary API

  • Flask is a Python microframework for web apps and APIs. It gives essential features without forcing infrastructure choices, and has a large plugin ecosystem.
  • The course covers authentication, database access, ORM, routing, Flask plugins, testing, and deployment to a cloud server.
  • An API receives requests and returns JSON. JSON is preferred over XML or custom formats because it needs no parsing and is supported natively by Python and most languages.
  • Prerequisites: basic Python 3, and how web apps work (form posts, request/response).
  • Tools: PyCharm (Professional has Flask tooling; Community works with manual venv/pip), Postman (tests all HTTP verbs), DB Browser for SQLite (inspect the DB file).
  • Database: SQLite. It is file-based and needs no server, which avoids PostgreSQL/MySQL setup.

  • Features: list planets, register users, authenticate users, add / update / delete planets (for example, deleting Pluto after reclassification).

jsonify RESTful API

RESTful API › 3. Returning JSON, Status Codes, URL Parameters and Variables › jsonify

jsonify turns keyword arguments or a dict into a JSON response and sets Content-Type: application/json. Without it, the endpoint returns plain text.

Several pairs are allowed: jsonify(message="...", status="success") returns {"message": "...", "status": "success"}.

  • Status codes are response metadata saying whether the request worked. Clients (web, mobile, desktop) branch on them.
  • 200 OK, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found. 400-499 are client errors, 500-599 are server errors.
  • Flask defaults to 200. Return a tuple to change it: return jsonify(...), 404. Setting 200 explicitly is optional but clearer.

  • Sent after ? as key/value pairs: ?name=Bruce&age=28. Read with request.args.get('name').
  • Values are strings, so cast them (int(...)).
  • Business rules stay in the API, so the frontend only builds the URL. Validate missing or non-numeric values, and sanitize anything that reaches a DB query.

URL variables and conversion filters RESTful API

RESTful API › 3. Returning JSON, Status Codes, URL Parameters and Variables › URL variables and conversion filters

  • Parts of the path become variables with <name>. URLs are cleaner (/url_variables/Bruce/28 instead of ?name=Bruce&age=28) and request.args.get() is not needed.
  • Variable names in the route must match the function parameters in name and count.
  • A converter restricts and converts the type: <converter:variable>.
ConverterAccepts
string (default)any text without slashes. It is string, not Python's str
int / floatnumbers, converted automatically
pathtext including slashes (file paths)
uuidUUID strings
  • Gotcha: in the route the converter comes before the name (int:age). In the signature the type hint comes after (age: int).

/url_variables/Bruce/28 returns 200. /url_variables/Bruce/14 returns 401. Document endpoints (Swagger/OpenAPI) with their expected types.

RESTful API › 4. Database with SQLAlchemy: Models and Seeding

  • APIs do CRUD against a database. SQLite is file-based, needs no server and ships with Python.
  • An ORM (SQLAlchemy) generates SQL behind the scenes and represents rows as Python objects. Benefits: no raw SQL, easy database switching (SQLite to MySQL), schema defined in code (version-controlled), support for several databases when shipping on-premises.
  • Install Flask-SQLAlchemy (with the dash; FlaskSQLAlchemy is a different package). It installs SQLAlchemy too.
