Why JWT RESTful API

RESTful API › 7. Security: Registration, JWT, Login, Email › Why JWT

  • JSON Web Tokens handle authentication and authorization and keep the API stateless. APIs avoid server-side session plugins such as Flask-Login or Flask-User.
  • JWT is an open standard supported across languages, and works for web apps (React, Angular), mobile and desktop clients.
  • Planetary API rule: login is required to add, edit or delete planets. Login is not required to list planets, view details, or register.
  • Library: Flask-JWT-extended. It can be used as a black box; see jwt.io for internals.

1. What GraphQL Is and Why GraphQL

GraphQL › 1. What GraphQL Is and Why

  • GraphQL is a query language for APIs. It is not a database, and it is not a client. It acts as a server-side layer that sits in front of data sources.
  • Created at Meta (Facebook) because REST could not handle deep queries (4-5 levels deep in a friend network). GraphQL handles any depth across multiple databases.
  • Ecosystem: Facebook's reference implementation, Apollo, Relay.
BenefitMeaning
Precise fetchingClient asks for exactly the fields it wants, so there is no over-fetching
Type checkingThe schema describes and enforces types (like TypeScript)
Multiple data sourcesOne request can pull from several databases
Single entry pointAll input is validated by the schema before it reaches the database

Type safety example: sending a Boolean for a String field (name: true) is rejected by GraphQL, and the database is never reached.

Tooling: VS Code with a GraphQL extension (general GraphQL, Apollo GraphQL, or Relay variants); WebStorm has built-in support.

10. Gotchas and Concept Comparisons GraphQL

GraphQL › 10. Gotchas and Concept Comparisons

ConceptKey point
buildSchemaParses a schema string (SDL) into a schema object
graphqlHTTPExpress middleware that mounts the endpoint
rootValueResolver object; resolver names must match schema field names exactly
type vs inputtype for output, input for mutation arguments; using type is a runtime error
[Type] vs [Type]! vs ID!optional list; mandatory list; mandatory scalar
Enum vs BooleanEnum is named and extensible; switching is a breaking change
Query vs Mutationread vs write
Aliases vs fragmentslabeled multi-query in one request vs reusable field set
GraphQL vs Mongoose typesAPI validation vs storage; they may differ

Common errors seen in the course:

  • creatProduct typo: the resolver name must match the schema name or the mutation does not resolve.
  • Forgetting to add a new resolver to the schema's Mutation/Query type, so GraphQL does not recognize it.
  • Adding a field to type but not to input (or to the model/constructor).
  • Using Widgets.remove() (deprecated) instead of deleteOne.
  • Forgetting { new: true } in findOneAndUpdate, which returns the pre-update document.
  • Not restarting the server or refreshing GraphiQL after schema changes.
  • SQLite sqlite::memory: data and the in-memory productDatabase object are lost on restart.

Python Automation › 4. Organizing Files by Type

A script that sorts files in the current directory into category folders, with unknown types going to MISC.

  • Flow: dictionary maps categories to extensions, pickDirectory looks up the category, organizeDirectory skips directories, creates missing category folders, and moves each file.
  • .lower() makes extension matching case-insensitive. Check the result with ls.

10. Selenium Browser Automation Python Automation

Python Automation › 10. Selenium Browser Automation

Selenium is an open-source framework that controls browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) from Python through WebDriver. It simulates user actions (click, type, navigate) and scales from one task to full test suites. Use it for testing, scraping JavaScript-rendered content, filling forms, and QA.

Browser-specific imports: Chrome uses ChromeService and ChromeDriverManager. Firefox uses FirefoxService and GeckoDriverManager. Safari has a built-in driver. webdriver_manager downloads the matching driver automatically, which avoids "driver not found" errors.

11. Selenium Waiting Strategies Python Automation

Python Automation › 11. Selenium Waiting Strategies

Problem: modern sites load content asynchronously (Ajax). WebDriver may look for an element before it exists, which causes exceptions such as ElementNotVisibleException and failed runs. Waiting strategies pause until the element is ready.

TypeBehaviorNotes
Explicit waitWaits until a specific condition is met, up to a timeoutPrecise, recommended for dynamic content
Implicit waitGlobal wait for elements to be availableSimpler, less precise
sleep()Always waits the full durationWasteful; fine only for viewing results while testing
← Previous22 / 40Next →
Explicit wait Python Automation

Python Automation › 11. Selenium Waiting Strategies › Explicit wait

The full lesson script repeats this on a page with Enable/Disable, Remove/Add buttons and a checkbox, using find_element for static elements, wait.until for elements that reappear after loading, and sleep(3) between steps to watch the result. wait.until(...) proceeds as soon as the condition is true, so it can finish well before the timeout. sleep(10) always costs 10 seconds.

Syntax: wait.until(condition((locator_strategy, 'locator_value'))). Note the locator is a tuple.

An API (Application Programming Interface) is a bridge between applications. Typical uses: weather, e-commerce product data, finance, social media, maps.

13. API Keys Python Automation

Python Automation › 13. API Keys

An API key is a unique identifier that unlocks an API. Providers require keys for authentication, access control, rate limiting and usage tracking, and abuse prevention.

Getting one: sign up on the provider's site (for example openweathermap.org/api), copy the key from the "API keys" section, and read the documentation for the required parameters. The documented request form is api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast?q={city}&appid={API_KEY}.

14. API Chaining Python Automation

Python Automation › 14. API Chaining

API chaining makes several API calls in sequence, where the output of one call is the input to the next. It builds complex workflows from small steps, enriches data from several sources, and needs little code. If calls are independent, run them in parallel instead.

Examples: weather app (geolocation API, then weather API), e-commerce (product, then inventory, then payment), recipes (SMS, then text analysis to extract ingredients, then recipe search).
